Optimize Topology-Aware Scheduling for CompositePodGroups with identical children

Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS) for CompositePodGroups currently schedules child workloads sequentially in `compositePodGroupSchedulingDefaultAlgorithm`:
- **Enumerate candidate placements**: For each child PodGroup (or nested CompositePodGroup), enumerate all candidate topology domains (e.g., zones, racks, or nodes) matching the group's topology constraints.
- **Evaluate candidate placements from scratch**: Iterate through every candidate placement, running simulated pod scheduling (`SignPod`, `PreFilter`, `Filter`, `Score`, and tentative `Reserve`) across candidate nodes, and computing placement scores via `PlacementScore` plugins.
- **Select best placement and commit**: Normalize placement scores, select the highest-scoring candidate (breaking ties randomly), tentatively commit the child's placement to the snapshot, and advance to the next child.

When scheduling CompositePodGroups representing distributed workloads (e.g., distributed AI/ML training or HPC jobs), the hierarchy frequently consists of multiple identical child PodGroups (e.g., homogeneous worker groups with identical pod templates, resource requests, and topology constraints).
While kube-scheduler already employs opportunistic batching at the **pod/node level** (KEP-5598: reusing node evaluation outcomes across consecutive identical pods and invalidating only the chosen node), no equivalent mechanism exists at the **PodGroup/placement level**.

Because candidate placements are evaluated independently from scratch for every child in the hierarchy:
- The scheduler re-evaluates feasibility and re-runs placement scoring plugins across all candidate placements for each child, even though cluster state and capacity outside the previously selected placement remain unchanged.
- For a CompositePodGroup with $M$ child groups and $P$ candidate placements, this results in $O(M \times P)$ simulated placement evaluations. On large clusters (e.g., thousands of nodes across tens of racks or zones), this produces thousands of redundant placement evaluations.
- Non-overlapping candidate placements (placements that share no nodes with the placement selected by the previous child) retain identical feasibility and raw placement scores, but are discarded and re-evaluated from scratch in each child iteration.

As a result, the scheduler spends significant time in redundant placement simulation, leading to:
- High scheduling latency for CompositePodGroup workloads (e.g., spending dozens to hundreds of seconds in `scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`).
- Excessive CPU and memory consumption in the scheduler from repeated pod filtering and scoring across unaffected nodes.
- Head-of-line blocking in the scheduler queue for subsequent workloads waiting for scheduling cycles.

Conceptually, the proposed solution **lifts opportunistic batching (KEP-5598) from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level**: instead of evaluating individual nodes for consecutive identical pods, it caches candidate topology placements across consecutive identical child PodGroups (or nested CompositePodGroups).

We propose introducing placement result and score caching in `scheduleOnePodGroup` for CompositePodGroups (guarded by an alpha feature gate `TopologyAwareCompositePodGroupOptimization`) that:
1. **Detect identical consecutive child groups**: Check equivalence between consecutive children (`arePodGroupsIdenticalWithRoot` / cached `QueuedPodInfo.PodSignature`) to determine if candidate placement evaluations can be reused across child iterations.
2. **Cache placement feasibility and unweighted raw scores**: Split placement scoring in the framework into raw plugin scoring (`RunRawPlacementScorePlugins`, computing raw scores in $[0, \text{MaxPlacementScore}]$) and normalization (`NormalizePlacementScores`). Cache feasibility outcomes and raw scores across candidate placements for identical child groups.
3. **Invalidate only overlapping candidate placements**: When child $i$ selects placement $p_{\text{last}}$, identify and invalidate only candidate placements that overlap (share nodes) with $p_{\text{last}}$ (analogous to invalidating the selected node in pod-level opportunistic batching). All non-overlapping candidate placements reuse their cached feasibility and raw plugin scores.
4. **Recalculate affected placements and re-normalize scores**: Re-evaluate feasibility and raw scores only for invalidated overlapping placements, update the cache, re-normalize scores across all surviving feasible placements, and break ties randomly to preserve identical placement distribution and quality.
5. **Support multi-level hierarchies**: Recursively propagate placement caching across both leaf `PodGroup`s and nested child `CompositePodGroup`s.

The AI based POC implementing this approach is available on [44past4/kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...44past4:kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization?diff=unified&w) branch (with benchmarks added to `test/integration/scheduler_perf/cpg/cpg_test.go`).

Minimizing scheduling algorithm latency for large multi-gang workloads is essential for cluster throughput and resource utilization. The current algorithm results in:
- High algorithmic latency scaling quadratically with the number of identical child groups and candidate topology domains.
- Thousands of redundant simulated placement evaluations on nodes whose capacity and state are unchanged.
- Head-of-line queue delay for subsequent workloads in multi-tenant environments.

Extending the opportunistic batching principles of KEP-5598 from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level eliminates these redundant evaluations while preserving identical placement quality and scoring semantics.

In [scheduler performance benchmarks](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1USEVtKRIKcOBdsa26qfaSGFMif4HlFVqcvtijAGx4hA/edit?usp=sharing) on a 5,000-node cluster (5 zones, 50 racks) with CompositePodGroups of 4 to 128 child groups:
- Placement feasibility evaluations were reduced by **`3.05x` to `35.56x`** (e.g., `12,800 → 360` evaluations for 256 PodGroups across 50 racks).
- Pure TAS algorithm execution time (`scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`) was reduced by **`64.1%` to `95.4%`** (**`2.79x` to `21.71x` speedup**).
- End-to-end workload scheduling duration improved by **`2.45x` to `3.90x`** with identical placement distribution.

Workload-Aware Preemption may result in unnecessary or cascading preemptions

Workload-aware (PodGroup) preemption currently operates in three steps during PodGroupPostFilter:
- **Remove all potential victims**: Identify all lower-priority workloads/pods in the cluster that the preempting PodGroup is eligible to preempt and remove them from the scheduling snapshot upfront.
- **Speculatively schedule the preemptor**: Run the standard PodGroup scheduling algorithm on this stripped snapshot to find a feasible node assignment for all pods in the preempting PodGroup.
- **Reprieve unnecessary victims**: Iterate through the removed victims (ordered from most important to least important via MoreImportantVictim) and restore any victim that can still coexist with the chosen PodGroup placement; evict the remaining victims.

During step 2, because all potential victims have already been removed from the snapshot, standard Score plugins cannot distinguish between:
- Nodes that already have sufficient free capacity (requiring no preemption).
- Nodes where capacity was only freed by removing high-priority or large PodGroup victims versus low-priority or small victims.
- Nodes whose victims have already been condemned by an earlier pod in the same preempting PodGroup (especially when preempting a victim PodGroup with DisruptionMode: PodGroup frees spots across multiple nodes).

As a result, the scheduler treats all freed nodes equally and scatters the preempting PodGroup across occupied and empty nodes alike. Step 3 (reprieveVictim) can only save victims on nodes that were not selected in Step 2, leading to:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.

Introduce victim-aware node scoring in DefaultPreemption active only during PodGroup preemption evaluation that:
1. Track surviving vs. condemned victims across the PodGroup scheduling pass
2. Compute per-node incremental ("delta") victims in PreScore
3. Prioritize nodes by preemption cost in Score, assigning the maximum score (100) to nodes that require no new victims (either genuinely free nodes or nodes whose victims were already condemned by an earlier pod in the PodGroup), deferring tie-breaking among zero-cost nodes to standard Score plugins.
For nodes where preemption is required, we score them accordingly to the "importance" of the victims - the more important victims needs to be preempted (priority, size, etc.), the lower the score of that node is.

The POC implementing this approach is in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142325 (together with the results from the benchmarks being introduced in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142679 ).

Minimizing the "cost" of preemptions is the goal for all users and current algorithm may result in:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.

which isn't acceptable for many users.

kubectl cp --retries does not resume when the exec returns an error

`kubectl cp --retries=N` resumes a copy only when the exec that runs `tar` ends with a nil error. `TarPipe.initReadFrom` runs the exec in a goroutine with `cmdutil.CheckErr(t.o.execute(options))`, so any error from the session exits kubectl before `TarPipe.Read` gets to retry; the resume only happens after the pipe was closed without an error.

Over WebSocket (the default since 1.30) a cut connection ends the exec with `error reading from error stream: ... close 1006`, so `--retries` has not resumed after a cut there. Over SPDY a cut ended the exec with nil, which is the client-go half of #142376 and the only reason `--retries` resumed. With the client-go change from that issue (part 1 of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142376#issuecomment-6003529603) a cut over SPDY is an error too, and `--retries` stops resuming there as well.

`kubectl cp` of a 3 GiB file from a pod on a stock kind v1.37.0 cluster, the connection between the apiserver and the kubelet killed 5 s in (`ss -K` on the node), one run per cell:

| | kubectl from master | kubectl with the client-go change |
|---|---|---|
| SPDY, `--retries=3` | `Resuming copy at 728108032 bytes, retry 1/3`, complete, exit 0 | `error: connection closed before the command's status was received; the output may be incomplete`, exit 1, no resume |
| WebSocket, `--retries=3` | `error: error reading from error stream: next reader: websocket: close 1006 (abnormal closure): unexpected EOF`, exit 1, no resume | same |

`--retries` resumes after a cut connection on either transport; that is what it was added for in #104792 (#60140).

1. A kind cluster and a pod with a large file (`head -c 3221225472 /dev/zero > /tmp/big`).
2. `kubectl cp --retries=3 pod:/tmp/big ./big`
3. A few seconds in, on the node: `ss -K sport = :10250`, which kills the apiserver's connection to the kubelet.

The fix is in `TarPipe.initReadFrom`: when `MaxTries != 0`, close the pipe with the exec's error instead of calling `CheckErr`, so that `Read` retries; an exit status from `tar` (`utilexec.ExitError`) stays fatal. That raises the question of which errors are worth a retry, and whether `--retries=-1` needs a backoff or a stop when no byte was copied since the last attempt, since a persistent error (the pod is gone) would otherwise retry in a tight loop. I can send the PR once the client-go change has landed.

WAS: exclusive topology placement for PodGroups (one PodGroup per topology domain)

An exclusive mode for PodGroup topology placement in kube-scheduler: a PodGroup lands in a topology domain (one value of a node label) that no other in-scope PodGroup occupies, and keeps that domain to itself while its pods run there.

JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) and DisaggregatedSet each implement this today by injecting pod affinity and anti-affinity. It came up in kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064 (graduating the LWS `exclusive-topology` annotation to a spec field), where the suggestion was to raise it here instead of implementing it in each controller. This issue asks a question; it does not propose an API.

`TopologyConstraint{Key}` puts all pods of one PodGroup in one domain. Its doc comment says "Different PodGroups can land on different domain instances" ([KEP-5732](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L252-L258), [v1beta1 types.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7708623c1a6c115ef1fd4f5f90b98cb7c49d337e/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L858-L868)). Nothing keeps another PodGroup out of that domain, and in the KEP review a reviewer noted that PodGroup replicas may land in different domains "but they can also share them" ([comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5733#discussion_r2610398971), [reply](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5733#discussion_r2623294009)). Exclusivity is not among the KEP's [Goals](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L137-L151) or [Future Extensions](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L474-L508). I did not find an existing issue asking for it.

For a PodGroup G with exclusive placement on node label key K:

1. All scheduled pods of G are on nodes with the same value d of K. This is what `TopologyConstraint` does today.
2. G is placed only in a domain that holds no pods of another in-scope PodGroup, and while G has pods in d, no other in-scope PodGroup is placed in d.
3. d is chosen for the whole group: at least `minCount` pods must fit, as KEP-5732 Phase 2 already checks for each Placement under the Gang policy ([README.md:377-386](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L377-L386)).
4. It is a hard constraint checked at scheduling time only, like `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`.

"In-scope" is the open part, and the three controllers define it differently:

| Controller | Unit | Kept out of the domain | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| JobSet, [`alpha.jobset.sigs.k8s.io/exclusive-topology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/api/jobset/v1alpha2/jobset_types.go#L42-L48) | child Job | pods of any other JobSet Job at the same priority, all namespaces | required affinity and anti-affinity on the leader pod ([pod_webhook.go:117-162](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L117-L162)); followers get the leader's domain as a nodeSelector ([:164-198](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L164-L198)) |
| LWS, [`exclusive-topology` and `subgroup-exclusive-topology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/api/leaderworkerset/v1/leaderworkerset_types.go#L28-L34) | replica, or subgroup | pods of any other LWS replica (or subgroup) in the same namespace | required affinity and anti-affinity ([pod_webhook.go:255-297](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/webhooks/pod_webhook.go#L255-L297)); at replica level only the leader carries them and workers get the leader's domain as a nodeSelector ([pod_controller.go:298-309](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/controllers/pod_controller.go#L298-L309)) |
| DisaggregatedSet, [`placementPolicy.type: ExclusiveTopology`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/api/disaggregatedset/v1/disaggregatedset_types.go#L147-L183) | slice (one copy of every role, across several LWS) | pods of any other DisaggregatedSet slice in the same namespace | required affinity and anti-affinity on every pod ([affinity.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/utils/disaggregatedset/affinity.go#L37-L103)) |

In all three, pods without the controller's labels (for example a plain Deployment) can still share the domain unless taints are used ([DisaggregatedSet docs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/site/content/en/docs/concepts/disaggregatedset/placement-policy/_index.md#L43-L45)).

Emulating exclusivity with pod affinity in each controller has known problems:

1. **No look-ahead.** The leader (JobSet, LWS) or the first pod (DisaggregatedSet) commits the domain, and the rest of the group stays Pending if it does not fit. KEP-5732 rejects pod inter-affinity for this reason ([Alternatives](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/e3340bf8f7eaa2566ff962fa425ec35d42a6d793/keps/sig-scheduling/5732-topology-aware-workload-scheduling/README.md#L935-L946)), and the DisaggregatedSet KEP documents the same risk and defers to gang scheduling ([KEP-848](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/keps/848-disaggregatedset-placement-policy/README.md#L194-L201)).
2. **No gang scheduling together with exclusivity.** LWS alpha rejects gang or WAS topology constraints combined with `exclusive-topology` ([KEP-666 rule 10](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/keps/666-gang-scheduling-in-lws/README.md#L544-L546), [phase_one.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/pkg/schedulerprovider/phase_one.go#L451-L453)). JobSet's docs say native gang scheduling will enable more robust topology-aware scheduling, which they call the core objective of the exclusive topology feature ([tpu_multislice.md](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/jobset/blob/a4fae2847493efda10cc427a572a778bf2f1fe1a/site/content/en/docs/tasks/tpu_multislice.md#L35)). The LWS docs ask users to pick either native exclusive placement or Kueue TAS bin-packing ([LWS docs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/lws/blob/8dd3fd54dd4f286bf115d9214372970633dcaae8/site/content/en/docs/examples/leaderworkerset/topology-aware-scheduling/_index.md#L19-L29)).
3. **Cost.** The Kubernetes docs advise against inter-pod affinity in clusters larger than several hundred nodes ([assign-pod-node.md](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/1c7aa9955e884879397ed15de88605f05eb61d1f/content/en/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node.md#L261-L263)). JobSet measured 58 vs 266 pods/s at 5,000 nodes with its exclusive-placement affinities (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#174), then moved to leader-only terms (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#310) and added a manual node-label and taint mode (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#312). DisaggregatedSet still puts the terms on every pod.
4. **Controller machinery.** JobSet rejects follower pod creation until the leader is scheduled, which loads the API server (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#482). It also needed race handling (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#341) and limited exclusivity to the same priority level as part of supporting preemption (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#682, kubernetes-sigs/jobset#687).
5. **Other placers cannot see it.** Kueue TAS picks nodes without seeing the injected anti-affinity, so it can assign exclusive LWS pods a domain their anti-affinity forbids (kubernetes-sigs/kueue#15057). The direction suggested there is the WAS integration (kubernetes-sigs/kueue#13149). Kueue TAS Topology Spreading caps a domain's share within one spreading group to a value in (0, 1), so it does not exclude other workloads ([KEP-13746](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/blob/df693920cb4be96ed909ab2292966a1c7635800e/keps/13746-tas-topology-spreading/README.md#L460-L463)).
6. **Diverging definitions.** Scope has been argued separately in each project (kubernetes-sigs/lws#539, kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1057). Graduating each controller's version on its own (kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064) would fix three different scopes into three APIs.

Should WAS support exclusive topology placement for PodGroups in kube-scheduler, so controllers can express it through their PodGroup topology constraints instead of injecting pod affinity?

If yes, scope needs a single answer: same namespace or cluster-wide, PodGroups only or all pods, whether priority matters, and whether it applies to CompositePodGroups (a DisaggregatedSet slice spans several LWS).

The answer will inform whether LWS graduates its annotation to its own spec field or maps it onto WAS (kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064). I will add this to the WG meeting agenda.

KEP: kubernetes/enhancements#5732
Related: kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064, kubernetes-sigs/kueue#15057, #136207

kube-apiserver: DELETE with a resourceVersion precondition permanently fails with 409 when the delete removes the object's last GC finalizer

A `DELETE` that carries a `resourceVersion` precondition fails **permanently** with `409 Conflict` when the object's only remaining finalizer is a garbage-collection finalizer that the same delete removes. The object is never modified, so every retry takes the identical code path and produces the identical conflict — the object can never be deleted through this API.

The diagnostic signature is that the apiserver reports an **empty** precondition:

```
Error from server (Conflict): Operation cannot be fulfilled on configmaps "fg-parent":
  StorageError: invalid object, Code: 4, Key: /registry/configmaps/default/fg-parent,
  ResourceVersion: 0,
  AdditionalErrorMsg: Precondition failed: ResourceVersion in precondition: ,
  ResourceVersion in object meta: 1627
```

`ResourceVersion in precondition:` is followed by nothing, while the object itself holds `1627`. The client sent `1627`, which was correct — the registry replaced it with `""` before handing it to the storage layer, and the storage layer then faithfully reported that the precondition did not match.

This is not a race and not a stale precondition. The precondition was verified twice before the failure — once in `rest.BeforeDelete` against the freshly-read object, and once inside `GuaranteedUpdate` against `origState.obj` — and it passed both times. The delete then fails only because the registry overwrote a satisfied precondition with an empty string.

**Real-world trigger.** An object left carrying `foregroundDeletion` because one of its dependents never finishes deleting. That is an everyday situation: a stuck child Pod, a child carrying a third-party finalizer, a child in a namespace that is itself terminating. Once the parent is in that state, any client that deletes it with a resourceVersion precondition — for example a controller using controller-runtime's `client.Preconditions{ResourceVersion: ...}`, or any client using `DeleteOptions.Preconditions` — can never delete it.

The `DELETE` should succeed. The client's precondition was valid when it was sent, the object did not change, and the whole point of a precondition on `DELETE` is to let a client be certain it deleted exactly the version it read.

If the precondition genuinely no longer held, a `409` would be correct. Here the `409` means "the apiserver corrupted its own precondition", which is not something a client can detect, retry past, or recover from.

No manual patching of finalizers is needed — the state arises from ordinary foreground deletion of an object with a stuck dependent.

```
# 1. A child that can never finish deleting.
kubectl create cm fg-child --from-literal=b=2
kubectl patch cm fg-child --type=merge \
  -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":["example.com/never-removed"]}}'

# 2. A parent that owns it.
kubectl create cm fg-parent --from-literal=a=1
PUID=$(kubectl get cm fg-parent -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
kubectl patch cm fg-child --type=merge -p "{\"metadata\":{\"ownerReferences\":[{\"apiVersion\":\"v1\",\"kind\":\"ConfigMap\",\"name\":\"fg-parent\",\"uid\":\"$PUID\",\"controller\":true,\"blockOwnerDeletion\":true}]}}"

[... 13 more lines]
```

Observed, on all three attempts, with `resourceVersion` unchanged at `1627` between them:

```
Error from server (Conflict): Operation cannot be fulfilled on configmaps "fg-parent": StorageError: invalid object, Code: 4, Key: /registry/configmaps/default/fg-parent, ResourceVersion: 0, AdditionalErrorMsg: Precondition failed: ResourceVersion in precondition: , ResourceVersion in object meta: 1627
```

The same delete **without** the precondition succeeds immediately:

```
kubectl delete --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/default/configmaps/fg-parent?gracePeriodSeconds=0" -f - <<EOF
{"apiVersion":"meta.k8s.io/v1","kind":"DeleteOptions","propagationPolicy":"Background"}
EOF
# -> {"kind":"Status",...,"status":"Success",...}
# -> configmaps "fg-parent" not found
```

A shorter variant that skips the owner setup, if you just want the failing delete:

```
kubectl create cm rv-precond-cm --from-literal=a=1
kubectl patch cm rv-precond-cm --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":["orphan"]}}'
RV=$(kubectl get cm rv-precond-cm -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion}')
kubectl delete --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/default/configmaps/rv-precond-cm?gracePeriodSeconds=0" -f - <<EOF
{"apiVersion":"meta.k8s.io/v1","kind":"DeleteOptions",
 "propagationPolicy":"Background",
 "preconditions":{"resourceVersion":"$RV"}}
EOF
```

`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go:1336-1349`, in `Store.Delete`:

```
shouldUpdateFinalizers, _ := deletionFinalizersForGarbageCollection(ctx, e, accessor, options)
if graceful || pendingFinalizers || shouldUpdateFinalizers {
    err, ignoreNotFound, deleteImmediately, out, lastExisting = e.updateForGracefulDeletionAndFinalizers(ctx, name, key, options, preconditions, deleteValidation, obj)
    // Update the preconditions.ResourceVersion if set since we updated the object.
    if err == nil && deleteImmediately && preconditions.ResourceVersion != nil {
        accessor, err = meta.Accessor(out)
        if err != nil {
            return out, false, apierrors.NewInternalError(err)
        }
        resourceVersion := accessor.GetResourceVersion()
[... 3 more lines]
```

The intent is correct: the preceding `GuaranteedUpdate` may have bumped the resourceVersion, so the precondition is refreshed from the object that update returned. The problem is that it trusts `out` unconditionally.

`updateForGracefulDeletionAndFinalizers` has an `errDeleteNow` path that returns **without ever populating `out`** — `store.go:1277-1280`:

```
case errDeleteNow:
    // we've updated the object to have a zero grace period, or it's already at 0, so
    // we should fall through and truly delete the object.
    return nil, false, true, out, lastExisting
```

`out` is allocated once at `store.go:1206` (`out = e.NewFunc()`) and handed to `GuaranteedUpdate` as the destination. The `errDeleteNow` sentinel originates inside the `SimpleUpdate` callback at `store.go:1251` (`return nil, errDeleteNow`), which returns a nil object, so the storage layer never writes to the destination. In `etcd3`, an error out of `updateState` short-circuits at `store.go:545-549` before the destination is ever decoded — the only two writes to it are `store.go:597` and `store.go:646`, both unreachable on this path.

So `out` is still the bare `e.NewFunc()` object, `accessor.GetResourceVersion()` returns `""`, and the caller's valid precondition is replaced with a pointer to the empty string.

Note that this branch returns `err = nil` and `deleteImmediately = true`, so the guard `err == nil && deleteImmediately` passes. There is no empty-RV check and no re-read of the object between here and `e.Storage.Delete` at `store.go:1371`, which then fails its own precondition check against `""` and surfaces as `409 Conflict`.

Contrast the sibling `case nil` at `store.go:1261-1276`, where `GuaranteedUpdate` did commit and `out` genuinely carries the new resourceVersion. That path is correct. Only the `errDeleteNow` path is broken.

**Reachability.** `errDeleteNow` is returned at `store.go:1251` when the strategy is non-graceful and the object has no pending finalizers *after* the finalizer rewrite — i.e. precisely when the object's only finalizer was the GC finalizer that this delete just removed. `deletionFinalizersForGarbageCollection` (`store.go:1135-1164`) strips `orphan`/`foregroundDeletion` for a `Background` or `Orphan` propagation policy, so
`shouldUpdateFinalizers` is true, the branch at `store.go:1338` is entered, and the finalizer list is emptied at `store.go:1239`.

**Why it loops forever.** On this path the `SimpleUpdate` is aborted before the write. The GC finalizer is never stripped and `deletionTimestamp` is never set, so the object stays byte-identical. Every subsequent `DELETE` re-enters the same branch with the same empty precondition and 409s identically.

Perform a limited read in the webhook authorizer

Right now, the `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/authorizer/webhook/webhook.go` file's `rest.Interface` under the hood does a `io.ReadAll` from the server, which means that a webhook authorizer that malfunctions could OOM the API server. The webhook authorizer is a highly privileged component, so this is not that much of an issue, but it'd still be better to enforce a limited read (e.g. 10MB or similar).

xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633 where this was discussed.

apimachinery yaml: YAMLOrJSONDecoder drops a trailing document shorter than 4 bytes

`YAMLOrJSONDecoder` fails to decode a document when fewer than 4 bytes remain in the stream. The same document decodes correctly if a single trailing space is added.

```
"{a}"          len=3  ->  error: json: offset 2: invalid character 'a' looking for beginning of object key string
"{a} "         len=4  ->  map[a:<nil>]
"{ab}"         len=4  ->  map[ab:<nil>]

`{"a":1}{b}`   ->  doc 1 decodes, doc 2 fails   (3 bytes remaining)
`{"a":1}{bc}`  ->  doc 1 decodes, doc 2 decodes (4 bytes remaining)
```

The cutoff is exactly 4 bytes, which is the read size in `consumeWhitespace`.

`consumeWhitespace` (`staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go:362`) discards a short read:

```
buf, err := d.stream.ReadN(4)
if err != nil && err == io.EOF { //nolint:errorlint
	return err
}
```

`ReadN` documents the opposite contract:

> If EOF is hit before n bytes are read, this will return the bytes read so far, along with io.EOF.

`Decode` only builds the YAML decoder when `consumeWhitespace` returns nil (`decoder.go:333`), so an early `io.EOF` means the YAML fallback never runs and the caller gets the JSON syntax error instead.

A document should decode the same whether or not it happens to be followed by padding. `{a}` should decode to `map[a:<nil>]`, as `{a} ` already does.

`staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml/repro_test.go`:

```
package yaml

import (
	"bytes"
	"testing"
)

func TestShortTrailingDocument(t *testing.T) {
	for _, in := range []string{"{a}", "{a} "} {
		var out interface{}
[... 6 more lines]
```

```
go test -run TestShortTrailingDocument ./pkg/util/yaml/
```

Scope: the decoder only takes this path when the stream begins with `{` (`IsJSONBuffer`); a stream that does not is given a YAML decoder directly in the constructor and is unaffected. So ordinary `apiVersion:`-style manifests do not hit this. It is reachable through `StreamVisitor.Visit` (`staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource/visitor.go:590`) for a JSON-prefixed stream whose last document is under 4 bytes and is not valid JSON.

This is the same defect class as #142527 ("apimachinery yaml: keep a final line returned together with io.EOF"), in the same package: bytes returned alongside `io.EOF` are discarded by the caller. That change fixed one instance; this is another.

Happy to send a PR.

kube-apiserver: /openapi/v3 is never gzip-compressed, unlike /openapi/v2

kube-apiserver serves `/openapi/v3` and `/openapi/v3/<group-version>` uncompressed even when the client sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip`. `/openapi/v2` on the same server is gzipped.

Same client and headers against a v1.34.11 kube-apiserver:

| Path | Identity size | With `Accept-Encoding: gzip` | `Content-Encoding` |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| `/openapi/v2` | 5,333,236 B | 484,949 B | `gzip` |
| `/openapi/v3` | 13,653 B | 13,653 B | none |
| `/openapi/v3/api/v1` | 1,452,085 B | 1,452,085 B | none |
| `/openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1` | 665,580 B | 665,580 B | none |

`/openapi/v3` and `/openapi/v3/<group-version>` honour `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, as `/openapi/v2` does.

The v2 endpoint is wrapped in a gzip handler in kube-openapi (`pkg/handler/handler.go`):

```
handler.Handle(servePath, gziphandler.GzipHandler(http.HandlerFunc(
```

The v3 handlers are registered without one, both in kube-openapi (`pkg/handler3/handler.go`, `RegisterOpenAPIV3VersionedService`) and in kube-aggregator, which serves these paths in kube-apiserver (`pkg/controllers/openapiv3/aggregator/aggregator.go`, `register`).

The apiserver's own response compression does not apply either: KEP-2338 scopes it to API object responses and lists "OpenAPI endpoints which provide their own compression" as out of scope. That is true for v2 but not for v3.

v3 is designed around client-side caching: the discovery document hands out `?hash=` URLs served with `Cache-Control: public, immutable`, and every response has an ETag. A client that uses them downloads each document once.

Not every client does. A client that requests group-version documents without the hash and without `If-None-Match` gets the full body each time. Helm does this when rendering a chart, so a Helm-based operator repeats it on every reconcile. At around 800 KB per response, one fetch every few seconds adds up to roughly 10 GB per day from a single controller, where gzip would make it about 1 GB.

Wrapping the two v3 handlers in kube-aggregator in the gzip handler v2 already uses is enough:

| Path | Before | After |
|---|--:|--:|
| `/openapi/v3` | 13,653 B | 5,295 B |
| `/openapi/v3/api/v1` | 1,452,085 B | 117,651 B |
| `/openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1` | 665,580 B | 77,036 B |

That compresses on every request. kubernetes/kube-openapi#646 moves v2 to gzip once per cache rebuild; the same could be done for v3 in `handler3`, which already caches the JSON and protobuf serializations per group-version.

```
for p in /openapi/v2 /openapi/v3 /openapi/v3/api/v1 /openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1; do
  curl -s --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key \
    -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' \
    -o /dev/null -D - -w "$p wire=%{size_download}\n" "https://$APISERVER$p" \
    | grep -i -E 'content-encoding|wire='
done
```

|---|---|---|---|
| control-plane | cadvisor (default) | 66285632 | 75044417 |
| worker | CRI | 74156229000 | 74196804 |

`total` in nanoseconds on both paths, as documented.

MemoryQoS TieredReservation: pod-level memory.low is not updated on a request-only in-place memory resize

With `memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation`, an in-place resize that changes only the memory request updates the container's `memory.low` but leaves the pod cgroup's `memory.low` at the old request. It doesn't recover on later syncs.

Measured on v1.37.0 (kind, containerd, cgroup v2), Burstable pod, limit 512Mi:

| step | container memory.low | pod memory.low | pod memory.max |
|---|---|---|---|
| created, request 256Mi | 268435456 | 268435456 | 536870912 |
| request-only resize to 400Mi | 419430400 | **268435456** | 536870912 |
| 90s later | 419430400 | **268435456** | 536870912 |
| limit resize to 768Mi | 419430400 | 419430400 | 805306368 |

A limit resize does refresh the pod-level value (that was fixed in #140262), so the gap is only the request-only case.

Pod-level `memory.low` should follow the pod's memory request after a request-only resize, as it does after a limit resize. KEP-2570 says that after an in-place resize, `memory.min`/`memory.low` "are recalculated during the next cgroup reconciliation cycle" ([KEP](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos)).

```
# kind node, KubeletConfiguration
featureGates: {MemoryQoS: true}
memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9
memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation
```

Create a pod with memory request 256Mi and limit 512Mi, then:

```
kubectl patch pod b --subresource resize -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"b","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"400Mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512Mi"}}}]}}'
# read memory.low in the pod cgroup (kubepods-burstable-pod<uid>.slice) on the node

### Anything else we need to know?

`setPodCgroupConfig` in `doPodResizeAction` returns early on a request-only memory resize ("Memory requests aren't written to cgroups"), but TieredReservation derives pod-level `memory.low` from the request, and nothing rewrites it later. The v1.38 `Soft`/`Hard` policies (kubernetes/enhancements#6362) go through the same path.

MemoryQoS: container memory.high is not reset when an in-place resize makes the memory request equal the limit

With MemoryQoS on and a `memoryThrottlingFactor` set, I resized a Burstable container's memory request up to its limit in place. The container kept the `memory.high` computed for its previous request, so it stays throttled below its limit. It doesn't recover on later syncs.

Measured on v1.37.0 (kind, containerd, cgroup v2, `memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9`), container with limit 512Mi:

| memory request | container memory.high |
|---|---|
| 256Mi (created) | 510025728 |
| 400Mi (resize) | 525123584 (recomputed, correct) |
| 512Mi = limit (resize) | 525123584 (stale, should be `max`) |
| 90s later | 525123584 |

I saw the same on v1.36.1.

When request equals limit the kubelet deliberately doesn't set `memory.high`, so after the resize the container should end up with `memory.high=max`, the same as a container created with request == limit.

```
# kind node, KubeletConfiguration
featureGates: {MemoryQoS: true}
memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9
```

```
kubectl run a --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"a","image":"registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"256Mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512Mi"}}}]}}'
kubectl patch pod a --subresource resize -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"a","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"512Mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512Mi"}}}]}}'
# then read memory.high in the container's cgroup on the node
```

I think the cause is in `generateLinuxContainerResources`. With MemoryQoS enforced, `memory.high` is added to `Unified` only when `memoryRequest != memoryLimitSpec` (and `memoryHigh > memoryRequest`). Otherwise the key is simply absent, and the runtime leaves an absent key untouched on `UpdateContainerResources`; CRI-O copies only the keys it's given. The MemoryQoS-off branch already writes `memory.high=max` for exactly this stale-after-resize reason, but the MemoryQoS-on branch has no equivalent.

This matters for VPA-driven resizes: a VPA `RequestsOnly` policy produces request == limit whenever the target is above the limit (kubernetes/autoscaler#9926).

Explore publishing an aggregated OpenAPI v3 schema for downstream consumers

Explore publishing a single, merged OpenAPI v3 document in the repo (or as a release artifact) alongside the existing per-group-version files under `api/openapi-spec/v3/`.

This would only be a static file for offline consumers, not a new endpoint served by `kube-apiserver`.

With `/openapi/v2` deprecation being discussed in #141455, many downstream projects still rely on `api/openapi-spec/swagger.json` instead of OpenAPI v3. For example, the official client generators in `kubernetes-client/gen` (Python, Java, JavaScript, C#, etc.), the Rust `k8s-openapi` crate, `kustomize`, and `pulumi-kubernetes` all consume `swagger.json`.

A big reason these consumers have not moved to v3 is that `api/openapi-spec/v3/` is split across dozens of per-group-version files with shared types like `ObjectMeta` duplicated in each file. Most code generators expect a single OpenAPI document, so migrating to v3 currently requires every downstream project to write custom logic to parse and merge all the group-version files themselves. Or they can adopt fetching each document separately and processing there but that's a bigger change.

Publishing a pre-merged OpenAPI v3 spec would make it much easier for client libraries and tooling to migrate off `swagger.json` without affecting `kube-apiserver` runtime memory.

Graceful Node Shutdown should allow admission of high priority pods

[Graceful Node Shutdown feature](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-shutdown/#configuring-graceful-node-shutdown) terminates pods in two stages: critical and non-critical pods. It is possible to specify a specific deadline for each of these stages.

```
shutdownGracePeriod: 3600s
shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods: 1800s
```

Terminating workloads on a node can take considerable amount of time.

Critical workloads (e.g. CSI driver, networking, monitoring, etc.) can terminate before the normal pods are terminated. This can happen for example during a DaemonSet rollout. Such disruption can have detrimental effect on the graceful termination of lower priority workloads.

[Pod Priority Graceful Node Shutdown](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-shutdown/#pod-priority-graceful-node-shutdown) also introduces a way to describe multiple termination stages according to arbitrary priorities. Allowing gradual admission could be useful there as well.

This also causes race between the daemonset controller and kubelet which has been discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122912

Critical priority pods (e.g. `system-node-critical`, `system-cluster-critical`) should still be admitted during GNS until it is their turn to terminate.

Node taints should also reflect this situation, either by removing

```
taints:
- effect: NoSchedule
   key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
   timeAdded: "2026-09-29T09:47:43Z"
```

or adding a custom taint for Graceful Node Shutdown that controllers can work with (e.g. daemonset controller) and add a default toleration. This is already an existing pattern:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/50b66f3c122cb1553cd4d46d4eba81a101e05b50/pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go#L48

Create a critical priority pod when `shutdownGracePeriod` is in effect.

Currently the pod is rejected with:

```
status:
  message: 'Pod was rejected: Pod was rejected as the node is shutting down.'
  observedGeneration: 1
  phase: Failed
  qosClass: BestEffort
  reason: NodeShutdown
  startTime: "2026-09-29T09:52:46Z"
```

Document that matchConditions cannot use namespaceObject or variables

The docs imply that admission policy `matchConditions` can use every CEL variable that validation expressions can. Two of those variables don't work in match conditions:

1. **`namespaceObject` compiles but is always `null`.** The CEL environment declares `namespaceObject` for every expression type ([`compile.go#L256`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/cel/compile.go#L256)). So a match condition that references it passes API validation. At runtime, however, the shared match condition evaluator always passes a `nil` namespace ([`matcher.go#L85`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/matchconditions/matcher.go#L85)). This happens even for ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, where the namespace has already been fetched and is passed to validations ([`validator.go#L104`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/policy/validating/validator.go#L104) vs [`#L127`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/policy/validating/validator.go#L127)).
   - With `failurePolicy: Fail`, every matching request is rejected with `no such key: metadata`.
   - With `failurePolicy: Ignore`, the policy is silently skipped.
2. **`variables` is rejected when the policy is created.** API validation compiles match conditions with a stateless compiler that has no `variables` declared ([`validateMatchConditionsExpression`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/pkg/apis/admissionregistration/validation/validation.go#L1100-L1112)). This matches the API field docs for `spec.variables` ("…except MatchConditions because MatchConditions are evaluated before the rest of the policy"). It contradicts the website docs.

Where the docs mislead:

- kubernetes.io, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy › Matching requests: `matchConditions` ([source](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/blob/049ffb8f2810d82a121b9cdaab94c907592d7526/content/en/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/validating-admission-policy.md?plain=1#L403)):
  > Match conditions have access to the same CEL variables as validation expressions.
- API reference for `MatchCondition.expression` ([`v1/types.go#L1570-L1583`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d3071315a65c453c861d06e9ad66d036a6413ec/staging/src/k8s.io/api/admissionregistration/v1/types.go#L1570-L1583)): the doc lists the available variables but doesn't say that `namespaceObject` is unavailable. Users reasonably assume the "Validation" variable list applies, since `namespaceObject` compiles.

This has been the behavior since `namespaceObject` was introduced in v1.28 (#118267). It affects ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, MutatingAdmissionPolicy, and the matchConditions of validating/mutating webhook configurations.

The docs should state which variables match conditions can use:

- `object`, `oldObject`, `request`, `authorizer`, `authorizer.requestResource`, and `params` (policies only).
- **Not** `namespaceObject`: it is not populated for match conditions and always evaluates to `null`.
- **Not** `variables`: it is rejected when the policy is created.

It should also point users to the supported alternatives: `namespaceSelector` on the policy or binding for namespace labels, or a guarded check inside `validations`, where `namespaceObject` is available.

Against `k8s.io/apiserver@master` (`v0.0.0-20260928183837-a21d4fc0471f`). The program compiles expressions the same way API validation does, then runs the shared match condition evaluator for a Pod in a namespace labelled `env: prod`:

DRA: ResourceSlice validation panics on a zero with an extreme negative exponent in capacity.requestPolicy.validValues

With `DRAFractionalCapacityRange` enabled (beta, on by default since 1.37), validating a ResourceSlice whose device capacity has `requestPolicy.validValues` containing `0e-2147483647` panics inside `ValidateResourceSlice`:

```
runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range
```

`ParseQuantity("0e-2147483647")` is accepted (a zero on the `inf.Dec` backend with scale 2147483647), and `validateRequestPolicyValidValues` keys the values with `quantityKeyAsDec`, which calls `AsDec().String()`; `inf.Dec.String` allocates `scale+2` bytes for a value below one (`gopkg.in/inf.v0/dec.go:442`) and overflows.

Reproduced on master (6c1c7702 and later) with a unit probe in `pkg/apis/resource/validation`:

```

bad := apiresource.MustParse("0e-2147483647")

Leverage remote partitions for exclusive CPUs (Linux 6.7+)

Linux 6.7 added support for ["remote partitions"](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#:~:text=partition%20is%20created.-,cpuset.cpus.partition,-A%20read%2Dwrite), which enables containers to allocate exclusive CPUs without modifying any other cgroups. With the deprecation of cgroups v1, we should migrate CPU manager to leverage this approach.

Currently, with static CPU policy, cpu_manager runs a reconcile loop (default 10s period) to sync CPU allocation to containers. It manages a default set, and every container that doesn't have exclusive CPUs gets assigned the default set. The default set is updated (for every container) to remove CPUs as they're allocated exclusively.

Problems with this approach:
1. Eventual consistency: When an exclusive CPU is assigned, there is up to 10s (or more!) delay before that CPU is removed from the default set of other containers.
2. No protection from system processes: Only containers managed by the Kubelet are excluded from using the assigned CPUs. System processes (e.g. the Kubelet itself) can still be scheduled to it.
3. Every static CPU assignment (or release) requires updating every other container on the node. These are all done through `UpdateContainerResources` requests, and are subject to global NRI locks.
4. Container reconciliation outside of SyncPod: the reconcile loop calls UpdateContainerResources directly. Normally, all direct container operations like that happen within SyncPod. Performing the operation outside of SyncPod makes this more prone to race conditions.

1. The full set of assignable CPUs is written to `cpuset.cpus.exclusive` on the full cgroup tree (`kubelet.slice`, `kubelet-kubepods.slice`), and pod-level cgroups.
2. When a container is assigned exclusive CPUs, it sets `cpuset.cpus.exclusive` to the assigned set, and `cpuset.cpus.partition=root` (some specialized workloads like DPDK may want `isolated`). This is set on container creation, or in `doPodResizeAction` on resize, both of which are in `SyncPod`.
3. Remove the cpu_manager reconciliation loop: it's no longer needed.

e2e_node: make ImageGCPeriod (and other e2e_node wait budgets) configurable for tests

﻿## What happened
While removing duplicated `[Slow]` spec execution between `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial` and `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-slow` (kubernetes/test-infra#37903), we looked into why the `[Slow]`-tagged ImageGC/GarbageCollect/MirrorPod specs in `test/e2e_node` cost ~30 minutes per host.

It's not image size or pull time — these use the standard few-MB e2e-test-images (pause, busybox, nginx-slim/agnhost). The time comes from wait/poll budgets hardcoded in the tests themselves, bound to production defaults:

- `image_gc_test.go`: two `[Slow]` specs poll for up to `checkGCUntil = 6 * time.Minute`, gated by kubelet's `ImageGCPeriod` (hardcoded to 5 minutes).
- `garbage_collector_test.go`: `setupDuration = 10 * time.Minute`, `garbageCollectDuration = 3 * time.Minute`.
- `mirror_pod_test.go`: several `2 * time.Minute` `Eventually` polls, plus a couple `5 * time.Minute` waits.

Polling more frequently doesn't help — these tests aren't slow because they check infrequently, they're waiting on a real kubelet-side event gated by a fixed period.

Make `ImageGCPeriod` (and whatever governs the GC/mirror-pod wait windows above) configurable for e2e_node tests, so these specs aren't bound to the 5-minute production default and can run with a much shorter period in test.

Some kube-apiserver histograms stay classic because ApplyFeatureGates() runs after informers and REST clients are built

First of all, thank you for landing native histogram support in v1.37 — it's been a really
welcome addition on my side.

While verifying it on a kind cluster, I noticed that within a **single kube-apiserver
process**, some histograms are exposed as native while others stay classic. The split does not
look intentional, so I wanted to report what I measured.

Scraping `kindest/node:v1.37.0` with Prometheus v3.13.2 and `scrape_native_histograms: true`
(`always_scrape_classic_histograms` left at its default of `false`):

| metric | native from | classic from |
|---|---|---|
| `apiserver_request_duration_seconds` | **kube-apiserver** | — |
| `workqueue_work_duration_seconds` | kubelet | **kube-apiserver** |
| `workqueue_queue_duration_seconds` | kubelet | **kube-apiserver** |
| `rest_client_request_duration_seconds` | kubelet | **kube-apiserver** |
| `informer_processing_latency_seconds` | — | **kube-apiserver** |
| `apiserver_admission_controller_admission_duration_seconds` | — | **kube-apiserver** |

The first row shows the feature gate is active for kube-apiserver
(`apiserver_request_duration_seconds` had 158 native series). So this isn't a gate or config
problem — only the metrics registered early stay classic.

The consequence is that **the same metric name is native from one component and classic from
another**. `workqueue_work_duration_seconds` had 4 native series from kubelet and 319 classic
series from kube-apiserver, and this query silently returns kubelet data only, with no warning:

```
sum(rate(workqueue_work_duration_seconds[10m]))
```

`toPromHistogramOpts()` reads the gate when `Create()` runs, i.e. at registration time, so
`ApplyFeatureGates()` has to run first. The doc comment says as much:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/features/kube_features.go#L51-L53

```
// ApplyFeatureGates propagates the current feature gate state to the metrics
// subsystem. It must be called after feature gates are finalised and before
// any histogram metrics are registered.
```

kubelet calls it before any client or informer is built:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/cmd/kubelet/app/server.go#L671-L673

kube-apiserver calls it inside `CreateConfig()`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/config.go#L303

but an informer is already instantiated nine lines earlier, at `server.go:230`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L230

```
endpointSliceGetter, err := proxy.NewEndpointSliceIndexerGetter(versionedInformers.Discovery().V1().EndpointSlices())
```

That calls `sliceInformer.Informer()`
([`endpointslice.go#L74-L76`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/proxy/endpointslice.go#L74-L76)),
which triggers the deferred registration in the fifo metrics provider. The REST clients behind
`versionedInformers` are built earlier still.

What makes me think this is unintended rather than a deliberate scoping decision is that the
workqueue and fifo providers already contain a workaround for exactly this ordering problem:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/prometheus/clientgo/fifo/metrics.go#L61-L66

```
// init only installs the provider with cache. The actual metric
// registration with legacyregistry is deferred until the first factory
// method is called (which happens at runtime when the first informer is
// constructed). This ensures Create() — and therefore the read of the
// NativeHistograms feature gate inside toPromHistogramOpts — runs after
// ApplyFeatureGates has propagated the gate state.
```

The deferral works, but in kube-apiserver the first informer is still constructed before
`ApplyFeatureGates()`, so the workaround doesn't have the intended effect there.

I'd expect a given metric name to be exposed in the same format regardless of which component
emits it, so that a query like `sum(rate(workqueue_work_duration_seconds[10m]))` covers every
component that reports it.

Moving the `ApplyFeatureGates()` call in kube-apiserver earlier — before the REST clients and
`SharedInformerFactory` are built — would line it up with what kubelet already does. I may well
be missing a constraint that forces the current placement, though.

1. Create a cluster:

```
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.37.0
```

2. Run Prometheus v3.x with native-only scraping for both the apiserver and the kubelet:

```
global:
  scrape_native_histograms: true
scrape_configs:
- job_name: kubernetes-apiservers
  # ... standard in-cluster apiserver scrape config
- job_name: kubernetes-nodes
  # ... standard in-cluster kubelet scrape config
```

3. Compare the native and classic forms of the same metric:

```
count by (job) (workqueue_work_duration_seconds)          # => kubernetes-nodes only
count by (job) (workqueue_work_duration_seconds_bucket)   # => kubernetes-apiservers only
```

4. Confirm the gate is actually on for the apiserver:

```
count(apiserver_request_duration_seconds{job="kubernetes-apiservers"})   # => 158
```

- With `convert_classic_histograms_to_nhcb: true`, the split becomes an exponential/NHCB schema
  mix instead, and `sum(rate(workqueue_work_duration_seconds[10m]))` returns an empty vector
  with a PromQL warning rather than partial data.
- Two other groups of histograms stay classic for different reasons, which I assume are out of
  scope here: `TimingHistogramOpts` metrics (e.g. `apiserver_flowcontrol_*_utilization`) never
  receive native options, and the `go_*` runtime metrics come from client_golang's Go collector
  and don't go through `component-base` at all.
- I couldn't find this discussed in KEP-5808 or in an existing issue, so apologies if I've
  missed it.
- Possibly related: #142377 (on `NativeHistogramMinResetDuration` being unset).

Happy to send a PR moving the call site if that's the direction you'd want to take.

Exec drops end of stdout when client reads slowly

I tried to take a backup of a pod's data using `kubectl exec`. When inspecting file sizes the files seemed not to be the same. After some testing and experiments, I found the issue to occur only when the client reads slower than the (in-pod) process writes (to stdout). Only the end of the stream was missing, the beginning was intact. `kubectl exec` often exited with 0, with nothing on stderr. So the truncated result could not be told apart from a complete one. `kubectl cp` fails the same way when the client is behind a slow link with `error: unexpected EOF` (copying to a fast local disk did not fail). The error occurred using the older SPDY transport as well as WebSockets.

kube-apiserver keep using a stale webhook configuration after an update

The kube-apiserver kept calling admission webhooks with an old version of `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration`, even though the object had been updated. It kept doing so until the object was updated again.

There is a recurring e2e flake in Cluster API, which most likely is related to this cache race. Right after the providers are installed, every webhook fails with:
```
failed calling webhook "validation.cluster.cluster.x-k8s.io": failed to call webhook: Post "https://capi-webhook-service.capi-system.svc:443/validate-cluster-x-k8s-io-v1beta2-cluster?timeout=10s": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
```

Following the time from one failing [run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/periodic-cluster-api-e2e-main-v2/2100268237257183232) :
* (17:22:15) cert-manager issues the serving certificate (signle revision)
* (17:22:16) `clusterctl` creates the `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` without a `caBundle`. In the same time, cert0manager caininjector sets the `caBundle` on all webhooks. The object ends at `generation: 2` and it is never modified again.
* (17:22:19) the webhook server loads the serving certificate.
* (17:22:23 --> end of the test) every call from the kube-apiserver fails with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority`. The webhook server logs remote error: tls: bad certificate for the same connections.

A dump of the objects after the failure shows `caBundle` equal to `ca.crt` of the serving certificate Secret, meaning that the stored object was correct for the failing duration, but the kube-apiserver, probably, kept serving with the version that had no `caBundle`.

It seems that the race is in `configurationsCache`, `sync.Map`, in the webhook managers code (validating/mutating). The cache is built with keys derived only by configuration name. The informer `UpdateFunc` runs `configurationsCache.Delete(name)` and then `lazy.Notify()`. `getValidatingWebhookConfigurations` builds accessors from a lister snapshot and runs `configurationsCache.Store(name, accessors)` without checking which version they were built from.

After a webhook configuration is updated, the kube-apiserver uses the latest version. Accessors built from an older version are never cached in the way that they will outlive an update event.

During the investigation for the kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api/issues/13300, we were trying to pinpoint if the source of flake was on the CAPI side or on the kube-apiserver side. I used the following unit test as way to reproduce it.

```
package configuration

import (
	"context"
	"testing"
	"testing/synctest"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/admissionregistration/v1"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	"k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook"
[... 55 more lines]
```
Using `k8s.io/apiserver` `v0.37.0`
```
=== RUN   TestValidatingWebhookConfigurationStaleCache
    stale_cache_simplified_test.go:62: caBundle = "", want "injected-ca"
```
The idea was to replicate the cert-manager `inject-ca-from` create the configuration and then patch the `caBundle` immediately (cainjector)

Testing a possible fix where we capture the `resourceVersion` next to the cached accessors and reuse them onky when it matches. That approach seems to fix the unit test above.

Another workaround was to trigger an update to the webhook configuration (eg. adding an annotation) clears the stale entry, without changing the current apiserver code.

Stale repos - gopkg.in/inf.v0 (github.com/go-inf/inf)

Following the same pattern as #132312, for a different dependency.

`gopkg.in/inf.v0` is a **direct** dependency of `k8s.io/apimachinery`, where `inf.Dec` backs the arbitrary-precision path of `resource.Quantity`:

```
type Quantity struct {
	// i is the quantity in int64 scaled form, if d.Dec == nil
	i int64Amount
	// d is the quantity in inf.Dec form if d.Dec != nil
	d infDecAmount
	...
}
```

It is also part of apimachinery's exported surface -- `func (q *Quantity) AsDec() *inf.Dec` and `func NewDecimalQuantity(b inf.Dec, format Format) *Quantity`, so it is compiled into essentially every Go program that talks to a Kubernetes API server, not only Kubernetes itself.

There is no CVE (OSV reports zero for `gopkg.in/inf.v0`), no bug report, and no urgency. The package is 760 lines across `dec.go` and `rounder.go`, has **no external dependencies at all**, just `math/big`, `fmt`, `io`, `strings`, and uses neither `unsafe` nor `reflect`. Decimal arithmetic is a stable problem, and "no commits since 2018" is not by itself alarming for code of this shape. This is materially lower-risk than the json-iterator situation in #132312, and I do not think it should be treated with the same urgency.

I am also not proposing removal. `inf.Dec` is in a GA Go API on one of the most widely used types in the ecosystem, so removing it would need `k8s.io/apimachinery/v2`. That is not what this issue is asking for.

It is bus factor, not code quality. As far as I can tell there is currently nobody able to publish a release under this import path:

- Last commit: **2018-03-27**. Last release: **v0.9.1, 2018-03-26**. Only two versions were ever tagged.
- Sole author is Péter Surányi (`@speter`, per the LICENSE copyright line); the only other commit in the repo's history is a one-line `gofmt` change from 2017. His last authored commit in any public repo is **2020-03-28**.
- The **`go-inf` organisation has zero public members**, no org email, and one repo. It was created in 2015 purely to back this vanity import path after Google Code shut down (see #26231). The original `speter.net` domain no longer resolves.
- [go-inf/inf#8](https://github.com/go-inf/inf/issues/8), "is it EOL ?", has been **open and unanswered since 2023-01-11**.
- [go-inf/inf#9](https://github.com/go-inf/inf/pull/9) was closed by its own author the day it was opened, unmerged, with no maintainer response.

So if a fix is ever genuinely needed under this path, a Go compatibility break, or an arithmetic bug found by the ongoing `Quantity` work, there is presently no mechanism to ship one, and downstream cannot route around it because the import path is in a public API.

I have tried the obvious things first: commented on go-inf/inf#8 on September, 05, 2026, and emailed the address in the repo's git history on September, 21, 2026. No response to either as of filing.

At what point, if any, is it worth acting on this proactively rather than waiting to need a fix we cannot ship? Roughly in increasing order of effort:

1. Someone with karma reaches Péter successfully and a maintainer gets added to `go-inf`, cheapest by far, and non-breaking, since the import path is unchanged.
2. Kubernetes adopts the package under an owned path, as was done for `google/gofuzz` → `sigs.k8s.io/randfill` and the `go-yaml` fork → `go.yaml.in/yaml`. The license is BSD-3, so this needs no one's permission, but note it is still a breaking Go API change, because `AsDec()` would return a different named type.
3. Deprecate `AsDec`/`NewDecimalQuantity` now and drop the dependency at a hypothetical apimachinery v2. Cleanest, slowest.

"The risk is acceptable, leave it alone" is a perfectly good answer too — I would just like it to be a decision on the record rather than something nobody has looked at. Happy to do the legwork on any of these if it is useful.

[FG:InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs] Need to track actuated changes

IIUC, CPUs are assigned during the admission stage when allocating a pod resize. During upsize, this is not a problem, but when downsizing the unallocated CPUs are returned to the available pool before the runtime has actually updated the container. This could cause a race condition where those CPUs are assigned to a different pod before the previous pod has actually released them.

I think CPU manager needs to track not-yet-released CPUs separately from what's been allocated to ensure they aren't reassigned before they're released.

Resize failure & start container

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140387 changed resize to happen before containers are started.

If resize fails, it adds the error to the sync result, but then proceeds with starting containers. This could cause resource oversubscription or OOMs if the resize was supposed to free up resources for the starting containers.

I'm not sure what the right way to handle this is. The simplest solution would be to simply return early and skip starting containers if the resize failed, but this could cause container start to be blocked indefinitely if, for example, a memory decrease was blocked by the usage > new limit check.

One possible solution is to look at the resource budget after the resize partial failure: actual pod-level limits - actual container requests (??), and only start the new containers that are budgeted for. But this approach breaks down in burstable pods, or burstable containers within a PLR envelope.

The solution requires more thought.

Pod validation: AllowIndivisibleHugePagesValues ratchets every hugepages entry, not just the stored one

`GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` sets `PodValidationOptions.AllowIndivisibleHugePagesValues` from `usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues(oldPodSpec)`, a single bool for the whole pod: true if *any* container, the pod-level resources, or the overhead in the old spec held a hugepages value that isn't a positive integer multiple of the hugepages size. `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` skips the divisibility check entirely for every hugepages entry in the *new* spec whenever that flag is true.

That means once one container's stored hugepages value happens to be indivisible (the known case is an old `2^64`-scale value that overflowed the divisibility check before it existed), a completely unrelated, brand-new indivisible hugepages value anywhere else in the same pod — a different container, a different hugepages size, a value that was never stored anywhere before — also passes validation. The flag is supposed to grandfather in a specific stored value; instead it opens the check for the whole object.

Only the exact stored `(container, resource name, quantity)` that was already accepted should be exempt from the divisibility check on update. A hugepages value that's new, or under a different resource name, or under a different container, should be validated in full — same as it would be on create.

Given a Pod (or a Deployment/ReplicaSet/etc. pod template, which goes through the same options builder) with two containers:

```
containers:
- name: a
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-2Mi: 18446744073709551616}   # already indivisible, already stored
    ...
- name: b
  resources:
    limits: {}   # no hugepages at all
    ...
```

Update it, leaving container `a` untouched, and adding a brand-new, itself-indivisible value to container `b`:

```
containers:
- name: a
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-2Mi: 18446744073709551616}   # unchanged
    ...
- name: b
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-1Gi: 3Mi}   # new, not a multiple of 1Gi
    ...
```

This update is accepted. It should be rejected the same way a fresh pod with `hugepages-1Gi: 3Mi` and no prior indivisible values anywhere is rejected (`3Mi is not positive integer multiple of hugepages-1Gi`).

RuntimeClass's `overhead` field had the identical pattern (a whole-object blanket flag) until kubernetes/kubernetes#142323, which narrowed it there to an exact stored-value match using `PodValidationOptions.StoredResourceQuantities` (already computed for the #141166 burndown). `GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` already builds that same `StoredResourceQuantities` set for pods, and `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` already checks it there — the only missing piece for pods is that `usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues` still sets the wider flag on top of it, which shadows the precise check. A fix (drops the blanket flag and its now-dead helpers, relies on the existing per-value match alone, adds a regression test) is ready and PR'd; it's stacked on #142323 since it depends on that PR's `StoredResourceQuantities` plumbing, and can't land before it.

Add roundtrip coverage of fuzzing an external version, ensuring a roundtrip through internal preserves data

Right now, we fuzz the internal version, then convert internal -> external -> internal and verify the object didn't lose data.
In some cases, e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633, internal -> external is lossy by design (e.g. new internal fields for non-serialized types), which means we need to add fuzzer funcs to clear any such data in the internal type when fuzzing.

This leaves a little bit of a coverage gap, that could be closed by also going the other way: fuzz external, then convert external -> internal -> external, and verify equivalence.

This would improve the coverage of some special cases of API conversion.

Informer cache lag on PVC claim state in pv_controller can trigger premature volume deletion

In `pv_controller` (`isVolumeReleased` in `pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller.go:1382`), the controller inspects the local informer claim cache (`ctrl.claims.Get(claimName)`) to verify if a claim bound to a PV is released before marking the volume released or performing volume cleanup.

**Race Window:**
If a claim state changes or is updated in the API server, but the local informer cache experiences watch delay, `pv_controller` reads stale claim state from its cache and can proceed to release or delete a persistent volume prematurely.

Before executing irreversible volume deletion or release actions, `pv_controller` should re-verify the live PVC object against the API server.

- #141891 (`pv_controller`: revalidate claim live before deleting released volume)

Informer cache lag on out-of-service taint causes premature force deletion / volume detachment

Controllers handling `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taints (`podgc` and `attachdetach`) rely on local informer caches (`nodeLister`) to inspect Node objects before executing non-reversible force operations (e.g., force-deleting terminating pods or force-detaching volumes):
- `podgc`: `pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go:127`
- `attachdetach`: `pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go:148` (`hasOutOfServiceTaint` → `rc.nodeLister.Get`)

**Race Window:**
Taint is removed in the API server (or node becomes Ready again) → watch event is delayed / not yet delivered to local informer store → controller reads stale node from cache → force-deletes pod or force-detaches volume.

This violates the safety guarantee of `out-of-service` taints and can produce split-brain scenarios (two running instances of the same pod on different nodes).

Before executing force deletion or force detachment authorized by out-of-service taints, the controller should re-verify the live Node object against the API server to ensure the `out-of-service` taint is still active.

- #141887 (`podgc`: revalidate node out-of-service taint live before force deleting)
- #141888 (`attachdetach`: revalidate out-of-service taint live before force detaching)

WAS: Gang-scheduled Job never completes if an index pod fails after another index has completed

The Indexed Job using `spec.scheduling.schedulingPolicy.gang` never finishes if any index's pod terminates after at least one other index has completed. The replacement pod is created but never scheduled.

The scheduler's pod informer excludes Succeeded/Failed pods, so completed members leave the PodGroup state (cache.removePod → removePodGroupMember). The gang plugin's PreEnqueue gate then rejects the replacement with waiting for minCount pods from a gang to appear in scheduling queue because `AllPodsCount() < minCount`, and nothing re-admits it.

The only requeue hints are a new group pod or a minCount change. The Job controller never lowers minCount as indexes complete (`syncGangMinCount` derives it from `spec.parallelism` only).

**Impact**
Any gang Job whose indexes finish at different times and then loses a pod (crash, eviction, node loss). Only exits are activeDeadlineSeconds or a manual minCount patch. This will eventually block kubernetes-sigs/kueue#13715 defaulting gang on managed Jobs.

The replacement schedules and the Job completes.

- Scheduler side: I added a new table entry in `TestPodGroupScheduling` to admit a gang of 3 (minCount: 3), UpdatePodStatus two members to Succeeded and one to Failed, and then create a replacement in the same PodGroup, WaitForPodsScheduled on it. The test times out after 30s with no scheduling attempt. (planning to add this test to the KEP update PR for beta https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6345).
- Job controller side: Verified by tracing the code. One PodGroup per Job, recreated indexes reference it, minCount unchanged.

In `syncGangMinCount`, when `minCount` was defaulted rather than user-set, use `max(1, parallelism - status.Succeeded)`. After the first completion the threshold tracks remaining work. This is controller-only and is not blocked on #136334.

Open point for review: a user-set `minCount` is left alone. A user who sets it on an Indexed Job will still hit this after the first completion. Weather documenting that vs clamping user-set values too, is the sig-apps call.

Note: Add the scheduler-side test case from the reproduction of this issue to kubernetes/enhancements#6345. This is in additon to Job-controller integration test asserting `minCount` drops as indexes succeed.

Originally listed here as the long-term fix via #136334. Per the WG Workload-Aware Scheduling meeting on 2026-09-24, that work is split:

- `PodGroupSatisfied` condition (`NeverSatisfied` / `Healthy` / `Degraded`) proceeds under #136334.
- The `minAvailable` threshold is deferred. The WG position is that a floor the group must not drop below is a disruption-policy concept, not a `GangSchedulingPolicy` field, and needs its own KEP after the disruption-mode design settles.

Neither piece changes the fix above. Revised design note: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wnV7XGWjt0pwDH_d67qvYxCtse5R_ZZylPxMHIJuOys/edit?tab=t.0

Pod inside its startup period becomes Ready after a kubelet restart

A container still in its startup period is NotReady, as expected. Restart the kubelet on that node and the pod goes Ready within a few seconds, without the startup probe ever succeeding, and it stays Ready.

`isContainerStarted` looks up the probe workers to tell whether a container has a startup probe. `SyncPod` builds the pod status before it calls `AddPod`, so right after a kubelet restart there is no worker yet and the container is marked started. That value is kept across syncs and `worker.doProbe` stops probing once it is set, so nothing puts it back.

With a readiness probe the pod stays NotReady, but the startup gate opens and the liveness probe starts running against a container that is still warming up.

Opened #142303 with a fix.

The pod stays NotReady until the startup probe succeeds. Restarting the kubelet should not change whether a container counts as started.

Create a pod with a startup probe that keeps failing and no readiness probe:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: slow-start
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    startupProbe:
[... 4 more lines]
```

Once it is running:

```
$ kubectl get pod slow-start -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'
false
```

Restart the kubelet on that node, wait a few seconds, then check again:

```
$ kubectl get pod slow-start -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'
true

$ kubectl get pod slow-start
NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
slow-start   1/1     Running   0          5m
```

The startup probe is not run again after this.
