[Feature][scheduler] Asynchronously or concurrently update (Composite)PodGroup status conditions to avoid scheduling cycle head-of-line blocking

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140670, status condition updates for `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` were integrated into the scheduler pipeline.
Currently, in `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go`), status updates for every group within a hierarchy are performed sequentially and synchronously on the main scheduling goroutine:
```
for _, podGroupResult := range podGroupResults {
    pgi := podGroupResult.podGroupInfo
    if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil {
        sched.submitCompositePodGroupResult(ctx, podGroupResult)
        continue
    }
    queuedPodInfos := rootPodGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos[pgi.GetKey()]
    sched.submitPodGroupResult(ctx, schedFwk, podGroupState, queuedPodInfos, podGroupResult)
}
```
Each call to `submitCompositePodGroupResult` / `submitPodGroupResult` issues an individual, synchronous status patch request to the API server (`util.PatchPodGroupStatus` / `util.PatchCompositePodGroupStatus`).

For larger or deeper hierarchies containing multiple intermediate composite groups and leaf pod groups, issuing sequential synchronous HTTP patch calls directly on the scheduling thread:
- Multiplies scheduling cycle latency linearly by the number of groups in the subtree.
- Contributes to head-of-line (HoL) blocking in the active scheduling queue, as the scheduler cannot pick up the next queued workload until all status updates complete.

- **Asynchronous dispatch**: Offload status patching to background goroutines (similar to `sched.runBindingCycle`) or a dedicated worker queue so the main scheduling goroutine can immediately proceed to the next cycle.
- **Concurrent patching**: If status updates must be bounded or completed within the cycle, patch group statuses concurrently (e.g., using an `errgroup` or bounded worker pool) rather than strictly sequentially.

GetDiskFormat in k8s.io/mount-utils returns ("", nil) for unreadable devices, leading callers to destructive mkfs

`GetDiskFormat` in the staging repo `k8s.io/mount-utils` (staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils/mount_linux.go) shells out to
`blkid -p -s TYPE -s PTTYPE -o export <disk>` and maps **exit code 2** to `("", nil)` ("disk is unformatted").

However, blkid also exits with code 2 when the device node **exists but its data cannot be read** (e.g. the storage backend is temporarily unavailable). As a result, `GetDiskFormat` returns the exact same result for two very
different situations:

1. A genuinely blank disk → `("", nil)` (expected)
2. An existing device with data whose data path is currently unreadable → `("", nil)` (misleading)

Any caller that uses an empty format to decide whether to initialize/format a device cannot distinguish the two cases.

Real-world impact: in Longhorn (a CNCF storage system using mount-utils via the CSI stack), this caused NodeStageVolume to attempt `mkfs.xfs` on existing volumes containing user data, because blkid probed them as unformatted while the engine data path was temporarily broken. The formatting only failed because mkfs itself hit read errors, so data loss was avoided by luck, not by design.
See longhorn/longhorn#14042 for the full incident log.

Relevant code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils/mount_linux.go#L667-L686

```
if err != nil {
    if exit, ok := err.(utilexec.ExitError); ok {
        if exit.ExitStatus() == 2 {
            // Disk device is unformatted.
            return "", nil
        }
    }
    ...
}
```
Impact: Potential Data Loss
This bug creates a data-loss window. If the underlying data path recovers between filesystem detection and the formatting operation, mkfs.xfs -f may succeed and overwrite existing filesystem metadata, resulting in permanent data loss.

`GetDiskFormat` should distinguish a blank disk from an unreadable device, for example:

- Perform a small read (e.g. first 4 KiB) on the device when blkid reports no filesystem, and return an error if the read fails, or
- Inspect blkid's stderr/exit-code semantics more precisely so that read failures are not reported as "unformatted".

Using the scsi_debug module to create a device whose reads fail:

```
# 1. Create a scsi debug device that fails READ commands (error=3: medium error)
modprobe scsi_debug dev_size_mb=16 every_nth=1 opts=2

DEV=$(ls -d /sys/bus/pseudo/drivers/scsi_debug/adapter*/host*/target*/*/block/* | xargs -n1 basename)
echo "Device: /dev/$DEV"

# 2. blkid behaves identically to a blank disk
blkid -p -s TYPE -s PTTYPE -o export /dev/$DEV
# → no output, exit code 2 (same as a zeroed blank disk)

[... 3 more lines]
```

A consumer calling `GetDiskFormat("/dev/$DEV")` receives `("", nil)`, so it will take the "unformatted disk" path although the device is not readable.
A zeroed blank disk returns the identical value.

(Any other way of producing an unreadable block device, e.g.
device-mapper `error` target, reproduces the same behavior.)

- The same `("", nil)` result is also produced for **non-block files**
  (e.g. an empty regular file), which is how the behavior was verified
  without kernel modules.
- Longhorn has worked around this at the CSI layer by re-verifying device
  readability before entering the formatting path
  (longhorn/longhorn#14042), but other in-tree and out-of-tree consumers
  of mount-utils remain exposed.
- Happy to submit a PR once the maintainers agree on the desired semantics.

Kubelet OOM score calculation collapses to 999 for small/medium containers on large-memory nodes and ignores per-container memory guarantees

This bug description was assisted by AI.

Update `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` in `pkg/kubelet/qos/policy.go` for `Burstable` QoS containers (guarded behind a new Kubelet feature gate) to fix precision collapse on large-memory nodes and recognize per-container memory guarantees:

1. **Replace linear node-capacity division with logarithmic scaling (`log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C)`)** so container memory requests (`R`) across multiple orders of magnitude maintain distinct `oom_score_adj` values on large nodes (1 TiB to 4 TiB+).
2. **Incorporate per-container memory guarantee ratio (`R / L`)** so "memory-guaranteed" containers (`memory.requests == memory.limits`, such as orchestrators or control agents) receive lower OOM score adjustments than containers configured to overcommit/burst far above their requests (`R << L` or unlimited).
3. **Reserve a safety gap between maximum `Burstable` baseline (`800`) and `BestEffort` (`1000`)** so mild bursts do not immediately invert kill priority against `BestEffort` workloads.
4. **Gate behind a Feature Gate** so operators can roll out or revert to the legacy calculation without risk.

Currently, `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` computes `oom_score_adj` for `Burstable` containers as:

```
oom_score_adj = 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequest) / memoryCapacity
```

clamped to `[3, 999]`, while the Linux kernel calculates process badness points as:

```
points = oom_score_adj + (usage_bytes * 1000) / memoryCapacity
```

When this heuristic was written in 2015, nodes typically had 4 GiB–64 GiB of RAM. On modern 1 TiB–4 TiB nodes running microservices, this formula breaks down in three ways:

Because the formula divides by `memoryCapacity` in integer arithmetic across 1000 buckets, any container requesting less than `memoryCapacity / 1000` evaluates to:

```
(1000 * memoryRequest) / memoryCapacity == 0  =>  oom_score_adj = 999
```

* On a **1 TiB (1024 GiB)** node, every container requesting **< 1.024 GiB** gets `oom_score_adj = 999`. A container requesting 50 MiB, 256 MiB, or 1 GiB receives the exact same score (`999`).
* On a **4 TiB** node, every container requesting **< 4.096 GiB** gets `oom_score_adj = 999`.
* Note: While #111356 observed this symptom and PR #128029 mitigated native sidecars by copying the minimum score of regular containers, regular containers themselves still collapse to `999` on large nodes (making the sidecar adjustment a no-op as well).

Because Kubernetes QoS is evaluated at the Pod level across both CPU and memory, a container that explicitly sets `memory.requests == memory.limits` (zero memory overcommit) is forced into `Burstable` QoS whenever:
* The Pod has another container that is burstable (e.g., an **Orchestrator + Executor** Pod), or
* CPU limits are unset or differ from CPU requests (previously noted in #78848).

Consider a `Burstable` Pod on a 1 TiB node with two containers:
* **Orchestrator (`O`):** `request = 500 MiB`, `limit = 500 MiB` (`R / L = 1.0`, memory-guaranteed). Steady usage = `200 MiB`.
* **Executor (`E`):** `request = 500 MiB`, `limit = 32 GiB` (`R / L = 0.015`, burst-heavy). Spikes to `1.5 GiB` (3x request).

Under the current formula:
* `oom_score_adj(O) = 999` => `points(O) = 999 + (0.2 / 1024) * 1000 = 999.2`
* `oom_score_adj(E) = 999` => `points(E) = 999 + (1.5 / 1024) * 1000 = 1000.5`

The kernel badness score between a memory-guaranteed orchestrator using 40% of its request and an executor bursting 300% over its request differs by **only 1 point**. If the executor spawns multiple worker processes, each worker process has fewer kernel points than the orchestrator, causing the kernel OOM killer to kill the orchestrator first.

Because small `Burstable` containers get `oom_score_adj = 999` and `BestEffort` containers get `1000`, the baseline margin is only **1 point** (0.1% of host RAM). On a 1 TiB node, a `Burstable` container exceeding its request by 1.1 GiB reaches score `1000.1`, making it more likely to be killed than an unreserved `BestEffort` container.

---

Replace the linear formula for `Burstable` containers with a two-factor formula combining **per-container memory guarantee ratio (`R / L`)** and **logarithmic request sizing (`log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C)`)**, anchored at a baseline of `800`:

```
oom_score_adj = 800 - 400 * (R / L) - 350 * (log2(1 + R) / log2(1 + C))
```

Where:
* `R` = effective container memory request (including pod-level / DRA share if enabled)
* `C` = node memory capacity
* `L` = effective container memory limit (if unset or `> C`, `L = C`)
* Result is clamped to `[3, 999]` (with sidecar clamping preserved).

In Go, integer `floor(log2(x)) + 1` can be computed in a single instruction via `math/bits.Len64(uint64(x))` without floating-point arithmetic.

---

| Workload Spec (`Request / Limit`) | Current `oom_score_adj` | Proposed `oom_score_adj` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| `50 MiB / 50 MiB` (Small Orchestrator) | `999` | **`176`** |
| `500 MiB / 500 MiB` (Std Orchestrator) | `999` | **`147`** |
| `500 MiB / 32 GiB` (Spiky Executor) | `999` | **`541`** |
| `500 MiB / unset` (Unbounded Worker) | `999` | **`547`** |
| `4 GiB / 8 GiB` (Medium Service) | `996` | **`320`** |
| `64 GiB / 64 GiB` (Large Database) | `938` | **`85`** |
| `500 GiB / 500 GiB` (Huge Database) | `512` | **`59`** |
| BestEffort (`0 / 0`) | `1000` | **`1000`** |

| Workload Spec (`Request / Limit`) | Current `oom_score_adj` | Proposed `oom_score_adj` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| `50 MiB / 50 MiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `997` | **`137`** |
| `500 MiB / 500 MiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `970` | **`103`** |
| `500 MiB / 4 GiB` (Bursty) | `970` | **`454`** |
| `2 GiB / 2 GiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `875` | **`81`** |
| `12 GiB / 12 GiB` (Memory-Guaranteed) | `250` | **`54`** |
| BestEffort (`0 / 0`) | `1000` | **`1000`** |

---

* **Feature Gate Protection:** The updated calculation in `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` will be guarded behind a Kubelet feature gate, allowing safe rollout and immediate fallback to the legacy formula if needed.
* **No Semantic or API Changes:** This change does not alter any Kubernetes API, CRI protocol, or documented QoS contract:
  * The strict ordering `Guaranteed` (`-997`) < `Burstable` (`[3, 999]`) < `BestEffort` (`1000`) is preserved.
  * Within `Burstable`, the documented intent—that containers reserving more memory and staying within their bounds are protected over containers consuming memory beyond their requests—is unchanged and preserved on small nodes, while fixing the integer truncation bug where containers collapse to `999` on large nodes.
  * Prior refinements to `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` (such as PR #128029 for sidecars) followed the same path without requiring a standalone KEP.

API Server Write Throughput: Address Allocation Ceiling and Degraded State Bottlenecks

Based on recent experiments with API server write throughput, we propose a multi-pronged effort to address severe allocation bottlenecks.

**1. Optimize the "Happy Path"**
* **Reduce PATCH Allocations:** Significantly reduce allocations for the PATCH path . Specifically, target `managedFields` patching and SSA tracking, which currently account for over half of allocations. Tracked in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142228
* **Storage Bytes Passthrough**: Provide safeguards allowing us to safely pass through objects serialized in etcd to clients. Tracked as part of KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6407

**2. Optimize the "Bad Path" (Degraded States)**
* **Resilient Watch Propagation:** Implement https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6268 to prevent watch breaking due to temporary CPU/network blips by allowing unsynchronized watchers to reread from cached objects.
* **Direct Watch Cache Reads for Informers:** Replace API server admission informers with Listers that read directly from the watch cache. This removes a heavy source of allocations while halving the memory needed by the API server. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142304
* **Serve All Gets from Cache:** Ensure all Gets are served from the cache (including Gets triggered by TXN conflicts). This makes load on etcd and allocations much more predictable by removing a costly fallback. Tracked as part of KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6407

While most of these improvements are optimizations, "Serve all Gets from cache" may require a KEP update. The main risk is lock contention; however, thanks to the major rewrites of the watch cache in 1.37, we have removed almost all copying from under the lock and now rely on immutable btree snapshots to efficiently scale reads.

Would like to get feedback on what is KEP worthy.

Implementing all those improvements allowed us reduce the allocation factor of API server from 100-180x to stable 50x and achieve over 4k QPS stable QPS on 30KB pods using single c4-standard-144 machine running kind cluster. Around that point we stopped seeing improvements from reducing allocations. Next stop: watch cache.

Following the SIG Scalability proposals to introduce Resource Size as a new dimension (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375) and establish a realistic "Pod Shape" (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415), we have updated the list benchmark https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-scalability-benchmarks#gce-benchmark-list and introduced new write throughput benchmarks https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-scalability-benchmarks#gce-benchmark-write-throughput using this new pod shape.

While investigating the bottlenecks in the write throughput benchmark (with help from @Jefftree), we identified the primary limiting factor: **Allocations**.

**The API server allocates over 1MB of memory to apply a trivial patch on a 10KB pod object. This is a >100x allocation factor on the *happy path*** (which includes storing it in etcd, observing on watch, storing in the watch cache, and propagating to 10-20 watchers).

During our investigation, we discovered that the Go runtime hits a hard ceiling around 6GB/s of memory allocations on a `c4-highmem-144` machine. At this ceiling, CAS operations during the GC sweep phase start burning >50% of the CPU, fully saturating the node. We are in contact with the Go team to reproduce this behavior. In the meantime, tuning the garbage collector (`GOGC=400`) provided some relief, allowing us to hit allocation rates above 11GB/s, but a fundamental fix in the API server is still necessary.

The >100x allocation factor only accounts for the happy path. On any short disruption (e.g., watch breaks, transaction conflicts), the API server enters a degraded state:
* Watch breaking prevents the watch cache serialization cache from working
* Built into API server admission policy informer can quickly start relisting
* Conflicting TXNs cause the API server to fetch objects directly from etcd and decode them

In each these scenarios, **allocations easily double, turning a short disruption into a persistent, sticky degradation.**

Hitting this allocation ceiling causes a sticky degradation that requires lowering the throughput by a factor of 2x-3x before the API server can recover. Consequently, improving QPS is only sustainable if the increase is gradual (<10% at a time) and at a steady state. Any burst immediately pushes the API server into a degraded state.

Only by systematically addressing these degradation factors can we achieve a robust state where the API server can instantly jump to max QPS and reliably recover from bursts.

Kubelet omits volume stats after all pod container cgroups are removed

The kubelet's cAdvisor stats provider can omit a Running pod's mounted volume stats after cAdvisor has removed every pod-managed container record.

PR #142249 preserves volume stats when all container samples are filtered as terminated, but `ListPodStats` still builds its pod map from cAdvisor records carrying pod labels. If every container cgroup has already been garbage-collected and cAdvisor reports only the unlabeled pod-level cgroup, the provider cannot build a `PodReference`. The pod and its cached volume stats are therefore absent from the Summary API and from `kubelet_volume_stats_*`.

A Running pod should retain cached stats for its mounted volumes while the kubelet still knows the pod and the resource analyzer still has volume data, even when no pod-managed container cgroup remains.

At the unit-test level:

1. Have the pod manager return a Running pod with a valid start time.
2. Have the resource analyzer return cached persistent volume stats for that pod.
3. Have cAdvisor return the root cgroup and the pod-level cgroup, with no labeled container records.
4. Call the cAdvisor provider's `ListPodStats`.

The current provider returns an empty pod list. A focused regression test fails with:

```
"[]" should have 1 item(s), but has 0
```

Use the kubelet pod manager as the fallback source of pod identity when cAdvisor has no labeled container record. Only seed a missing pod when cached volume stats exist, then apply the existing start-time and Running-phase validation before returning it.

This is a follow-up to #141350 and #142249.

Pod-level limit defaulting is skipped for pods that have an ephemeral container

With `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting` enabled, `DefaultPodLevelResources` defaults pod-level limits from the aggregated container limits when every container specifies a limit for that resource. The function deliberately builds the pod it aggregates from `Containers` and `InitContainers` only, and says so:

> Ephemeral containers are excluded here as they cannot specify resources and do not contribute to QoS or pod-level resource defaulting.

But the candidate filtering in `aggregateContainerLimits` walks the spec with `VisitContainers(spec, AllContainers, ...)`, and `AllContainers` includes `EphemeralContainers`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/pkg/api/pod/util.go#L2419-L2429

An ephemeral container can never carry a limit (`resources` is not an allowed ephemeral container field), so visiting one deletes every candidate resource and pod-level limit defaulting silently becomes a no-op for that pod.

Ephemeral containers cannot be present on create, so this shows up on the `/resize` path (`podResizeStrategy.PrepareForUpdate` calls `DefaultPodLevelResources`): after `kubectl debug` has attached an ephemeral container, a resize that adds a pod-level request no longer gets the pod-level limit defaulted, whereas the identical resize on the same pod before debugging does. The pod ends up with different effective pod-level limits depending on whether it was ever debugged.

Ephemeral containers do not affect pod-level limit defaulting, as the comment in `DefaultPodLevelResources` states. The resize result should not depend on whether an ephemeral container exists.

Unit level (both feature gates on): a pod with container `c1` requesting `cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi` with limits `cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi`, and `spec.resources.requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}`.

- Without an ephemeral container, `DefaultPodLevelResources` sets `spec.resources.limits` to `{cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}` (this is the existing "single container limit defaulting" test case in `pkg/registry/core/pod/strategy_test.go`).
- With `spec.ephemeralContainers: [{name: debugger, image: busybox}]` added, `spec.resources.limits` stays unset.

A regression test that fails against the `v1.37.0` tag is in the linked PR.

End to end, on a cluster with the two gates enabled and `InPlacePodVerticalScaling`:

```
$ kubectl run app --image=busybox --requests=cpu=100m,memory=128Mi --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi -- sleep 3600
$ kubectl debug -it app --image=busybox -- true          # attaches an ephemeral container
$ kubectl patch pod app --subresource resize -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"}}}}'
$ kubectl get pod app -o jsonpath='{.spec.resources}'
{"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"}}          # no limits defaulted
```

The same resize on a pod that was never debugged yields `{"limits":{"cpu":"200m","memory":"256Mi"},"requests":{...}}`.

Introduced with pod-level limit defaulting in f8cb15ce549 (v1.37). PR to follow: visit `InitContainers|Containers` in `aggregateContainerLimits`, matching the comment and the pod that is actually aggregated.

Eviction of healthy pods does not pin pod ResourceVersion between PDB check and Delete

Hi, I hit a race in the eviction path on master. I've checked the healthy-pod delete block here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3551fa84d739d7e0ceb1954025d61c43e504e97f/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L291-L305

```
// pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go (L291-L305, master @ 3551fa8)
deleteOptions := originalDeleteOptions

// Set deleteOptions.Preconditions.ResourceVersion to ensure
// the pod hasn't been considered healthy (ready) since we calculated
if updateDeletionOptions {
    // Take a copy so we can compare to client-provied Options later.
    deleteOptions = deleteOptions.DeepCopy()
    setPreconditionsResourceVersion(deleteOptions, &pod.ResourceVersion)
}
[... 3 more lines]
```

Root cause: `updateDeletionOptions` is only set to `true` inside the `!podutil.IsPodReady(pod)` branch (unhealthy cases). The healthy-pod path that just passed `checkAndDecrement` falls through with it still `false`, so the guard above is skipped and `deleteOptions` stays as `originalDeleteOptions` with no RV precondition when it hits `Delete`.

What that means:
1. Pod is Running and Ready, covered by PDB with `disruptionsAllowed=1`.
2. `POST /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/foo/eviction` passes `checkAndDecrement`.
3. Before the delete, the PDB is tightened to `disruptionsAllowed=0` or the pod changes.
4. Delete still succeeds because there's no RV pin. It allows one excess disruption.

The unhealthy path already does `DeepCopy + setPreconditionsResourceVersion(pod.RV)`. I'd copy that pattern to the healthy path too and re-fetch on conflict.

Doesn't need a KEP, it's a small fix in `Create`. Happy to put up a PR if you agree with the approach.

[HPA] ReplicaCalculator evaluates unactuated pod.spec instead of pod.status during In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling

In `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go`, `ReplicaCalculator` evaluates pod and container resource requests strictly from `pod.spec`:
- In [`calculatePodRequestsFromContainers`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L510-L536): reads directly from `container.Resources.Requests[resource]` in `pod.Spec.Containers`.
- In [`calculatePodLevelRequests`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L498-L505): invokes `resourcehelpers.PodRequests(pod, resourcehelpers.PodResourcesOptions{})` where `UseStatusResources` and `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScalingEnabled` default to `false`, reading directly from `pod.Spec.Resources.Requests`.
When a workload undergoes **In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling** ([KEP-1287](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/1287-in-place-update-pod-resources) / [KEP-2837](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2837-pod-level-resource-spec)), `pod.spec` requests are mutated immediately by the user or an autoscaler (e.g. VPA), but physical capacity actuation via Kubelet cgroups is asynchronous. The capacity currently running on the node is reported under `pod.status.containerStatuses[*].resources` and `pod.status.resources`.
Evaluating HPA utilization strictly against `pod.spec` during in-flight or failed resizes leads to severe recommendation skew:
1. **Scale-Up (Request Increase):** When requests are increased (e.g., CPU request 1 core $\to$ 4 cores), the denominator jumps immediately to 4 cores before Kubelet accommodates the resize. HPA divides actual usage (e.g., 0.9 cores) by 4 cores instead of 1 core, artificially collapsing calculated utilization from $90\%$ to $22.5\%$. This can cause HPA to trigger premature **scale-in** (reducing replicas) while the application is under heavy load.
2. **Scale-Down (Request Decrease):** The denominator drops immediately to the lower value before cgroups are throttled. This creates an artificial utilization spike, prompting HPA to trigger unnecessary horizontal **scale-out**.
3. **Infeasible Resizes (`PodResizePending: Infeasible`):** If the node cannot accommodate the resize, `pod.spec` remains updated with the unreachable requested value while the pod permanently runs with the original allocated resources. HPA calculations remain permanently distorted.

During in-flight in-place vertical scaling, HPA should evaluate the request baseline using the capacity actually provisioned on the node (`pod.status`), ensuring:
- Workloads scaling up vertically do not trigger premature horizontal downscales before node capacity is allocated.
- Infeasible resizes continue to scale horizontally based on actual running capacity rather than the unfulfilled spec.

1. Deploy a workload targeting CPU utilization with an HPA (target 80%).
2. Generate load such that the pod consumes ~0.9 cores against an initial request of 1 core (90% utilization $\to$ scale-out pending).
3. Trigger an in-place pod resize updating `spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu` from `1` to `4` (or `pod.spec.resources.requests.cpu`).
4. While Kubelet is resizing (or if the resize is blocked / marked `Infeasible` due to node capacity), observe HPA's calculated utilization:
   - **Observed:** HPA divides current usage (`0.9`) by `4` ($22.5\%$), cancelling scale-out and recommending scale-in.
   - **Expected:** HPA should evaluate usage against the actuated capacity reported in `status` until Kubelet finishes resizing.

Relevant code references:
- Container-level request summation: [`calculatePodRequestsFromContainers`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L510-L536)
- Pod-level request calculation: [`calculatePodLevelRequests`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L498-L505)
- Component helper logic:
  - [`PodRequests`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go#L152-L173)
  - [`AggregateContainerRequests`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16f2372dd50524c61f7bd752315c5ecb8490ef9e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go#L295-L335)

Reusing component-helpers' `PodRequests` for HPA inherits `determineEffectiveRequests`, which was designed for node scheduler reservations. It works well for scale-down and infeasible resizes, for HPA scale-up it causes the denominator to jump immediately to desired spec before node actuation, leading to premature horizontal scale-in.

[Declarative Validation] Support config-driven custom formats and named validations

Downstream consumers of Declarative Validation (e.g., Substrate) need a low-friction way to define reusable custom formats (like URI) and named validations. Today, `+k8s:customValidation` requires writing a separate wrapper function for every field, and we want to avoid maintaining custom `validation-gen` binaries due to upstream drift.

Add a flag to `validation-gen` (e.g., `--validator-definitions=<config.yaml>` or `--custom-validators`; discussed conceptually as a "profile", though `--profile` collides with `kubectl --profile` pprof flags) to load custom validation definitions at codegen time:
- **Custom Formats**: Defined via regex, custom error message, and optional min/max length (or a shared Go function).
- **Named Validations**: Mapped directly to reusable Go functions or CEL expressions without per-field wrapper boilerplate.
- **Typo Safety**: `validation-gen` fails at codegen time if a tag references an unregistered format or rule name.

*(Note: Continue using `+k8s:customValidation` as a workaround in the meantime.)*

Eliminate the usage of empty/short secrets for `ComputeDetachedSignature()` for kubeadm/cluster-bootstrap operations

As part of the review process for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142012 we found that existing secrets for computing detached signatures using https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/467cf7b5cb246a95604681915f3b84f538c0110b/staging/src/k8s.io/cluster-bootstrap/token/jws/jws.go#L29 are not long-enough to satisfy the requirement that secrets for HS256 signatures must be at least 32 bytes in length as per https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7518#section-3.2

This issue is spun out of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142012 to be tracked as follow-up work.

OIDC token authenticator should expire cached JWKs based on server-provided cache headers

During the review process of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142012 we found that JWKs don't have an expiration associated with them, meaning that there is no mechanism for a JWK publisher to indicate a maximum time in which that JWK data should remain valid before needing a cache refresh.

This issue is spun out of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142012 for this to be tracked as a follow-up.

resource quota controller leaks informer event handlers when a monitored resource is removed

The resource quota controller's `QuotaMonitor` registers an event handler on the shared informer for every monitored resource (`pkg/controller/resourcequota/resource_quota_monitor.go`, `controllerFor`), but when a monitor is torn down in `SyncMonitors` (and on shutdown) it only stops the monitor — it never removes the handler:

```
_, _ = shared.Informer().AddEventHandlerWithOptions(handlers, ...) // registration discarded
```

The informer factory caches informers per resource, so the informer outlives the monitor. When a resource such as a CRD is deleted and later recreated with the same `GroupVersionResource`, a new handler is added to the same cached informer each time and the old ones are never removed. On a started informer every handler is a `processorListener` with its own goroutines, so the handlers (and their goroutines) accumulate and kube-controller-manager memory grows.

This is the same class of bug as the garbage collector's graph builder (#114066); the quota monitor's `controllerFor` was copied from it and has the identical omission.

Removing a monitored resource should also remove its event handler from the shared informer; repeatedly adding and removing the same resource should not leak handlers.

Run kube-controller-manager with `--controllers=resourcequota` and repeatedly create and delete a set of CRDs, watching the informer's per-handler goroutines (`k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache.(*processorListener).run`/`.pop`) via `/debug/pprof/goroutine`. Create 40 CRDs, wait for the quota monitor sync, delete them, repeat.

On a kind cluster (processorListener goroutines):

| step | count |
|------|-------|
| baseline | 66 |
| after creating 40 CRDs | 146 (+80) |
| after deleting them | 146 (not released — leak) |

With the handler removed on teardown the count returns to 66 after deletion.

The fix follows the same approach used for the garbage collector: store the informer and the handler registration on the monitor and call `RemoveEventHandler` on teardown (in `SyncMonitors` and on shutdown). A unit-level regression test (a counting fake informer asserting no net handlers remain after add/remove cycles) is included in the PR.

kube-proxy iptables: nfacct probe doesn't cover xt_nfacct match, all syncs fail

kube-proxy in **iptables mode** decides whether to emit `-m nfacct --nfacct-name ...` rules based only on a probe of the **nfacct netlink subsystem** (`nfnetlink_acct`, kernel option `CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_ACCT`). It never checks that the **iptables `nfacct` match extension** (`xt_nfacct`, kernel option `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_NFACCT`) is usable.

On a kernel that has the first but not the second, the probe passes, the two counters are created successfully over netlink, and every generated ruleset contains `-m nfacct` rules. `iptables-restore` is all-or-nothing, so the **entire filter+nat restore fails on every sync**, and the node ends up with **no Service rules at all** (no `KUBE-SERVICES` jump, no ClusterIP/NodePort DNAT). kube-proxy keeps running and reporting healthy to `kubectl`, retrying the identical (still failing) restore every `syncPeriod`.

Observed on an arm64 embedded vendor kernel (5.10 series) where `CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_ACCT` is enabled but `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_NFACCT` is not set (`modinfo xt_nfacct` -> not found). Symptoms on that node: every pod that talks to a ClusterIP (`dial tcp <kube-apiserver ClusterIP>:443: i/o timeout`), CoreDNS / metrics-server crash-looping, namespace deletion hanging on the metrics APIService. Pods with `hostNetwork: true` were unaffected, which made it look like a CNI problem at first. The only kube-proxy log line is:

```
"Failed to execute iptables-restore" err=<...>
```

(with iptables-legacy the reported failing line is the table's `COMMIT` line, so the 3 lines of context that get logged do not even show the `-m nfacct` rule - see below.)

The workaround we ended up with is backwards: **blacklist `nfnetlink_acct`** (`install nfnetlink_acct /bin/false` + `rmmod`) so that `nfacct.New()` fails and the documented fallback ("Failed to create nfacct runner, nfacct based metrics won't be available") kicks in. Removing a working kernel feature to make kube-proxy work is not something a user should have to discover.

Either of:

- kube-proxy detects that the `nfacct` iptables match is unavailable and falls back to the same behaviour as when the netlink subsystem is missing: skip the `-m nfacct` rules, keep programming Services, log once that the two nfacct-based metrics are disabled; or
- at minimum, when a restore fails while nfacct rules are enabled, kube-proxy retries **without** them instead of leaving the node with zero Service rules forever.

The nfacct rules exist only to feed two metrics (`kubeproxy_iptables_ct_state_invalid_dropped_packets_total` and `kubeproxy_iptables_localhost_nodeports_accepted_packets_total`). Losing those metrics is vastly preferable to losing all Service networking on the node.

On any Linux node where `xt_nfacct` is built as a **module** (most distro kernels), running kube-proxy in iptables mode (`--proxy-mode=iptables`, default `conntrackTCPLiberal=false` so the `KUBE-FORWARD ... --ctstate INVALID` rule is emitted):

```
# make the iptables nfacct match unavailable, but leave the netlink subsystem alone
modprobe -r xt_nfacct
echo 'install xt_nfacct /bin/false' > /etc/modprobe.d/no-xt-nfacct.conf
# sanity: netlink side still works (this is all kube-proxy probes)
nfacct add probe_ok && nfacct list && nfacct del probe_ok

# restart kube-proxy on that node, then:
iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SERVICES      # -> "No chain/target/match by that name" / chain never populated
kubectl -n kube-system logs <kube-proxy-pod> | grep -i "iptables-restore"
curl -m3 https://<kube-apiserver ClusterIP>:443   # from a non-hostNetwork pod on that node -> timeout
```

kube-proxy logs `"Failed to execute iptables-restore"` on every sync and `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_iptables_restore_failures_total` climbs, but the pod stays Running/Ready.

What `iptables-restore` actually returns in this situation (checked by hand with a ruleset containing one `-m nfacct --nfacct-name <counter>` rule that the kernel cannot satisfy; iptables 1.8.10):

```
# legacy backend: the failing line is the COMMIT line of the table, not the rule
iptables-restore: line 4 failed

# nf_tables backend
iptables-nft-restore v1.8.10 (nf_tables):
line 3: RULE_APPEND failed (No such file or directory): rule in chain TESTNF
```

To blame the missing match rather than a missing counter object, create the counter first (`nfacct add <name>`) - kube-proxy does this in `syncProxyRules` before generating the rules; on a kernel that *has* `xt_nfacct` the same restore then succeeds in both backends.

Code on master @ `d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7` (all in `pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go` unless noted):

1. [`NewProxier` L257-259](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L257-L259): `nfacct.New()`; on error the runner is nil and the fallback message is logged.
2. [`nfacct_linux.go` `New()` L66-84](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/util/nfacct/nfacct_linux.go#L66-L84): the only capability check is a netlink `NFNL_MSG_ACCT_GET` for a dummy counter over `NETLINK_NETFILTER`. Nothing here (or anywhere else) exercises the iptables `nfacct` match.
3. [`syncProxyRules` L702-711](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L702-L711): `nfacct.Ensure(name)` for both counters; on success `nfAcctCounters[name] = true`. This succeeds on the affected kernel because `nfnetlink_acct` is present.
4. [L1015-1023](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1015-L1023) (localhost NodePort accept rule) and [L1326-1330](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1326-L1330) (`KUBE-FORWARD --ctstate INVALID ... DROP`) append `-m nfacct --nfacct-name <counter>` whenever the corresponding `nfAcctCounters` flag is true. The second rule is emitted on essentially every node (only `conntrackTCPLiberal=true` suppresses it), so the failure is unconditional.
5. [L1384-1394](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1384-L1394): the single `RestoreAll` covers both `*filter` and `*nat`; on error it logs, bumps `IPTablesRestoreFailuresTotal` and returns. The deferred block at [L657-670](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L657-L670) sets `needFullSync = true`, so the next sync regenerates the identical payload and fails identically. There is no fallback path and `nfAcctCounters` is never cleared.
6. [`pkg/util/iptables/iptables.go` `parseRestoreError` L588-612](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/pkg/util/iptables/iptables.go#L588-L612) only recognises `<cmd>: line N failed`. With the legacy backend `N` is the `COMMIT` line, so the context logged at L1387-1388 does not show the nfacct rule; with the nf_tables backend the message has extra colons and is not classified as a `ParseError` at all. So a fix cannot rely on "ParseError pointing at an `-m nfacct` line".

The nftables proxier (`pkg/proxy/nftables`) has no nfacct references and is unaffected.

Prior reports I could find are different failure modes: #126951 / #125866 / #126952 handle the case where the **netlink subsystem** is missing (that fallback works, and it is what the workaround above abuses); cri-o/cri-o#8270 was a kernel with **both** `CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_ACCT` and `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_NFACCT` unset, so the existing probe caught it. I found no issue or PR covering the split configuration (netlink present, match absent).

**Proposed fix** (happy to send a PR once maintainers pick a direction):

- **(a) Probe the match, not just the subsystem.** After `Ensure()` succeeds in `syncProxyRules` (a counter must exist for the match to load), run a one-time check that the iptables `nfacct` match works - e.g. add and immediately delete a rule such as `-m nfacct --nfacct-name <counter> -j RETURN` in the existing `KUBE-PROXY-CANARY` chain via `EnsureRule`/`DeleteRule`. If that fails, set both `nfAcctCounters` entries to false and log once ("iptables nfacct match unavailable; nfacct based metrics won't be available"). Cheap, backend-agnostic, and reuses the same fallback that already exists for the netlink case.
- **(b) Defensive fallback on restore failure.** In the `RestoreAll` error branch at L1385, if any `nfAcctCounters` flag is true, clear them all, log that nfacct rules are being disabled, and return (needFullSync is already set). The next sync then succeeds. This is a heuristic (it disables the metrics on *any* restore failure) but it guarantees a node never stays without Service rules because of an optional metric.

Doing (a) with (b) as a safety net seems reasonable. A unit test can drive either path with `FakeIPTables` returning an error for rules containing `-m nfacct` and asserting the following sync succeeds with no nfacct rules and both counters disabled.

kube-apiserver: the watch cache retains every object fully decoded, costing several times their serialized size

Some kind of fix so kube-apiserver does not consume unbounded memory when resources are added to K8S.

**Status:** hypothesis confirmed by measurement (see [Evidence](#evidence)).
**Affects:** `kube-apiserver` v1.35.5 (reported), reproduced on `master` @ `def9a441f5` (v1.38.0-alpha.0). The mechanism is unchanged between the two.
**Component:** `sig-api-machinery`, `k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher`

*Disclosure*

This RFE/REPORT was written in part with the assistance of generative AI (Claude Opus 5).

I'm not intimate with the K8S source code. But I've read this report and tweaked it so it aligns with what I do know.

- I *did not* test any proposed fix yet.
- I *did* test pruning resources on live data: that works.
- I *did* test the workaround using ``--watch-cache-sizes`` on live data: that seems to work and have no adverse effects.

When the watch cache is enabled (`--watch-cache=true`, the default), kube-apiserver keeps **every object of every cached resource resident in memory, fully decoded**, for the lifetime of the process.

Three properties combine to make this much more expensive than it looks:

1. **The stored representation is a decoded `runtime.Object`, not bytes.** For custom resources that is `*unstructured.Unstructured` — a `map[string]interface{}` tree — which costs **~5.2x** its serialized size on the Go heap.
2. **The cost is unconditional.** It is not proportional to the number of watchers, and it is not driven by watchers at all. One client request against a resource is enough to pin that resource's entire contents in RAM permanently.
3. **Asking for less does not get you less.** A client that requests metadata only (`PartialObjectMetadataList`) — which is exactly what the kube-controller-manager garbage collector does for every resource in the cluster — still causes and reads through the full-object cache. The projection to metadata happens at response-serialization time, long after the full object has been materialized.

The result: a cluster holding ~1 GB of large custom resources (`trivy-operator` SBOM/vulnerability reports, Helm release Secrets) pays **several gigabytes** of apiserver RSS for it, with no way to bound the cost short of disabling the watch cache for those resources entirely.

*Important observation: nobody needs instant access to the Trivy SBOM reports, but because the GC is watching them, they go into memory verbatim. This seems like a complete waste.*

* Reported on kube-apiserver **v1.35.5**; reproduced on **master** (`def9a441f5`, v1.38.0-alpha.0).
* Resources involved in the original incident:
  * `sbomreports.aquasecurity.github.io`, `vulnerabilityreports.aquasecurity.github.io` (trivy-operator)
  * `secrets` — Helm release history (`sh.helm.release.v1.*`), ~157 KB each, 10 revisions retained per release by default
* Clients: kube-controller-manager (garbage collector; metadata-only informers over **all** resources) and ArgoCD (full-object watches).
* Observed: kube-apiserver RSS **12+ GB**, dropping to **~2 GB** after pruning the SBOM reports and Helm history.

Original sizing, from the cluster:

```
$ kubectl get sbomreports.aquasecurity.github.io -A -o json | wc -c
1122584175            # ~1.1 GB of JSON for all the sbomreports
```

`StorageWithCacher()` wraps each resource's storage in a `Cacher`
([`registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go:36`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go#L36)).
`NewCacherFromConfig` immediately starts a reflector performing a full LIST + WATCH of the resource
([`storage/cacher/cacher.go:475`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L475)).

For CRDs the storage is built lazily, on the first request that touches the resource — so the trigger is a single request, after which the cost is permanent.

```
// staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/store/store.go
type Element struct {
	Key    string
	Object runtime.Object   // <-- the fully decoded object
	Labels labels.Set
	Fields fields.Set
}
```

`watchCache.Replace()` builds one of these per object during the initial LIST
([`watch_cache.go:584`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L584)),
and `processEvent()` does the same per update ([`watch_cache.go:227`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L227)).

In v1.35.5 this is the identically-shaped `storeElement` in `storage/cacher/store.go:93`.

CR storage decodes into `*unstructured.Unstructured`
([`apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/registry/customresource/etcd.go:48`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/)staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/registry/customresource/etcd.go#L48)).
An SBOM is a long array of small objects with many short string keys — the worst possible shape for
`map[string]interface{}`, where every key, every boxed value and every map bucket carries overhead.
Measured cost: **5.2x the serialized size**, stable across object sizes.

`transformResponseObject` → `asPartialObjectMetadataList` projects to metadata at **response serialization** time
([`endpoints/handlers/response.go:435`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d5cbb79be9160faa3a7d7323e3294c3781c16ae7/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/response.go#L435)),
reading from the already-materialized full object. There is no metadata-only path through the storage layer.

So the garbage collector — which by design only needs `ownerReferences`, `uid`, `name`, `namespace` — is enough
on its own to force every resource in the cluster, at full fidelity, into the apiserver's heap.

This was reproduced with Claude and locally added tests.

`TestUnstructuredHeapAmplification` — decode N copies of a realistic SbomReport and measure retained heap:

| SBOM components | Serialized (JSON) | Decoded (`Unstructured`) | Amplification |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | 0.6 MiB | 3.4 MiB | **5.20x** |
| 2 000 | 2.6 MiB | 13.5 MiB | **5.20x** |
| 8 000 | 10.4 MiB | 53.7 MiB | **5.19x** |

`TestWatchCacheMemory` — 100 SbomReports (~1.3 MiB each) seeded into etcd, one `Cacher` built over them:

| | Retained heap | vs. wire size |
|---|---:|---:|
| 129.5 MiB of JSON in etcd | **737.6 MiB** | **5.69x** |

No client is connected. The memory is consumed purely by the cacher's initial LIST.

`repro/run.sh` — 200 SbomReports (161 MiB of JSON; 202 MB etcd database) against a real kube-apiserver.
A **single** `GET /apis/…/sbomreports?limit=1` with `Accept: …as=PartialObjectMetadataList`:

| Case | RSS before | RSS after | Go heap before | Go heap after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| watch cache ON, **no watchers at all** | 258 MiB | **1459 MiB** | 87 MiB | **1261 MiB** |
| watch cache ON, 20 metadata-only watchers | 253 MiB | 1488 MiB | 101 MiB | 1285 MiB |
| watch cache OFF for this resource | 254 MiB | 256 MiB | 102 MiB | 112 MiB |

(Every sample is taken after forcing a GC via `/debug/pprof/heap?gc=1`, and only once the heap has settled, so
these are live-heap figures rather than wherever the collector happened to be.)

Three things to read off this:

* **161 MiB of submitted JSON became ~1.17 GB of additional live heap** — a 7.3x multiplier on what was sent,
  and consistent with the controlled 5.69x of experiment B once the `managedFields` the apiserver adds to every
  object are accounted for.
* **Twenty concurrent watchers cost no more than none** (+1%). The cache is shared, and it is populated by the
  first request to touch the resource whether or not anyone goes on to watch it. Watchers are the trigger, not
  the cost.
* **With the cache off for that resource the growth disappears entirely** — +2 MiB RSS, +10 MiB heap.

The trigger was one `GET …/sbomreports?limit=1` asking for a single object's metadata. Repeated runs put RSS
growth between 1.2 GB and 1.7 GB depending on GC timing; live heap growth is stable at ~1.0–1.3 GB.

It scales linearly, and accounts for the reported incident: ~1.1 GB of SBOM reports alone would be expected to
cost on the order of 6–8 GB of heap, before the vulnerability reports, config-audit reports and Helm Secrets are
counted.

* Apiserver memory is driven by **total bytes stored in large-object resources**, at a ~5–9x multiplier, rather than by request or watch load. (Note that secrets and other core resources might multiply by a smaller number because they have their own structs.)
* The cost is invisible in the usual places: no watcher is required, and the resource may never be read again after the request that populated it.
* Operators have no bounded control. `--watch-cache-sizes` only accepts an object count, and the count is ignored except for the special case of `0`, which disables caching for the resource outright. There is no byte budget, and no eviction.
* It is an availability risk: a controller that creates large CRs (a security scanner, a backup tool) can OOM the control plane without any change to cluster workload, and the blast radius is the apiserver.

These need no patch and are worth applying regardless:

1. **Disable the watch cache for the offending resources.** Size `0` is the documented way to opt a resource out:
   ```
   --watch-cache-sizes=configauditreports.aquasecurity.github.io#0,exposedsecretreports.aquasecurity.github.io#0,sbomreports.aquasecurity.github.io#0,vulnerabilityreports.aquasecurity.github.io#0,certificaterequests.cert-manager.io#0,orders.acme.cert-manager.io#0,policyreports.wgpolicyk8s.io#0
   ```
   Verified in experiment C: the growth disappears entirely. The cost is that LIST/WATCH for those resources go to etcd directly, which is acceptable for resources that are written often and read rarely.
2. **Reduce what is stored.** Trivy-operator report TTLs; `helm --history-max` (default 10) — a 157 KB Secret × 10 revisions × every release is substantial on its own.
3. **Prune unused resources.** Helm revisions, replicasets.apps (Deployment revisionHistoryLimit), controllerrevisions.apps (Ds/Sts revisionHistoryLimit).
4. **Watch the right signal.** `apiserver_storage_objects` × mean object size predicts the cost far better than watch counts do. Example:
   ```bash
   # Show the resources taking up the most space (json byte counts).
   kubectl get --raw /metrics |
     grep '^apiserver_storage_objects' |
[... 49 more lines]
```

kubelet: containers that fail before ever running don't get exponential CrashLoopBackOff treatment

When `startContainer` fails before the container ever reaches a running state — e.g. `CreateContainer` is rejected by the CRI because a resource limit (such as memory) is below the runtime's floor, or a pre-create/pre-start hook fails , no container status is ever recorded for that attempt.

`kubeGenericRuntimeManager.doBackOff` decides whether to apply `CrashLoopBackOff` by looking for an *exited* container status in `podStatus.ContainerStatuses`. Since these pre-run failures never produce a container status, `doBackOff` never finds one to back off against.

The pod is still retried (the pod-worker's flat ~10s backoff on `SyncPod` errors still applies , see `backOffPeriod` in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go`), but these container-start failures never get the *exponential* backoff or the `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event that other persistently-failing containers get once they've run and exited at least once. This is inconsistent: two containers that both fail forever are treated differently depending on whether the failure happened before or after the container briefly started.

Containers that repeatedly fail to start , even before ever reaching a running state — should get the same exponential backoff escalation (up to the standard cap) and `CrashLoopBackOff` status/event reporting as containers that repeatedly exit after starting.

1. Create a Pod with a container whose resource request/limit is set below what the container runtime enforces as a floor (e.g. a memory limit below the runtime's minimum).
2. Observe that `CreateContainer` is rejected on every retry.
3. Observe that kubelet retries at a flat ~10s cadence indefinitely, without back-off escalating over time, and without a `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event ever appearing ,unlike a container that starts and then repeatedly exits

kubelet: cut PLEG relist memory with CRI field projection + delta listing

Two additive, opt-in changes to the CRI container/pod list calls so the kubelet's PLEG can stop decoding data it doesn't use:

1. **Field projection** Let the client request only the fields it needs (container id, state, and the `io.kubernetes.*` identity labels). The runtime omits everything else; older runtimes ignore the request field and behave as today.
2. **Delta listing** Let the client receive only the containers that changed since the last relist, instead of the full set every cycle.

This came out of a hallway conversation at gRPCConf after my talk on CRI list streaming: a few gRPC maintainers and I got into why server-streaming a big response doesn't actually cut memory and the receiver still decodes the whole object graph. That pointed back at the kubelet's own CRI list path, so I went and measured it.

PLEG relists every container on the node about once a second and the kubelet decodes the entire
result each time. On dense or high-churn nodes this is large, mostly-redundant memory and CPU:

- Measured on master: ~18k containers with realistic annotations ≈ **1.57M allocations / ~79 MB
  held per relist**, re-paid every second.
- A full "fat" response can cross the 16 MiB CRI client cap (`maxMsgSize`), so `ListContainers`
  fails → PLEG stalls → node NotReady → and container GC can't run because it needs the same list
  (the "PLEG is not healthy" failure on high-churn nodes).
- The list is dominated by accumulated terminated containers that never change, re-decoded every
  second for nothing.

Existing work doesn't cover this axis: KEP-5825 (CRIListStreaming) fixes the per-message size cap but, in its own words, "does not reduce kubelet memory usage"; KEP-3386 / PLEGOnDemandRelist change relist *frequency*, not per-object payload.

I have a small benchmark harness (happy to push it) that measures decode + hold cost for full vs projected vs changed-only responses on representative payloads:

- **Projection** (measured): −45% memory, −65% wire, −34% allocations.
- **Changed-only** reduces it much further, since the list is mostly static terminated containers, the mechanism is measured and linear, and the exact factor depends on per-relist churn, which isn't instrumented upstream today (I model it at ≤1% for the accumulated-dead-container case, giving ≥99%; grounding that number would be step one of an alpha).
- **Correctness:** projection is client-declared per call, so it can't remove a field a consumer is reading and safe by construction. For the PLEG path specifically, the needed set is small and verified in code (event generation uses only id + state; container→pod mapping uses only `pod.uid`; the restart hash comes from `ContainerStatus`, not the list).

I'd like to bring this to sig-node as a KEP; opening this to track the problem and gather input.

Proposal: Lifecycle-Aware Persistence for Dormant Kubernetes Custom Resources

Hi SIG API Machinery,

I was hoping to bring a design question to today's SIG meeting, but it looks like the meeting didn't happen, so I wanted to ask here.

We're exploring a pattern for high-cardinality, relatively short-lived CRs where Kubernetes is primarily needed while the resource is actively being reconciled.

The lifecycle we're considering is:

**active → CR stored in Kubernetes/etcd → reconcile → dormant → persist durable state externally + remove CR → new activity → materialize CR back into Kubernetes → reconcile**

The motivation is that we may have a large number of resources whose active reconciliation lifetime is short, while their logical lifetime is much longer. Keeping all dormant resources in Kubernetes can create unnecessary etcd, watch, informer/cache, and control-plane overhead.

I'd love to get the SIG's guidance on a few questions:

1. Is treating a Kubernetes resource as an **active/materialized view of externally persisted state** an established or recommended pattern?
2. For reactivation, is delete/re-create of the CR the expected approach, or are there other API Machinery mechanisms we should consider?
3. If we need the logical resources to remain addressable through a Kubernetes-style API while not being stored in kube-apiserver's etcd, would an **aggregated API server backed by external storage** be the better abstraction?
4. Is there any existing work or KEP around lifecycle-aware/externalized persistence of API resources that we should look at?

Happy to write up a short design doc or bring this to a future SIG meeting if this is something the group would be interested in discussing.

In-tree FC block teardown skips current-device cleanup when the recorded device path is stale

For an in-tree Fibre Channel raw block volume, kubelet records the resolved raw or device-mapper path used while mapping the volume.

If that recorded nonempty path is no longer present during teardown, `DetachBlockFCDisk` currently treats the missing path as successful teardown. It therefore returns before using the WWN/LUN or WWID encoded in the FC global-map path to discover a current device.

As a result, current-device SCSI or multipath cleanup may be skipped while the caller proceeds as though device teardown completed.

When the recorded nonempty path is missing:

- attempt the existing stable-identity discovery already used for empty paths;
- if the identity resolves a current device, perform normal cleanup;
- if both the remembered path and stable identity are gone, retain idempotent success; and
- keep permission, I/O, and cleanup failures as errors so teardown can retry.

A deterministic regression test, `TestTearDownDeviceRecoversFromStaleDevicePath`, models:

- an absent recorded `DevicePath`;
- persistent WWN/LUN identity in the FC global map; and
- a matching `/dev/disk/by-path` entry resolving a current device.

On the affected baseline at `39d3afacbeca5074fb54c1af5469ad11d6ddd78e`, the test observes that teardown:

- does not search the identity directory;
- does not flush the current device;
- does not write to `/sys/block/<current-device>/device/delete`;
- returns success; and
- removes the FC global-map metadata.

The regression matrix also covers WWID lookup through `/dev/disk/by-id`, raw and multipath cleanup, identity disappearance, originally empty paths, remembered paths that still exist, permission and cleanup errors, and global-map cleanup ordering.

FC/SCSI path loss or re-enumeration is the production-shaped trigger. Physical SAN hardware was not used to reproduce the trigger in this investigation.

The deterministic regression proves that a stale recorded path causes an early successful return, stable-identity recovery is skipped, current-device cleanup is skipped, and FC global-map metadata is subsequently removed. It strongly supports that kubelet can then proceed as though device teardown completed. This report does not claim data corruption, storage loss, a guaranteed Multi-Attach failure, or guaranteed orphaned physical SAN state.

- #141839 / #141863: related iSCSI missing-by-path case.
- #57153 / #57155: historical FC empty-`DevicePath` recovery. In #57155, `devicePath` is empty, so FC uses global-map identity recovery. Here, `devicePath` is nonempty but stale, so current code returns success before reaching that same recovery.
- #101862: historical retry after FC cleanup errors.
- #97014 / #97013: historical FC multipath cleanup.
- #121937: unrelated CSI reconstruction/global-mount residue.
- #55314: related path changes in FlexVolume.
- #94780 / #94781: historical filesystem-mode FC idempotency.

Memory Manager accepts an incomplete pod-level checkpoint as a restored allocation after kubelet restart

With the static Memory Manager, pod-scope Topology Manager, and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, pod-level allocation is persisted through independent checkpoint updates: `PodMemoryAssignments` first, then per-container assignments, then `MachineState`. If kubelet stops after the real `SetPodMemoryBlocks` write completes but before the first `SetMemoryBlocks`, the resulting checkpoint is structurally valid but contains a PodEntry for UID `podUID`, no container assignments for that pod, and the pre-allocation machine state.

On restart, `validateState` reconstructs expected accounting by iterating `ContainerMemoryAssignments`. Because this pod has no container entries, the orphan pod assignment is not inspected and startup succeeds. `GetPodTopologyHints` then regenerates a hint from the PodEntry, and pod-scope admission calls `AllocatePod`. `AllocatePod` sees `GetPodMemoryBlocks(podUID) != nil` and returns success as though allocation were complete. The container `MemoryBlocks` and machine reservation remain absent.

This is an ordinary functional-correctness issue. No security impact is being claimed.

An incomplete pod-level allocation must not be treated as a completely restored allocation. Restart handling should reject the inconsistent checkpoint, repair it, or safely reconstruct/reallocate the missing state before successful admission is reported.

A deterministic unit reproducer, `TestMemoryManagerRestorePartialPodCheckpoint`, uses pod name `pod1` and UID `podUID`. It:

1. enables `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`;
2. creates the real static Memory Manager with the real checkpoint backend and a real best-effort, pod-scope Topology Manager;
3. wraps the state so `SetPodMemoryBlocks` first invokes the real setter and only then simulates process interruption;
4. verifies that the PodEntry is durable, container assignments are empty, and `MachineState` is unchanged;
5. creates new managers against the same checkpoint directory; and
6. performs normal pod-scope Topology Manager admission.

With the proposed validation guard removed on current master, the restored manager starts and admission succeeds, followed by these invariant failures:

```
successful restored pod allocation left container "container1" without memory blocks
successful restored pod allocation left machine state without the pod reservation
```

This constructs the precise checkpoint through production state APIs; it does not claim that a live production node was intentionally crashed.

Related but distinct work:

- #140906 / #141077 preserve a fully completed restored pod allocation; this issue concerns a PodEntry-only partial checkpoint.
- #141070 restores pod topology hints from the pod-level allocation, which is why the orphan PodEntry can supply the post-restart hint.
- #141261 addresses a sibling CPU Manager partial-state cleanup problem.
- kubernetes/enhancements#5526 is the Pod Level Resource Managers design context.

A deterministic regression test and minimal startup-validation fix are prepared, and I intend to open a PR shortly.

kubelet ignores the configured subordinate ID range for a local kubelet account when getent is not on PATH

Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870, which replaced `user.Lookup("kubelet")` with a `getent passwd` shell-out.

[`getentUserExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L188-L191) returns early when `LookPath` fails:

```
getent, err := exec.LookPath("getent")
if err != nil {
	return false, nil // no getent: same as "not configured"
}
```

[The caller](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L151-L158) reads that as "no kubelet account", skips `getsubids` and returns the built-in default range. The account itself is never examined, so a local `/etc/passwd` entry is affected the same way, which is wider than the directory-service case the PR body describes.

Same node, with `getent` on PATH and then off it:

```
getent on PATH   firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608
getent off PATH  firstID=65536   rangeLen=4294901760
```

Before 6bb4235 the cgo `user.Lookup` resolved a local account without `getent`, so a node in this state used to get its configured range. I ran the two versions of that branch side by side against a real local account with `getent` off PATH: `user.Lookup` reports the account, `getentUserExists` reports it missing.

The configured subordinate IDs to still be used when the account is in `/etc/passwd`, or something in the log saying they were skipped. Today it is a `V(5)` line and no error.

@kginonredhat suggested a fallback during review: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870#discussion_r3966541751

That shape looks right to me with one adjustment. I would gate it on `exec.ErrNotFound` only, since `LookPath` also returns `ErrDot` alongside a usable path, and swallowing that turns a resolvable `getent` into a missing account.

Run from anywhere inside a checkout of master. No root, cleans up after itself.

repro.sh

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
W=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$W" pkg/kubelet/zz_getent_repro_test.go' EXIT
mkdir -p "$W/with" "$W/without"

# stand-ins for a node whose /etc/passwd has a kubelet account and whose
# /etc/subuid delegates 1048576/8388608 to it
cat > "$W/with/getent" <<'G'
#!/bin/sh
[... 34 more lines]
```

```
--- getent on PATH ---
    zz_getent_repro_test.go:14: firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608 err=<nil>
--- getent off PATH ---
    zz_getent_repro_test.go:14: firstID=65536 rangeLen=4294901760 err=<nil>
```

Two things a fix would have to deal with.

[`TestGetentUserExists`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods_test.go#L8595-L8598) has a `"getent not installed"` case expecting `wantFound: false`, so that case has to change with the behavior. It also only asserts `found`, never the range `getKubeletMappings` ends up with, which is the part that matters here.

The second one is smaller. [The comment above the lookup](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6bb42350227f0a714f4730165e7ba622c69bd99e/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L145-L150) says the account is checked first so a getsubids backend that is unreachable can be told apart from one that simply has no entry. glibc's `getent` sets exit 2 whenever `getpwnam()` returns NULL without consulting errno, while the cgo `os/user` gave `UnknownUserError` for a genuine miss and a plain error otherwise. So an account-backend error that used to stop kubelet can now arrive as exit 2 and select the default range instead. I have not reproduced a real directory-service outage, so I would treat that as a question about the contract, not a second bug.

I am happy to send the PR if the fallback is the direction people want.

Deployment controller enters infinite ReplicaSet churn when a gated PodTemplateSpec field is disabled while in use , affects any feature using the standard "preserve if in use" drop pattern

When a feature-gated PodTemplateSpec field (e.g. GRPCAction.mode from [KEP-4939](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/4939), or Container.restartPolicyRules) is disabled on kube-apiserver while a Deployment's template already has that field set, triggering the Deployment controller to create a new ReplicaSet (e.g. kubectl rollout restart) causes an infinite reconcile loop. A new ReplicaSet is created and replaced continuously, never converging.

Root cause:

- The standard drop-field convention (!gateEnabled && !fieldInUse(oldPodSpec)) is used by many features to avoid silently deleting data from objects that already legitimately use the field on direct updates. That part works correctly.
- But ReplicaSetStrategy.PrepareForCreate (pkg/registry/apps/replicaset/strategy.go:87) always calls pod.DropDisabledTemplateFields(&rs.Spec.Template, nil), passing nil as the old template for any newly created ReplicaSet, since from the ReplicaSet's own perspective it has no "old" version. This means the "in use" exception never applies to it, and the field is stripped the instant the ReplicaSet is persisted, even though it was copied verbatim from a Deployment template that still has the field.
- This leaves the Deployment's desired template and the persisted ReplicaSet's template permanently disagreeing, which the Deployment controller can never reconcile, so it keeps creating new ReplicaSets forever.

Disabling the gate should drop the field from newly created/updated objects, that's documented, expected behavior. Triggering a new ReplicaSet in that state should produce exactly one new ReplicaSet (with the field stripped) and settle into a stable state. Instead, the Deployment never converges.

- Enable a feature gate for a PodTemplateSpec field that uses the "preserve if in use" drop pattern (e.g. GRPCContainerProbeTLS + livenessProbe.grpc.mode: TLS, or ContainerRestartRules + restartPolicyRules).
 - Create a Deployment using it.
 - Disable that feature gate on kube-apiserver only (kubelet untouched).
- Run kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>.
kubectl get replicaset -w shows continuous churn — a new ReplicaSet every ~0-1s, indefinitely, for both features tested.

This is not specific to any one feature. It's a structural gap between the drop-field convention and how PrepareForCreate handles controller-managed child objects. Likely affects every feature currently using this pattern in pkg/api/pod/util.go, most of which have simply never had this exact scenario (disable gate while a live Deployment depends on it, then trigger a new ReplicaSet) exercised or tested.

kubelet can fail to start when the user namespace ID pool changes while pods with user namespaces exist on the node

If the subordinate ID pool kubelet uses for user namespaces changes between restarts, and a pod on disk holds a mapping that falls outside the new pool, the kubelet does not start:

```
create user namespace manager: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
```

[`record()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L252-L255) rejects a persisted mapping outside the current pool, and [the replay loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L185-L189) returns on the first such pod, so `MakeUserNsManager()` fails and `NewMainKubelet()` with it. As far as I can tell the only ways out are to restore the previous pool or to delete the pod directory by hand, and the message points at neither.

Several ordinary things change the pool. Editing `/etc/subuid` to move kubelet's range does it. So does installing `getsubids` on a node that did not have it, or creating the `kubelet` account on a node where it did not exist, since both move the node from the built-in default range to whatever `getsubids` then reports. None of these involve cgo or #135870; that PR just adds one more way to get here, which is where I ran into it.

Whether a given node survives is luck. Blocks come from `allocator.NewAllocationMap`, which picks at random, so it depends on where the running pod happens to sit relative to the new pool. Going from the default pool to a delegated one is close to a certainty: the default holds 65535 blocks against a typical delegated pool of ~128.

`UserNamespacesSupport` has been GA with `LockToDefault` since 1.36, so the path is active on every Linux kubelet, but only nodes running pods with `hostUsers: false` are affected, since pods without a user namespace write no mapping file and are skipped on replay.

Something recoverable. Failing the whole kubelet over one pod whose persisted mapping no longer fits seems heavy next to, say, refusing that pod and saying why, and either way the error could name the pod directory an operator would have to clear.

I do not know which is right, and it overlaps with #140190, which is looking at persisted-mapping replay from the terminal-ID angle and deliberately kept its guard on the allocation side so that older on-disk mappings stay replayable.

Drop this in `pkg/kubelet/userns/` and run `go test ./pkg/kubelet/userns/ -run TestPoolChangeReplay -v`. No cgo, no NSS, no changes to the host.

```
package userns

import (
	"testing"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/types"
	utilfeature "k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/feature"
	featuregatetesting "k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/testing"
	pkgfeatures "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/features"
[... 35 more lines]
```

One run:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608      block 112    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 7340032 is out of range
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks      block 131    FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 8585216 is out of range
default pool -> delegated pool             block 15363  FAILS: record pod mappings for existing pod "p": id 1006829568 is out of range
```

All three depend on where the pod happened to land, so one run understates it. Over 20 runs:

```
subuid range moved 1048576 -> 8388608   19 fail,  1 restarts OK   [16..143] -> [128..255], survives on 16 of 128 blocks
subuid range shrunk 128 -> 110 blocks    2 fail, 18 restart OK    [16..143] -> [16..125],  survives on 110 of 128
default pool -> delegated pool          20 fail,  0 restart OK    [1..65535] -> [16..143], survives on 128 of 65535
```

which matches the geometry in each case. The third row is the one that matters in practice: a node coming from the default pool has roughly a 0.2% chance per userns pod of sitting somewhere a delegated pool can still replay.

This is a unit-level reproduction in a checkout rather than something I have watched a real node do. It came out of #135870, where I raised it before @dims suggested splitting it into separate issues, but the PR is a trigger rather than the cause, so it stands on its own.
