StatefulSet controller never recovers from an adopted pod with a mismatched volumeClaimTemplate set: endless FailedUpdate retries instead of delete

**What happened?**

A StatefulSet was deleted with `--cascade=orphan` and re-created with an additional `volumeClaimTemplates` entry (the API rejects adding one by update, so delete-and-recreate is the documented workaround path). The surviving, adopted pod did not have a volume for the new claim template. The statefulset controller then retried an in-place update of that pod forever, emitting `FailedUpdate` events, and never fell back to deleting the pod. The rollout wedged until the pod was deleted by hand.

Code path, at v1.30.5 and unchanged through v1.33 and current master:

- `pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go` `storageMatches` returns false for the adopted pod, because the pod's volumes do not cover the set's (new) volumeClaimTemplates.
- `pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go` `processReplica` therefore calls `UpdateStatefulPod`, which rewrites `pod.Spec.Volumes` and calls UpdatePod. The API server rejects it: `spec.volumes` is immutable in `ValidatePodUpdate` (`pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go`, "pod updates may not change fields other than ...").
- `processReplica` returns the error, `updateStatefulSet` returns at the `runForAll(replicas, ...)` call, and the rolling-update loop that deletes pods not matching the update revision (`getPodRevision(pod) != updateRevision.Name` -> `DeleteStatefulPod`) is never reached. Every resync repeats the identical failing update.

So for a storage mismatch the controller's only remediation is an in-place pod update, and when that update is impossible (volumes are immutable), there is no path that deletes and recreates the pod, even though the ordinary rolling-update path would have.

**What you expected to happen?**

Either the in-place storage reconciliation skips fields that cannot be updated in place and lets the revision-based rollout delete/recreate the pod, or an `Invalid` (non-conflict) error from the in-place pod update causes the controller to fall back to deleting the pod, as the rolling-update path does. A legal cluster state (orphaned pod adopted by a recreated StatefulSet with a different claim-template set) should not wedge the rollout permanently.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?**

1. Create a StatefulSet with one replica and no volumeClaimTemplates (or with a volume mounted from an emptyDir), wait for `web-0` running:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: web, namespace: default }
spec:
  serviceName: web
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
[... 1 more lines]
```

2. `kubectl delete sts web --cascade=orphan` (pod `web-0` keeps running).
3. Apply the same StatefulSet with `volumeClaimTemplates` added (e.g. a `data` template, 1Gi) and `replicas: 3`.
4. Observed: `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep FailedUpdate` fills with `FailedUpdate` for `web-0`; `web-1`/`web-2` are created normally; `web-0` never converges. The PVC `data-web-0` is created.
5. `kubectl delete pod web-0` unblocks it; the recreated pod has the volume and binds the claim.

**Anything else we need to know?**

Related but distinct from #69041 (that issue tracks relaxing the apiserver restriction on updating `volumeClaimTemplates`; this one is about controller recovery when the set legitimately ends up different from an adopted pod, which delete-and-recreate with orphaning makes reachable today).

For chart authors the trigger is common: a helm chart that renders a volumeClaimTemplate only under an HA flag will produce exactly this sequence when someone enables HA on a live release and follows the delete-and-recreate workaround. Filed dapr/dapr#10468 for one such chart.

**Environment**

- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): observed on v1.30.5; code path identical at v1.33.3 and current master (2026-09-05).

$ kubectl version
Client: v1.31.14
Server: v1.30.5+k3s1 (k3s)

[1.36] Kubelet retries DRA health streams for plugins that do not advertise health support

On Kubernetes 1.36, kubelet starts a `NodeWatchResources` health stream for every registered DRA plugin whenever `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled. It does this even when the plugin does not advertise the optional `DRAResourceHealth` service in its registration response.

When the service is not implemented, kubelet receives `codes.Unimplemented`, logs it as an error, and retries every five seconds:

```
E0902 21:16:20.306285 manager.go:1045] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = device health reporting is not supported by this driver" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="compute-domain.nvidia.com"
```

`ResourceHealthStatus` is Beta and enabled by default in 1.36, so this occurs on the default feature-gate configuration when a DRA plugin does not implement health reporting.

This does not appear to affect DRA workload correctness, but it continuously emits error-level kubelet logs. At one retry every five seconds, each unsupported plugin produces 17,280 error records per day per node. This creates unnecessary log storage and ingestion costs and makes genuine kubelet errors harder to identify.

Kubelet should only start the health stream when the plugin advertises a supported `DRAResourceHealth` service.

If a plugin advertises the service but returns `codes.Unimplemented`, kubelet should treat that as a terminal indication that health reporting is unsupported and stop retrying until the plugin re-registers.

This is the behavior in Kubernetes 1.37.

This was reproduced with a kind v1.36.1 cluster using the head of:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/pull/1243

The GPU plugin streams health normally when its health reporting feature is enabled. Kubelet nevertheless continues attempting `NodeWatchResources` every five seconds for `compute-domain.nvidia.com`, which does not advertise the health service.

The same driver configuration is quiet on kubelet 1.37.

Full reproduction findings and logs:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/issues/1423#issuecomment-5532233065

Although the report uses the NVIDIA DRA driver, the behavior is generic to any DRA plugin that registers without the optional health service.

In release-1.36, `RegisterPlugin` receives the plugin's `supportedServices`, but the health stream is started without checking that list:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L324-L334

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L387-L407

Kubernetes 1.37 fixed this as part of #139477 by:

- selecting an advertised health service during registration;
- starting the stream only when such a service was advertised;
- stopping retries when the stream returns `codes.Unimplemented`.

This issue is intended to track a targeted backport of that behavior to release-1.36, not the larger v1 health API and kubeletplugin helper changes from #139477.

The proposed 1.36 fix would:

1. Start `NodeWatchResources` only if the plugin advertises `v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth`.
2. Treat `codes.Unimplemented` as non-error and stop retrying.
3. Add regression tests for an absent health service and an `Unimplemented` stream.

A backport to 1.35 or earlier is not requested because `ResourceHealthStatus` was Alpha and disabled by default there.

DeploymentController: int64 overflow computing the next revision when an adopted ReplicaSet has deployment.kubernetes.io/revision = math.MaxInt64

A ReplicaSet whose `deployment.kubernetes.io/revision` annotation is set to `"9223372036854775807"` (`math.MaxInt64`) is adopted by a Deployment as soon as it matches the selector and has no other controller owner.

When the controller computes the next revision in `pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go` (`strconv.FormatInt(maxOldRevision+1, 10)`), the `int64` addition overflows: `math.MaxInt64 + 1` wraps to `math.MinInt64`. There is no panic, the wrap is silent.

The negative value is not persisted, but the revision history ends up corrupted. `SetNewReplicaSetAnnotations` compares the new ReplicaSet's current revision (`0`, unset) with the computed `newRevision` (`math.MinInt64`): `0 < math.MinInt64` is false, so the negative revision is never written to the new ReplicaSet. On the next sync the controller updates the Deployment's revision annotation from the new ReplicaSet's (still empty) revision, which clears the Deployment annotation. The observable end state is a Deployment with no revision annotation and a `kubectl rollout history` showing the current revision as `0` alongside the orphan ReplicaSet at `9223372036854775807`.

An out-of-range `deployment.kubernetes.io/revision` value on an adopted ReplicaSet should be ignored when computing the next revision, exactly like an unparseable value already is (`MaxRevision`/`LastRevision` skip ReplicaSets whose revision does not parse). It should never overflow nor clear the Deployment's revision history.

1. Create a Deployment with a selector.
2. Create a ReplicaSet matching that selector, with no controller owner reference and `deployment.kubernetes.io/revision: "9223372036854775807"`.
3. Trigger a rollout of the Deployment.
4. Observe:
   - `kubectl get deployment <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.deployment\.kubernetes\.io/revision}'` becomes empty.
   - `kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>` shows the current revision as `0` and the orphan ReplicaSet at `9223372036854775807`.

A deterministic manifest-based repro and an equivalent Go unit test are available.

`MaxRevision` already skips ReplicaSets whose revision annotation does not parse, but `math.MaxInt64` parses cleanly, so it is used as-is and overflows on `+ 1`. The parsing happens in a single place, `Revision()` in `pkg/controller/deployment/util/deployment_util.go`, so treating an out-of-range value as unparseable there (reject `< 0` and `>= math.MaxInt64`) fixes it at the source. With `math.MaxInt64` rejected, the largest usable revision is `math.MaxInt64 - 1`, and `(math.MaxInt64 - 1) + 1` does not overflow.

Dynamic Resource Allocation (DeviceClass/Device) is not supported on Windows nodes

Support for Dynamic Resource Allocation - **structured parameters** (KEP-4381; `DeviceClass`/`Device`) - on Windows nodes, defined by a real Windows enhancement KEP and a Windows-specific device-assignment design. Today the kubelet's Windows container manager stubs every DRA accessor to nil and registers only the device-plugin handler.

DRA exists because the device-plugin + extended-resource model only advertises an integer count of a node-local resource. It cannot express device init/cleanup (e.g. reprogramming an FPGA), partial partitions (Nvidia MIG / SR-IOV), dynamic/network-attached devices, or structured property-based matching. The motivating scenario - device-centric accelerator workloads (GPU/AI, NIC/DPU, edge/batch) - applies to Windows containers exactly as on Linux (Windows GPU/AI is a real, growing use case). So the gap is real and worth closing.

- Base DRA today is **KEP-4381 (structured parameters)**, not KEP-3063. KEP-3063 (the original 'classic' DRA) was **withdrawn** in Kubernetes 1.32 and its code removed; #4381 now defines the base functionality and driver interface.
- The Windows TODO in the code references `kep.k8s.io/4680`, which **does not exist** (no such KEP in kubernetes/enhancements; no Windows-DRA KEP in the sig-windows index). So DRA-on-Windows is not only unimplemented but also untracked.

- `pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_windows.go` `GetPluginRegistrationHandlers`: `// DRA is not supported on Windows, only device plugin is supported`; only the device-plugin handler is registered.
- DRA accessors are stubs on Windows: `GetAllocatableDevices` -> nil, `GetDynamicResources` -> nil, `PrepareDynamicResources`/`UnprepareDynamicResources` -> nil.

- Linux DRA injects devices via **CDI** (/dev + mount + runtime config) into the container; Prepare/Unprepare stage host devices. This depends on Linux /dev/mount/CDI semantics.
- In process-isolated (shared-kernel) Windows containers there is no /dev tree and no mount-based CDI injection; device exposure is per-Job-Object / device-interface / GPU-PV handle. The CDI mechanism is not portable.

Because the same scenario occurs on Windows and a viable mechanism exists, this issue is kept open. Proposed Windows-specific model under KEP-4381 structured parameters:
1. **Reuse the control plane unchanged**: the existing `ResourceClaim`/`Device`/`DeviceClass` API + scheduler-side allocation. No API divergence.
2. **Device injection - the real difference**: replace CDI + /dev-mount with **per-Job-Object / container device assignment**:
   - GPU: assign the Windows GPU adapter / device-interface (GPU-PV surface) to the container.
   - Generic: expose device handles into the container's Object Manager namespace (host-process sidecar or per-Job-Object device-permission model).
3. **Prepare/Unprepare map to Windows APIs**: open/close handles + device lease, not mount/unmount.
4. **podresources**: `GetDynamicResources`/`GetAllocatableDevices` surface the assigned device + claim, matching the contract.

- Open a real **Windows DRA enhancement KEP** (under the KEP-4381 structured-parameters model) covering registration, claim prepare/unprepare, and device exposure on Windows - the referenced kep.k8s.io/4680 does not exist.
- Get sig/windows + sig-node + sig/apps direction on device-assignment vs reusing devicemanager plumbing.
- Implement the DRA accessors and wire DRA device registration, replacing the stubs.

Please add `sig/windows`, `sig/node`, `kind/feature` for discovery (the filing account cannot add them; they are applied via `/sig` and `/kind` commands).

k8s master. Evidence: `container_manager_windows.go:260-263` (handler), `:336` (GetAllocatableDevices nil), `:392-400` (DRA stubs); base DRA: KEP-4381; Windows isolation: MS Learn.

---
AI-assisted analysis; verified against source; corrected to the KEP-4381 structured-parameters base (KEP-3063 withdrawn). Reconcile with sig/windows + sig-node maintainers.

[Umbrella] Supporting ML-DSA for PQC requirements

This issue is intended to be used as a scoping/tracking issue for all the changes that would be necessary to support configuring ML-DSA for PQC adherence within Kubernetes.

Adding support for configuring the usage of ML-DSA was discussed in the September 3rd, 2026 sig-arch community meeting.

- Bump to Go 1.27 - Go 1.27 introduced native support for ML-DSA crypto: https://go.dev/doc/go1.27#crypto_mldsa . This is actively being done in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141663

Support for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) with ML-DSA is a proposed standard: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9964

In order to support verification of JWTs, support for this standard will need to be added to the underlying libraries we rely on for JWT verification:
- `gopkg.in/go-jose/go-jose.v2`. We currently rely on v2 of this package which is now considered obsolete. Support for the proposed standard is already being proposed for v4 of this package in https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/issues/272 .
- `github.com/coreos/go-oidc`. This package will first need to be updated to pickup and support the new ML-DSA algorithms as part of it's token verification logic. It will also need to be bumped to use the lastest changes from `gopkg.in/go-jose/go-jose.v4` with support for the ML-DSA standard. We currently rely on an old release of the package (v2.5.0) which relies on an older version of the go-jose package. We will need to bump this dependency to the latest version.

Additionally, we will need to update https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/62a78fd86a6c100edae95f159d31fb4b435075c8/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/authenticator/token/oidc/oidc.go#L246-L257 to add the ML-DSA algorithms to the list of supported algorithms.

In order to support generation of JWTs signed with ML-DSA we will need to support the standard proposed in https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9964 for the OpenID JWKS data. In order to do this, we will need to use a version of the go-jose library that supports this. Once we are using the new go-jose library with support for this standard, we can update https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/62a78fd86a6c100edae95f159d31fb4b435075c8/pkg/serviceaccount/openidmetadata.go#L311-L334 to return the correct algorithm based on the public key type.

Additionally, we will need to add a new signer to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/62a78fd86a6c100edae95f159d31fb4b435075c8/pkg/serviceaccount/jwt.go#L64-L91 for the new [`*mldsa.PrivateKey`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/mldsa#PrivateKey) type.

For the most part, anywhere that verifies certificates using Go's native crypto libraries will inherently be able to verify ML-DSA signed certificates when using Go 1.27.

kubelet itself will need to be updated to support configuring the type of private key that should be used when generating its bootstrap certificates. The logic for generating the CertificateSigningRequest for bootstrapping certificates will need to be updated to generate new private keys for signing its CSR data based on the configured private key type.

Similarly to the bootstrap certificates, the PodCertificates functionality within the kubelet will need to be updated to generate an ML-DSA private key when specified.

Similarly to kubelet, kubeadm will need updates to allow specifying that bootstrap certificates should be generated using ML-DSA. This will require a new encryption type option and additional key generation and signer implementations for kubeadm. When using ML-DSA, kubeadm must not add `keyEncipherment` to the certificate.

The PodCertificate API will need to be updated to allow a PKCS#10 CSR using the ML-DSA subject public key types.

Additionally, the PodCertificateProjection API will need to be updated to allow specifying the ML-DSA key types.

CertificateSigningRequest spec validation should be updated to not allow the `usage` field to contain any of the following usages as defined by https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9881.html#name-key-usage-bits:
- `key encipherment`
- `key agreement`
- `data encipherment`
- `encipher only`
- `decipher only`

        - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142038 (client-go changes)
        - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142037 (kubeadm changes) (blocked on client-go changes)

Note: Items at the top-level can be done in parallel. Anything nested below these top-level items are blocked on the top-level items (and may be blocked on other top-level items).

Both subtests synchronize with a goroutine blocked on `cq.pop()` using the
same fragile pattern:

\`\`\`go
go func() {
    poppedCall, popErr := cq.pop()
    // ...
    poppedCallCh <- poppedCall
}()

time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond) // "give the goroutine time to block on pop()"

cq.add(call) // or cq.close()

select {
case poppedCall := <-poppedCallCh:
    // ...
case <-time.After(100 * time.Millisecond):
    t.Fatal("Pop() should have returned an added call, but it timed out")
}
\`\`\`

Two independent 100ms windows are used purely as synchronization, with no
polling or explicit signal that the goroutine actually reached the blocking
call. On a loaded or throttled CI runner (shared vCPUs, cgroup CPU
throttling, GC pause, or many parallel `go test` packages), the combined
round trip of goroutine scheduling + `pop()` unblocking + channel send +
`select` wake-up can exceed 100ms with no bug in the code under test — only
in the test's timing assumptions. That produces a spurious:

\`\`\`
Pop() should have returned an added call, but it timed out
\`\`\`
or
\`\`\`
Pop() should have been unblocked by close(), but it remained blocked
\`\`\`

**Locations:**
- `pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher/call_queue_test.go:359-391` (`TestCallQueue`)
- `pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher/call_queue_test.go:574-598` (`TestCallQueueClose`)

This is the same class of bug SIG Scheduling has fixed before in this same
package family — see #74611 ("fix the flake in scheduling_queue_test",
moved off sleep-based sync onto a `FakeClock`) and #125581 (client-go
workqueue test timing out under `-race -count=10000` for the identical
reason).

Replace the sleep-then-race-timeout pattern with an explicit synchronization
signal (a "goroutine started" channel closed right before the blocking
`cq.pop()` call) so the test doesn't depend on wall-clock timing to know the
goroutine is ready, and give the completion `select` a generous, non-racing
timeout — `wait.ForeverTestTimeout` (30s), the constant already used
elsewhere in the codebase for exactly this purpose, rather than a hardcoded
100ms.

Reproduce locally with:

\`\`\`
go test ./pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher/... -run TestCallQueue -race -count=200
\`\`\`

Running under `-race` and with other packages competing for CPU (e.g.
`go test ./... -race -p 8` in parallel) makes the window much easier to

NodeResourcesFit / NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation score real node load as 0 when a scheduler extender is configured (regression from #130537)

When a `KubeSchedulerConfiguration` profile has an HTTP extender configured with `nodeCacheCapable: false` (the default), `NodeResourcesFit.Score()` and `NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation.Score()` treat every node as if it has zero requested CPU/memory, regardless of its actual load. This makes those plugins unable to differentiate a busy node from an idle one whenever an extender is in the scheduling profile.

These plugins should score nodes based on their real current resource usage, same as when no extender is configured.

1. Configure a `KubeSchedulerConfiguration` profile with an HTTP extender (`filterVerb: filter`, `nodeCacheCapable` unset/false — this is the standard/default extender wiring, e.g. used by https://github.com/libopenstorage/stork's volume-aware scheduling).
2. Make one node much busier than the others (e.g. a filler pod requesting most of its CPU).
3. Schedule a pod through that profile.
4. Observe: `NodeResourcesFit`/`NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation` score the busy node the same as idle nodes, and the pod may land on the busy node.

We confirmed the exact mechanism:
- `HTTPExtender.Filter()` (`pkg/scheduler/extender.go`), in the `nodeCacheCapable == false` branch, builds a brand-new empty `NodeInfo` (`framework.NewNodeInfo()` + `SetNode()`) for each node in the extender's response, instead of reusing the real, already-computed `NodeInfo` it has in the `fromNodeName` map (built a few lines earlier, keyed by node name — which the returned `v1.Node` objects also have).
- Before #130537, this didn't matter: `Score()` took a node name and did its own independent lookup from the scheduler's snapshot, ignoring whatever `NodeInfo` had been threaded through the extender-filter pipeline.
- #130537 changed `Score()` to accept and directly trust the `NodeInfo` it's handed. For extender-filtered nodes, that's now the hollow one from `HTTPExtender.Filter()`, so `Score()` sees zero requested resources for every node.

We verified this by building kube-scheduler from the commit immediately before #130537 merged and from the merge commit itself, and running both against the same live cluster, same extender config, same busy node, same test pod — only the scheduler binary changed:
- Pre-#130537 binary: busy node scored 29 vs ~80 for idle nodes (`LeastAllocated`). Pod scheduled on an idle node.
- Post-#130537 binary (this PR): busy node scored 99, identical to every idle node. Pod scheduled on the busy node.

We also confirmed this on real clusters, not just the isolated before/after build: v1.34.9 (OCP 4.21) reproduces the bug; v1.31.14 (OCP 4.18), running the exact same extender config, correctly differentiates busy vs. idle nodes — consistent with the bug only existing from v1.33+ (when #130537 first shipped).

We also confirmed that switching the extender config to `nodeCacheCapable: true` (with the extender updated to resolve node names to real `Node` objects itself) avoids the bug — because that routes through the *other* branch of `HTTPExtender.Filter()`, which correctly reuses `fromNodeName`. This confirms the mechanism, but we don't think it should be required just to keep default (`nodeCacheCapable: false`) behavior correct.

Filed alongside a comment on #130537: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130537 — that's the PR we believe introduced this. We think the fix belongs in `HTTPExtender.Filter()`'s `nodeCacheCapable == false` branch: look up the returned node by name in `fromNodeName` (same as the `nodeCacheCapable == true` branch already does) instead of constructing a new empty `NodeInfo`.

keyutil.ParsePublicKeysPEM rejects PKCS#8-encoded ECDSA keys

**What happened?**

`keyutil.ParsePublicKeysPEM` / `PublicKeysFromFile` (in `k8s.io/client-go/util/keyutil`) reject an ECDSA private key encoded in unencrypted **PKCS#8** form (a `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----` block), failing with:

```
data does not contain any valid RSA or ECDSA public keys
```

The internal `parseECPrivateKey` only calls `x509.ParseECPrivateKey` (SEC1 / RFC 5915) and never falls back to `x509.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey`. Its sibling `parseRSAPrivateKey` *does* fall back to PKCS#8, and `ParsePrivateKeyPEM` explicitly treats a PKCS#8 `PRIVATE KEY` block as a valid "RSA or ECDSA" key — so PKCS#8-encoded EC keys are expected to be supported. Only the EC path in `ParsePublicKeysPEM` misses it.

**What did you expect to happen?**

A PKCS#8-encoded EC key is accepted, exactly like the SEC1 (`BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY`) form and like RSA PKCS#8.

**How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?**

Generate a PKCS#8 EC key (the default output of modern OpenSSL):

```
openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 > ec_pkcs8.pem
```

Pass it to `keyutil.PublicKeysFromFile("ec_pkcs8.pem")` (or use it as `--service-account-key-file`, which accepts a public or private key file). The identical key in SEC1 form works; an RSA key in PKCS#8 works; only the PKCS#8 EC key is rejected.

**Anything else we need to know?**

Fix: add a `x509.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey` fallback to `parseECPrivateKey`, mirroring `parseRSAPrivateKey`.

kubelet reports a volume as healthy when a CSI driver returns only unknown health conditions

`mapVolumeHealthStatus` drops any `VolumeHealthErrorType` it does not recognize, and the caller skips that entry:

```
status, ok := mapVolumeHealthStatus(entry.GetStatus())
if !ok {
	continue
}
```

When every entry in a reply is unknown, the mapper hands back an empty set. `volumehealth.manager` takes that as the new desired set and calls `SetPodVolumeHealth`, which clears whatever the driver reported before. What lands on `pod.status.volumeHealth` is then identical to a driver that reported no adverse condition at all.

Measured against master, asking for one volume each time:

| driver reply | conditions kubelet records |
| --- | --- |
| `[]` (no adverse condition) | 0 |
| `[DEGRADED, 9999]` | 1 (`Degraded`) |
| `[9999]` | 0 |
| `[UNKNOWN_VOLUME_HEALTH_TYPE]` | 0 |

Row 2 is what the spec asks for. Rows 3 and 4 are the problem: a driver reporting only values this kubelet does not know looks healthy, and an `Inaccessible` recorded a moment earlier is erased.

`mapStorageHealthStatus` has the same shape, so `csinode.status.storageHealth` behaves the same way.

Not to be read as healthy. KEP-1432 says it directly:

> COs MUST tolerate values they do not recognize. A CO that does not recognize a value SHOULD surface it for observability and MUST NOT misclassify it as healthy.

Nothing is surfaced today either. The value is dropped with no log line and no metric, so an operator has no way to tell this is happening.

With a node client that returns `VolumeHealth{VolumeId: "vol-A", HealthStatuses: [{Status: 9999, Reason: "MultipathLoss"}]}`:

```
conds, err := client.NodeGetVolumeHealth(ctx, "vol-A", "/staging", "/publish")
// conds is empty, err is nil
```

Feed that through `volumehealth.manager` after a probe that recorded `Inaccessible` and the condition is gone.

The mixed case has to keep working the way it does now. The spec example is explicit that an older CO "still acts on DEGRADED as before and surfaces the unknown value for observability without taking automated action on it", so failing a whole reply because it carries one unknown value would break that.

That leaves a choice I would rather not make on my own: when a reply has entries but none of them are recognized, should kubelet return an error so the previous conditions stay, or record something that says the driver reported a condition it cannot read? The first is the smaller change and needs no new API value.

One more thing while looking at this: `csi_volume_health_probe_total` is named in the KEP monitoring section as a kubelet metric, but I don't find it in tree. If it lands, a count of unknown values fits as an outcome label on it.

Pods stuck in ImagePullBackOff hold their resource requests on the node indefinitely, with no way to reclaim the capacity

A supported way to bound how long a Pod may sit in `ImagePullBackOff` before it becomes terminal, so that the node capacity its resource requests reserve is released. For example a kubelet-level `imagePullBackOffDeadline` (or an equivalent pod-level field): once exceeded, kubelet fails the Pod (`status.phase: Failed`) instead of retrying the pull forever, and the scheduler stops charging its requests to the node.

A Pod in `ImagePullBackOff` is already **bound** (`spec.nodeName` is set) and **non-terminal** (`status.phase: Pending`). kube-scheduler charges the requests of every bound Pod against the node's allocatable, and the only predicate anywhere in that path is "does it have a node name":

- [`pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L452-L454`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L452-L454) — `assignedPod()` is `len(pod.Spec.NodeName) != 0`
- [`pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L136-L138`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L136-L138) — assigned Pods go to the scheduler cache, unassigned ones to the scheduling queue
- [`pkg/scheduler/backend/cache/cache.go#L437-L448`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/backend/cache/cache.go#L437-L448) — `addPod()` → `n.info.AddPod(pod)`
- [`pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L439-L452`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L439-L452) — `NodeInfo.update()` → `n.Requested.MilliCPU += ...`
- [`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit.go#L699-L707`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit.go#L699-L707) — `fitsRequest()` rejects on `allocatable - requested`

Nothing in that chain inspects `status.phase`, container state, or the waiting reason. `assignedPod` has had the same one-line body at least since v1.28.

That accounting is correct on its own terms — the Pod is bound, and its requests must be honored the moment the image does become pullable. The gap is that **nothing ever reclaims the reservation when it never will be**: kubelet retries the pull indefinitely, the Pod never reaches a terminal phase, no eviction path applies, and cluster-autoscaler/descheduler see a legitimately-requesting Pod. So a Pod that can never start holds CPU and memory on a node forever while using none of it.

Real-world effects: unschedulable Pods behind a broken image reference (a typo, a rotated pull secret, a registry ACL, a purged tag), autoscaler scale-up to satisfy the phantom demand, and a permanent requests-vs-usage gap that breaks bin-packing and rightsizing. It is worst when a Job/CronJob controller keeps replacing failing Pods, since each replacement latches more capacity.

Existing workarounds are all outside the core behavior: `activeDeadlineSeconds` (Jobs only), a custom controller/descheduler policy, or deleting Pods by hand.

kind v1.34.0, single node, 20 CPU allocatable, 950m already requested by system Pods.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hog-unpullable
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: hog
    image: registry.invalid/does-not-exist:v0   # unpullable
    resources:
[... 16 more lines]
```

`hog-unpullable` is bound and stuck; `victim` cannot be scheduled:

```
$ kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,NODE:.spec.nodeName
NAME             PHASE     NODE
hog-unpullable   Pending   ipbo-proof-control-plane
victim           Pending   <none>

$ kubectl get pod hog-unpullable -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].state.waiting.reason}'
ImagePullBackOff

$ kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=victim
FailedScheduling   0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu. no new claims to deallocate,
[... 1 more lines]
```

The stuck Pod's 18 CPU are charged to the node:

```
$ kubectl describe node ipbo-proof-control-plane
  default   hog-unpullable   18 (90%)   0 (0%)   0 (0%)   0 (0%)   53s
Allocated resources:
  Resource   Requests
  cpu        18950m (94%)
```

Deleting only the stuck Pod releases the reservation and `victim` schedules immediately, with no other change:

```
$ kubectl delete pod hog-unpullable
pod "hog-unpullable" deleted from default namespace

$ kubectl get pod victim -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,NODE:.spec.nodeName
NAME     PHASE     NODE
victim   Running   ipbo-proof-control-plane

Allocated resources:
  Resource   Requests
  cpu        2950m (14%)
```

So the reservation held by the `ImagePullBackOff` Pod, not anything else, was what made the node unschedulable.

Related but not the same ask: #21657 asks the workload controllers to reschedule Pods that sit in `ContainerCreating`/image-not-ready. This issue is about the capacity the stuck Pod holds, and about giving kubelet a bounded pull-failure lifetime so the Pod becomes terminal and the requests are freed.

Open questions for the SIGs:

1. Should the deadline live in kubelet config (cluster-wide, with a per-Pod override) or as a Pod spec field?
2. Should it apply only to Pods that have never had a container start, so a running Pod restarting with a newly-broken image is not killed?
3. Would a `PodScheduled`/`Ready` condition carrying "capacity reserved but unstartable" be enough for a descheduler plugin to act on, without core changes?

[Scheduler] Redundant async preemption with already-deleted victim leaves preemptor stuck in unschedulable pool until 5-min flush

With `SchedulerAsyncPreemption` enabled (default since 1.32), a preemptor pod can be parked in the unschedulable pod pool for the full `DefaultPodMaxInUnschedulablePodsDuration` (5m0s) even though its preemption completed successfully milliseconds after it started.

Race chain (log quotes are from a captured kube-scheduler v=5 log, v1.33.0):

1. Cycle N fails filter → PostFilter picks node X, starts async preemption, victim V is evicted successfully ("Async Preemption finished completely ... result=success").
2. The victim-deletion event immediately requeues the preemptor → cycle N+1 runs *before* the scheduler cache observes V is gone → filter fails again → PostFilter starts a **second, redundant async preemption** for the same node and victim.
3. The second preemption finds V already deleted ("Victim Pod is already deleted") → issues zero API calls → **no PodDelete event is emitted**.
4. The deletion event from the first preemption *did* fire, but arrived while cycle N+1 was in-flight; it was consumed during in-flight event evaluation ("Checking event for in-flight pod ... hint=1"), and the pod still landed in the unschedulable pool because cycle N+1's PostFilter had already synchronously re-inserted the preemptor's UID into the preempting set, latching DefaultPreemption's PreEnqueue pending gate: "waiting for the preemption for this pod to be finished".
5. The gate's release mechanism is a victim-deletion event (`DefaultPreemption.EventsToRegister` returns nil). None will ever come. In a quiet cluster (no unrelated pod/node churn), the pod sits untouched until the 5-minute flush:

```
21:50:55.472  "Async Preemption finished completely" result=success
<total silence for this pod>
21:55:55.337  next "Update event for unscheduled pod" (external teardown)
```

Related: #140082 / #140054 fixed the sibling variant where the victim is preempted in-memory (WaitingPod / PreBind cancel). That fix explicitly does NOT cover this variant: the "Victim Pod is already deleted" path in `PreemptPod` returns `preemptedInMemory=false, nil`, on the assumption that the earlier deletion event suffices. Under redundant preemption + in-flight event consumption, it does not.

Once all async preemption work for a preemptor completes (successfully or as a no-op), the preemptor should be requeued promptly — the pending gate must not depend on a specific cluster event that a no-op preemption never produces.

Conditions required: SchedulerAsyncPreemption on (default); a high-priority pod P that needs preemption of a lower-priority victim V on node X; P fails filter again in a retry cycle that runs after V's deletion is issued but before the scheduler cache reflects it (cache-lag window) → PostFilter re-runs and re-selects the same (node, victim) pair.

We hit this repeatedly in an integration environment: kwok-simulated cluster (kwok v0.7.0, k8s v1.33.0 binaries, --runtime=binary), a scheduler extender that keeps rejecting P's alternative nodes so P keeps retrying against node X, and a slow control plane (containerized CI on overlayfs) that widens the cache-lag window. When the race hits, the preemptor stalls for exactly 5 minutes (matches DefaultPodMaxInUnschedulablePodsDuration to the second).

A targeted scheduler integration test (test/integration/scheduler/preemption) that drives a redundant preemption against an already-deleted victim and asserts the preemptor leaves the unschedulable pool without waiting for the flush would reproduce it reliably.

Suggested fix: in the async preemption goroutine (`prepareCandidateAsync`), treat the already-deleted last victim the same way #140054 treats the in-memory case — i.e. Activate the preemptor when no deletion event will be produced for the last victim. More generally, consider releasing the pending gate on async-preemption *completion* rather than on the eviction's observable side effect.

Why production clusters rarely notice: any unrelated cluster event whose QueueingHint returns Queue requeues the pod and the gate re-evaluates clean (the preemption finished long ago), so busy clusters self-heal in sub-second time. The full 5-minute stall only manifests in quiet clusters/queues — but the mechanism guarantee is still "worst case 5 min scheduling delay for a pod whose preemption already succeeded".

Evidence: full kube-scheduler v=5 log from the failing run is available on request (contains the complete cycle trace with in-flight event consumption).

Consider a stronger explicit warning against re-encoding SignJWTRequest.claims (KEP-740 ExternalJWTSigner)

**Context:**
The `SignJWTRequest.claims` field comment currently reads:

    // URL-safe base64 wrapped payload to be signed.
    // Exactly as it appears in the second segment of the JWT
    string claims = 1;

This is technically correct and, on a careful read, unambiguous — the payload is already base64url-encoded and must be used as-is.

**The issue:**
While implementing an `ExternalJWTSigner` from scratch, I initially misread this and re-encoded the already-encoded `claims` value before signing (assuming I was being handed raw JSON). This produced a structurally valid gRPC response and a structurally valid-looking JWT, but the signature was computed over the wrong byte string — the token failed verification silently, with no error surfaced anywhere in the pipeline (gRPC call succeeds, apiserver accepts it, only the final `kubectl` auth check fails).

I want to be clear this is a documentation-clarity suggestion, not a claim that the current wording is wrong — a second, careful read confirms it says what it needs to say. But because this failure mode is silent and hard to debug (no error at any layer points back to the encoding step), a small addition could save future implementers real debugging time.

**Suggested fix (optional, low-priority):**
Consider adding a one-line explicit warning, e.g.:
> "Do NOT base64url-encode this value again before use — it is already encoded."

or a short example showing correct usage (`signingInput := header + "." + claims`) directly in the proto comment or the KEP-740 README.

**Related:** KEP-740 tracking issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/740. Filed alongside a related finding on the `SignJWTResponse.signature` encoding requirement (RFC 7518 IEEE P1363 vs ASN.1 DER) — see #141669.

ExternalJWTSigner (KEP-740) proto doc doesn't specify required signature encoding (RFC 7518 IEEE P1363), causing silent verification failures

**What happened:**
The `ExternalJWTSigner.Sign` RPC's `SignJWTResponse.signature` field comment states only that the value must be "Already wrapped in URL-safe base64, exactly as it appears in the final segment of the JWT." It does not specify the required byte-level signature encoding for ECDSA algorithms (ES256/ES384/ES512).

RFC 7518 (JOSE, §3.4) requires ECDSA JWS signatures to be encoded as the fixed-length concatenation `R || S` (IEEE P1363/"raw" format) — e.g. 64 bytes for P-256. This is distinct from ASN.1 DER encoding, which Go's `crypto/ecdsa.Sign`/`SignASN1` produce by default (and which many other standard libraries default to as well).

An external signer implementation that signs with `crypto/ecdsa` and base64url-encodes the DER output directly will produce a structurally valid-looking gRPC response. `kube-apiserver` accepts the RPC call without error. However, `go-jose` (used by kube-apiserver for JWT verification) enforces the RFC 7518 fixed-length constraint and silently rejects the DER-encoded signature — no error surfaces to `kubectl` or the caller; the issued token simply fails all downstream authentication.

**Why this matters:**
This is a silent failure mode with no diagnostic signal at either the signer or the apiserver side. It's only detectable by manually verifying an issued token end-to-end. Any from-scratch `ExternalJWTSigner` implementation in a language whose ECDSA library doesn't default to IEEE P1363 (Go being the most obvious given it's Kubernetes' own implementation language) will hit this.

**Suggested fix:**
Add an explicit comment on `SignJWTResponse.signature` (and/or the `Sign` RPC doc) stating that ECDSA-algorithm signatures MUST be encoded per RFC 7518 §3.4 (raw `R || S`, fixed-length per curve), not ASN.1 DER. Optionally reference this same constraint in the KEP-740 README/design doc.

**Environment:** Encountered against `release-1.32` proto (`staging/src/k8s.io/externaljwt/apis/v1alpha1/api.proto`), Kubernetes v1.36 GA of KEP-740.

Related to KEP-740: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/740

Introduce model-based correctness and linearizability testing for k8s storage

We would like to introduce model-based correctness testing suite for Kubernetes storage (`k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage`), modeled after the [robustness testing approach used in etcd](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/tree/main/tests/robustness#etcd-robustness-testing).

This initiative introduces exploratory property-based and linearizability testing alongside existing table-driven tests to continuously verify consistency and watch invariants across concurrent reads, writes, watches, and cache invalidations.

- Build a formal sequential specification (`KVModel`) for Kubernetes key-value semantics with `ResourceVersion` tracking using [Porcupine](https://github.com/anishathalye/porcupine).
- Implement a concurrent exploratory traffic harness to execute randomized operations against storage implementations and verify strict blackbox linearizability.
- Validate baseline `etcd3` and `cacher` implementations under concurrent workloads.

Progress:

- Classify operations across four core verbs (`Get`, `List`, `Watch` .. ) across ~80 distinct API states (covering `ResourceVersion` variations, `ResourceVersionMatch` modes, pagination/continue tokens, selector predicates, preconditions, and terminal error codes).
- Provide a zero-dependency, non-invasive decorator (`coverage.Wrap`) to quantify and report API state coverage scorecards on existing and new storage test suites.

- Expand the model and test harness to cover:
  - Multi-level key hierarchies and prefix listings.
  - Watch stream invariants: event ordering, bookmark continuity, label/field selector transitions (`Added`, `Modified`, `Deleted`), and slow watcher ring buffer overflow (410 Gone handling).
  - Disruptive lifecycle events: watch cache reinitialization (`watchCache.Replace()` / `terminateAllWatchers`), compaction, and reflector resets.

---

```
staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/testing
    ├── coverage/                 # Standalone classification and scorecard library (zero external deps)
    └── correctness/              # Formal models and traffic generation
testing/integration/apiserver/correctness - Location of the test
```

As testing linearizability requires dependency on `github.com/anishathalye/porcupine` we will try to put the test under testing package to avoid introducing additional dependency on all users of apiserver library

1. **Blind Spots in Table-Driven Tests**: Existing storage unit and integration tests primarily target specific known code paths. They do not effectively explore race conditions, lock contention, or interleaved state changes across concurrent readers, writers, and watchers.
2. **Confidence in Advanced Storage Features**: With ongoing optimizations (e.g., `WatchList`, `ListFromCacheSnapshot`, `EtcdRangeStream`), subtle correctness bugs (such as stale list returns, broken bookmark continuity, or silent event drops during reflector relists) can easily go undetected without model-driven verification.
3. **Quantifiable Test Coverage**: Storage APIs have a high-dimensional configuration space (`ResourceVersionMatch`, `Continue`, `Limit`, `Predicate`, `Preconditions`). Classifying requests directly from `storage.Interface` allows measuring coverage of existing test suites and ensures no critical API state combinations are left untested.

e2e_node image configs use a negated character class instead of excluding the -cgroupsv1 suffix

The GCE node-e2e image selection filters candidate images with `image_regex` from the image config. `pickNewestImage` in `test/e2e_node/remote/gce/gce_runner.go` compiles it and keeps only images whose name matches:

```
imageRe := regexp.MustCompile(imageRegex)
...
if imageRegex != "" && !imageRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
```

The Ubuntu configs, and about nineteen image-config files in total, set:

```
image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"
```

The intent, from kubernetes/test-infra#35723, is to drop the `-cgroupsv1` suffix and force cgroup v2. The problem is that `[^-cgroupsv1]` is a negated character class. It constrains the final character to be none of `-`, `c`, `g`, `r`, `o`, `u`, `p`, `s`, `v`, `1`, so it does drop `-cgroupsv1`, but it also drops any image whose name ends in one of those characters. A build tagged `...v20260801` ends in `1` and gets filtered out.

An image should be excluded only when its name ends in `-cgroupsv1`. A normal newest image that happens to end in one of those characters should still be selectable. As written, the filter can silently skip the real newest image and fall back to an older one whose name ends in an allowed character.

Point a config's `image_regex` at `.*[^-cgroupsv1]$` and give the family a newest image whose name ends in `1`, such as a `v2026...01` build. `pickNewestImage` skips it and returns an older image.

RE2 has no negative lookahead, so `^(?!.*-cgroupsv1$).*` is not available. A separate exclude field matches the suffix directly and reads clearly:

```
ImageExcludeRegex string `json:"image_exclude_regex,omitempty"`
```

```
includeRe, err := regexp.Compile(imageRegex)
excludeRe, err := regexp.Compile(imageExcludeRegex)
...
if includeRe != nil && !includeRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
if excludeRe != nil && excludeRe.MatchString(instance.Name) {
    continue
}
```

A config then reads:

```
image_exclude_regex: "-cgroupsv1$"
```

This also gives a reason to switch the current `regexp.MustCompile` to `regexp.Compile`, so a bad config regex reports a clear error instead of panicking.

The `[^-cgroupsv1]$` pattern appears in about nineteen image-config files, so the config change spans several jobs once the field exists. This is separate from the image-resolution memory work in #141590 and #141434.

Namespace controller cleanup bottlenecks

When cleaning up namespaces under load or in clusters with complex resource graphs (multiple CRDs, APIServices, custom finalizers, stuck pods), the namespace controller suffers from several structural bottlenecks that cause worker pool starvation, cascading retries, and stuck namespaces.

This can be reproduced just with the integration test framework

```
diff --git a/test/integration/namespace/cleanup_bottlenecks_test.go b/test/integration/namespace/cleanup_bottlenecks_test.go
new file mode 100644
index 00000000000..64139bc1e63
--- /dev/null
+++ b/test/integration/namespace/cleanup_bottlenecks_test.go
@@ -0,0 +1,571 @@
+/*
+Copyright The Kubernetes Authors.
+
+Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the "License");
[... 569 more lines]
```

1. Discovery called on every sync iteration in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86c14f40a00aa91b672fe1f914d7b7920053af44/pkg/controller/namespace/deletion/namespaced_resources_deleter.go#L510 `d.discoverResourcesFn()` is called on every sync of every namespace without sharing or caching discovery results across workers.

If an aggregated APIService or CRD discovery endpoint is degraded or timing out, worker goroutines block in discovery (up to the 30s HTTP timeout). With the default 10 workers (`--concurrent-namespace-syncs=10`), a few slow discovery calls starve the entire controller worker pool.

 2. Sequential GVR deletion loop ( O(N) HTTP calls)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86c14f40a00aa91b672fe1f914d7b7920053af44/pkg/controller/namespace/deletion/namespaced_resources_deleter.go#L564-L588 , the deleter iterates over all namespaced GVRs sequentially. For every GVR, it runs:
1. `deleteCollection` (or fallback to `list` + per-item `delete`)
2. `listCollection` to verify removal

3. Pod head-of-line blocking, If a pod is stuck on something external, all other resources in the namespace sit untouched and un-deleted. Although this is on purpose because of security issues with network policies https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5080-ordered-namespace-deletion/README.md

4. Operator in-namespace teardown can deadlock if:
   1. An in-namespace controller/operator pod is deleted.
   2. Custom resources managed by that operator that have finalizers (e.g. `example.com/cleanup`) are processed *after* the pods are gone.
   3. With the operator dead, no controller is left to remove the finalizer on the CRs, leaving the namespace stuck in `Terminating` indefinitely.

5. "Unexpected items still remain" false error on async deletes
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86c14f40a00aa91b672fe1f914d7b7920053af44/pkg/controller/namespace/deletion/namespaced_resources_deleter.go#L484-L488, if `listCollection` finds remaining items that have no finalizers, the deleter returns `fmt.Errorf("unexpected items still remain...")`.

, non-`ResourcesRemainingError` errors cause `AddRateLimited(key)`, which triggers exponential backoff (up to 60s) and consumes tokens from the global workqueue rate limiter instead of using the normal requeue delay.

6. Global 10 QPS workqueue token bucket , https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9871c88769e2fe2ef940c9ad2a7b5734ff411c05/pkg/controller/namespace/namespace_controller.go#L75-L84 , `nsControllerRateLimiter()` uses a `TypedBucketRateLimiter` configured with 10 QPS / 100 bucket size shared across *all* namespace keys in the controller. Under burst namespace deletions with retries, the global rate limiter throttles requeue throughput across all namespaces.

Some potential solutions, although we need to evaluate the trade offs or make them tunable so operators can tune their systems accordantly to their environments

1. Use a cached discovery client with TTL or shared discovery invalidation rather than querying full server discovery on every single namespace sync.
2. Concurrent GVR deletion: Parallelize GVR cleanup within a namespace using a bounded worker pool.
3. Treat storage deletion lag as estimated wait: Return `ResourcesRemainingError` with a short wait when items without finalizers are still draining from etcd, rather than a hard failure with exponential backoff.
4. Per-namespace rate limiting: Avoid throttling all namespace retries against a single 10 QPS global bucket.

cgroup v2: Node Allocatable memory.max update can trigger reclaim/OOM before eviction

On cgroup v2, kubelet can lower the Node Allocatable `memory.max` for the pod cgroup while existing pod usage is already above the new limit.

`enforceNodeAllocatableCgroups` assumes that this update will fail until pod eviction reduces usage, and retries the cgroup update once per minute:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fbb9a10c7a0469a6f076873289e18bd680402c80/pkg/kubelet/cm/node_container_manager_linux.go#L101-L119

However, cgroup v2 documents that writing a lower `memory.max` triggers reclaim. If reclaim cannot bring usage below the limit, the memcg OOM killer is invoked; the write itself does not have to fail:

https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-max

This means a Node Allocatable change can cause synchronous reclaim and, when reclaim is insufficient, OOM kills before kubelet eviction has reduced pod usage. The behavior is specific to cgroup v2 and is not guaranteed to happen on every update.

Kubelet should not apply a lower Node Allocatable `memory.max` in a way that can OOM existing pods before eviction, or should use an explicit coordination mechanism between cgroup enforcement and eviction. A successful cgroup update should also mean that the requested limit was applied safely.

1. Use a Linux node with cgroup v2, `cgroupsPerQOS` enabled, and Node Allocatable enforcement for `pods`.
2. Run a pod workload whose cgroup usage is close to the current pod Node Allocatable memory.
3. Increase `systemReserved` or `kubeReserved` so the new Node Allocatable memory is below current pod usage, then restart kubelet.
4. Observe the `kubepods` cgroup `memory.max`, `memory.current`, and `memory.events`, together with kubelet eviction events.

The expected observation is that the cgroup limit write can succeed and reclaim starts immediately; if usage cannot be reduced far enough, `memory.events` may report `oom`/`oom_kill` before eviction completes.

This is separate from the InPlacePodVerticalScaling memory-resize discussion in #135670: this path updates the Node Allocatable pod cgroup during kubelet startup/enforcement.

Kubernetes master at `fbb9a10c7a0`.

core/v1: PodLogOptions.Stream has the wrong protobuf wire type in its struct tag

PodLogOptions.Stream is a string, but its Go struct tag says it is a varint (a number).

The tag is only a label. The generated proto and marshaller both treat the field as a string, and the wire format is correct. But libraries that read these tags at runtime believe the label, decide the field holds a number, then find a string in the Go struct and panic.

```
staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/types.go:
  Stream *string `json:"stream,omitempty" protobuf:"varint,10,opt,name=stream"`
```

It should say `bytes`, not `varint`

Argo Workflows hit this on every ?logOptions.*= log request after trying to move to grpc-gateway v2 (argoproj/argo-workflows#16796).

Build protoreflect message info for the type with google.golang.org/protobuf (its legacy/aberrant descriptor path derives descriptors from these tags). Any reflective set on a PodLogOptions field, for example populating it from URL query parameters through grpc-gateway v2, panics with `invalid Go type string for field k8s_io.api.core.v1.PodLogOptions.stream`

This is hopefully verifyable just by code inspection.

I'll put up a fix.

Claude tells me there are other inconsistencies, so I'll do a second PR for those.

nodelifecycle controller panics leaving master disruption mode when a node has no nodeHealthMap entry

kube-controller-manager can panic with a nil pointer dereference in the node lifecycle controller when a zone leaves master disruption mode while some nodes have no entry in the controller's nodeHealthMap.

With NodeControllerLeaseCircuitBreaker (Beta, default on since 1.37), when `consistencyStore.EnsureReady` reports a stale lease cache, `tryUpdateNodeHealth` short circuits and returns before building health data for any node that does not already have an entry. Its deferred writeback (`nc.nodeHealthMap.set(node.Name, nodeHealth)`) then stores an explicit nil for such nodes. Independently of that stored nil, an absent key behaves identically through `getDeepCopy`, because `deepCopy` on a nil receiver returns nil.

`handleDisruption` dereferences the result unconditionally when exiting full disruption mode:

```
v := nc.nodeHealthMap.getDeepCopy(nodes[i].Name)
v.probeTimestamp = now   // nil deref when the node has no entry
```

A node whose update was skipped in the cycle that observes recovery (for example because the breaker was open mid-cycle while other workers finished) reaches that loop with no entry, and the panic takes down the whole controller manager via HandleCrashWithContext. This is most likely to occur exactly during cluster recovery from a large outage, which is also when the lease cache is behind and disruption mode is active.

Unit-level reproduction against master:

```
--- FAIL: TestHandleDisruptionExitDoesNotPanicOnMissingNodeHealthEntry
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
        ...node_lifecycle_controller.go:1120
```

Leaving master disruption mode must tolerate nodes without nodeHealthMap entries; they simply get their entry built on the next successful cycle.

Construct the controller as in pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller_test.go, set `nc.zoneStates = {"": stateFullDisruption}`, leave `nodeHealthMap` empty, and call `handleDisruption` with one healthy node in zone "". The exit-disruption branch iterates the node list and panics at `v.probeTimestamp = now`.

Two-part fix: skip storing nil entries on the short circuit path, and skip nodes without health data in the exit loop instead of dereferencing them. I have a prepared branch with regression tests and will open a PR referencing this issue.

[Declarative Validation] Track beta→stable graduation of validation rules

A tracking issue for the beta→stable graduation of declarative validation rules, per KEP-5073.

Every DV rule currently at beta carries `since: "1.37"`, and there are no older ones, so nothing was eligible until v1.37 shipped. It has, which opens the wave.

Settled in [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141532#issuecomment-5403123232):

- **One API type per PR**, not one group. The type is the kind: a nested struct such as `IPBlock` goes with `NetworkPolicy`, not in a PR of its own. Deleting handwritten validation has no per-rule rollback and costs the mismatch comparison its baseline, so diffs stay small enough to read line by line.
- **`+k8s:beta` to stable only.** Dropping the prefix. `+k8s:alpha` promotion is out of scope and handled separately.
- **`meta` / ObjectMeta is out of scope** and tracked separately. This catches whole rows: `lifecycle`'s two rules are both on the embedded `metav1.ObjectMeta` (`lifecycle/v1alpha1/types.go:59` and `:251`), so that group is not claimable here.

Counts move as the wave lands. The total was 592 at filing, then 588, then 574 after #141533 (`discovery`) and #141677 (`batch`), and is 549 now: #141967 took `storage` 28 to 12 and #142119 took `node` 9 to 0. Only `types.go` carries the markers, so this returns the same number:

```

```

Comment here naming the **API type** you are taking, then open one PR for it. I will keep the table current.

On sourcing Owner from the tag's `owner:` field: that field does not exist. `+k8s:alpha` and `+k8s:beta` accept at most one argument and it has to be `since`, matching a version regex, so anything else is a generator error (`staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/levels.go:64-74`). A `grep -rho 'owner:' staging/src/k8s.io/api` returns nothing. So Owner comes from claims in this thread instead, unless you would rather the tag grew the field.
