**The only variable changed between the two runs was creation order.** The eviction target flipped exactly with it both times, with zero regard for which pod happened to be the DaemonSet.

Traced and confirmed against the `v1.36.1` tag (the same logic, unchanged in the relevant lines, is present at least as far back as `v1.35.0`, the tag used for #140984 — this is mature, long-standing scheduler code, not a recent regression).

**The only comparator used to choose a victim among equal-priority candidates:**

`pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go`, `MoreImportantPod` ([L89-L96](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go#L89-L96)):

```
// MoreImportantPod return true when priority of the first pod is higher than
// the second one. If two pods' priorities are equal, compare their StartTime,
// treating the older pod as more important.
func MoreImportantPod(pod1, pod2 *v1.Pod) bool {
	p1 := corev1helpers.PodPriority(pod1)
	p2 := corev1helpers.PodPriority(pod2)
	if p1 != p2 {
		return p1 > p2
	}
	return GetPodStartTime(pod1).Before(GetPodStartTime(pod2))
[... 1 more lines]
```

This is the sole ordering function `SelectVictimsOnNode` ([`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go#L207-L291`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go#L207-L291)) uses to sort potential victims and decide which to "reprieve" (keep) versus actually evict. At equal priority, the only signal is `StartTime` — nothing else. The node-level tiebreak functions in `pickOneNodeForPreemption` ([`pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L651-L731`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/pkg/scheduler/framework/preemption/preemption.go#L651-L731)) — fewest PDB violations, lowest highest-priority victim, smallest sum of victim priorities, fewest victims, latest start time — are equally blind to pod ownership. Grepping both files for `DaemonSet` or `OwnerReference` returns zero matches.

The only other axis considered anywhere in this logic is `PodDisruptionBudget` violation status (`filterPodsWithPDBViolation`, same file) — `SelectVictimsOnNode` tries hard to reprieve PDB-violating pods first, only evicting them if no other victim combination lets the preemptor fit. This is a real, existing lever, but non-default (DaemonSets essentially never carry a PDB — an odd fit for a one-pod-per-node workload), and even with one configured, the pod is still evicted as a last resort if genuinely necessary. It doesn't touch the underlying recoverability-cost blindness described here.

**Putting it together:** each function here is working exactly as documented — `MoreImportantPod`'s doc comment describes precisely the age-based behavior observed. The gap is that this heuristic has no way to express "this eviction is essentially free" versus "this eviction may be unrecoverable," and a DaemonSet pod hard-pinned to one node (via the same `NodeAffinity` mechanism traced in `#140984`) is the sharpest example of the latter.

`#140984` is about `isPreemptionAllowed`'s strict `<` — equal-priority pods can never preempt each other, full stop. This issue is about a different function (`SelectVictimsOnNode`/`MoreImportantPod`) that only runs *after* a genuinely higher-priority pod has already established it's allowed to preempt something — it's about which of several equally-valid victims gets picked. A complete fix to `#140984`'s equal-priority gate would not touch this at all; the two are independent gaps in different parts of the preemption code path that happen to produce the same user-visible symptom (a permanently stuck DaemonSet pod).

In Run 2 above, the stuck DaemonSet replacement's own inability to self-heal is fully explained by correct, working-as-intended behavior elsewhere (`#140984`'s equal-priority gate against `R`, and correctly-designed inability to preempt a genuinely higher-priority pod) — the actual root cause is one step earlier, at the original preemptor's victim-selection decision.

- The fake extended resource (`example.com/dummy`) technique was used instead of real CPU/memory specifically for determinism — `kind` nodes on a shared Docker host don't have genuinely scarce CPU/memory, which would make exact capacity control unreliable. This is a repro-methodology choice with no bearing on whether the underlying scheduler behavior is real; it reproduces identically with real resource requests sized against genuinely constrained nodes.
- Full manifests, the `kind` config, and complete raw `kubectl get events`/pod-state output from both runs are available and can be attached if useful for triage.

KCM supports start informer before acquiring a lease

The scheduler can start the informer before obtaining the lease and cache data, so that the standby instance can quickly perform scheduling when obtaining the lease. Can the KCM also start the informer to synchronize data, so that related work can be quickly started when the lease is obtained?

In some fault scenarios, quick recovery is indeed necessary.

kube-apiserver exits on startup when a nodeport repair reconcile error lands inside the 60s PostStartHook window

`kube-apiserver` exits roughly 60s after start, repeatedly:

```
F hooks.go:204] PostStartHook "start-service-ip-repair-controllers" failed: unable to perform initial IP and Port allocation check
```

The process fails its own PostStartHook via `klog.Fatal`, restarts, and can fail
again. On one cluster two replicas only became ready after 177 and 66 restarts.

The underlying condition is not exotic. **The nodeport repair loop failing is routine.** Its own counter: `apiserver_nodeport_repair_reconcile_errors_total` shows ~96 errors in 7 days on a healthy cluster.
After start-up they are harmless: `doRunOnce()` returns an error, `wait.Until` sleeps `IPRepairInterval` and retries.

**The bug is that the same error is fatal if it happens in the first 60 seconds.**

A transient first-attempt failure in the repair loop is retried rather than
terminating the apiserver.

`pkg/registry/core/service/portallocator/controller/repair.go` `doRunOnce()` LISTs
Services with no retry:

```
list, err := c.serviceClient.Services(metav1.NamespaceAll).List(context.TODO(), metav1.ListOptions{})
if err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("unable to refresh the port block: %v", err)
}
```

The `c.alloc.Get()` call immediately above it *is* defensively wrapped in a 30s
`wait.PollUntilContextTimeout`, with the comment "If etcd server is not running we
should wait for some time and fail only then." The LIST never got the equivalent.

On error, `RunUntil` skips `onFirstSuccess` and `wait.Until` sleeps
`IPRepairInterval` (`repairLoopInterval = 3 * time.Minute`), but the hook in
`pkg/registry/core/rest/storage_core.go` waits only:

```
case <-time.After(time.Minute):
	return goerrors.New("unable to perform initial IP and Port allocation check")
```

**Retry interval (3m) > deadline (60s)**, and there is no retry of the first
attempt, so a single error inside the window can never be recovered from.

`retry.RetryOnConflict` in `runOnce` does not help - it only retries Conflict.

Only the nodeport half is exposed. The ClusterIP repair is informer-backed via
`NewRepairIPAddress` when `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is enabled, so it waits for
cache sync properly. One `wg.Done()` fires and the other never does.

Removing the services watch cache (`--watch-cache-sizes=services#0`) stopped the
crashloop on the affected cluster: 6 days, 0 restarts, where previously it took
177 restarts to get one replica up. Since that flag's only effect is bypassing the
services cacher, the error consuming the window was coming from that path - i.e.
the LIST hitting a cacher that was not ready yet.

Relevant here: since `ResilientWatchCacheInitialization` went GA +
`LockToDefault: true` in 1.34, the not-ready-cache etcd fallback in
`CacheDelegator.GetList` only applies when `shouldDelegateListOnNotReadyCache()`
is true, which requires `pred.Limit > 0`:

```
func shouldDelegateListOnNotReadyCache(opts storage.ListOptions) bool {
	pred := opts.Predicate
	noLabelSelector := pred.Label == nil || pred.Label.Empty()
	noFieldSelector := pred.Field == nil || pred.Field.Empty()
	hasLimit := pred.Limit > 0
	return noLabelSelector && noFieldSelector && hasLimit
}
```

This LIST sets no limit, so it is not eligible.

I want to be explicit that this is the trigger we can demonstrate by experiment,
not one I can show you a captured log line for - see Evidence status below. The
retry gap is the bug regardless of which error consumes the window.

The failing hook name, from the apiserver's own log. The reconcile error counter above. That removing the services cacher resolves it. etcd p99 on the affected cluster is `list` 165ms / `get` 99ms - nothing in this path is slow,
which is why the fix is a retry rather than a larger timeout.

Wrap the Services LIST in `wait.PollUntilContextTimeout` (1s interval, 30s
timeout), mirroring the `alloc.Get()` call above it. Covers every cause of a
first-attempt failure. No import changes needed.

Alternatives that look attractive but are not:

- **Raising the 60s deadline** - hides the bug and still fails on slower clusters.
- **Adding a `Limit`** to satisfy `shouldDelegateListOnNotReadyCache` -
  `doRunOnce` does not paginate, so a partial list would make the repair conclude
  that live nodeports had leaked. Worse than the crash.
- **A startupProbe** - irrelevant, the process fails its own hook.

Any unpaginated in-process LIST during cacher initialization is exposed by the same
`Limit > 0` condition, and in-process callers generally do not paginate.
Independently, a PostStartHook whose deadline is shorter than the retry interval of
the work it waits on is a fragile pattern wherever it appears.

`--watch-cache-sizes` has applied to custom resources since v1.28, contrary to its documentation

The `--watch-cache-sizes` flag is documented as having no effect on custom resources:

> This option is only meaningful for resources built into the apiserver, **not ones defined by CRDs** or aggregated from external servers […]

In practice, since v1.28 the flag *does* take effect for custom resources served by the built-in apiextensions-apiserver. Passing `--watch-cache-sizes=<plural>.<group>#0` for a CRD disables the watch cache for that resource: the apiserver logs `Not using watch cache` for it at `-v=3`, and no `apiserver_watch_cache_*` series are reported for that resource.

More interestingly, the code appears to *intend* the documented behaviour, but the intent is not effective. In [`NewCRDRESTOptionsGetter`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4f5591ab57b75c0b8cabbff3031c9b956075c1ed/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/cmd/server/options/options.go#L138-L160):

```
etcdOptionsCopy := etcdOptions
etcdOptionsCopy.StorageConfig.Codec = ...
etcdOptionsCopy.StorageConfig.StorageObjectCountTracker = tracker
etcdOptionsCopy.WatchCacheSizes = nil // this control is not provided for custom resources
return etcdOptions.CreateRESTOptionsGetter(
    &genericoptions.SimpleStorageFactory{StorageConfig: etcdOptionsCopy.StorageConfig}, resourceTransformers)
```

`WatchCacheSizes` is cleared on `etcdOptionsCopy`, but the getter is built from the original `etcdOptions`; only `StorageConfig` is taken from the copy. [`CreateRESTOptionsGetter`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4f5591ab57b75c0b8cabbff3031c9b956075c1ed/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/etcd.go#L338-L346) stores `Options: *s` — i.e. the receiver's options, with `WatchCacheSizes` still populated. The assignment is dead code.

From there the flag reaches custom resources through the ordinary path: `crdHandler` passes its `restOptionsGetter` to `customresource.NewStorage`, which calls `store.CompleteWithOptions`, which calls `GetRESTOptions(e.DefaultQualifiedResource, …)` with the CRD's group/resource. [`StorageFactoryRestOptionsFactory.GetRESTOptions`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4f5591ab57b75c0b8cabbff3031c9b956075c1ed/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/etcd.go#L507-L523) does not distinguish built-in resources from custom ones — it only looks up a `schema.GroupResource` in the parsed sizes map and picks `UndecoratedStorage` vs `StorageWithCacher()`.

In kube-apiserver, the options handed to the apiextensions server are a plain copy of the command-line etcd options, so the user-supplied value is carried through: [`pkg/controlplane/apiserver/apiextensions.go#L52`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4f5591ab57b75c0b8cabbff3031c9b956075c1ed/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/apiextensions.go#L52) and [#L75](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4f5591ab57b75c0b8cabbff3031c9b956075c1ed/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/apiextensions.go#L75).

Either the documentation or the code should be authoritative — right now they disagree, and have for eight releases.

I'd like to raise the question of *which* one should change, because I don't think the answer is obvious:

1. **Bless the current behaviour** and fix the docs. `--watch-cache-sizes` has no remaining function other than switching the watch cache off for individual resources — as noted in #90058, that is precisely why the flag cannot be removed. There's no evident reason why that capability should be available for built-in resources but denied for custom ones, and #75677 previously reached the conclusion that supporting CRDs here "seems like a good thing". Large, high-churn custom resources are exactly the case where an operator may want to trade the watch cache's memory for direct etcd reads. This would mean deleting the dead `etcdOptionsCopy.WatchCacheSizes = nil` line and rewording the flag description.

A concrete case where this matters. Consider a custom resource used as chunked
transport for large payloads: a manifest archive produced during a backup or
snapshot operation is split across many objects, each carrying one chunk in its
`data` field. Such a resource has a combination of properties that makes the
watch cache pure overhead rather than an optimization:
- objects are numerous and individually large;
- they are written once and consumed once, so there is no repeated-read pattern
  for a cache to serve;
- the only client is the controller that produced them — there is no general
  population of watchers to amortize the cache across.

Since the watch cache keeps a complete decoded copy of every object of the
resource in the API server's memory (the btree-backed store, on top of the event
history), enabling it here duplicates the entire archive in the API server heap
for no hit-rate benefit at all. Disabling it for that single resource keeps the
API server's memory footprint independent of the size of the data being moved
through it.

There is currently no other way to achieve this: `--watch-cache=false` is global
and disabling the cache for every resource is obviously not acceptable, and no
per-CRD control exists. This is the same shape of problem as #96049 (the watch
cache being enabled for events, where it also brings no benefit) — except that
for custom resources the flag *does* work today, and the proposal is simply to
acknowledge that.

2. **Restore the pre-1.28 behaviour**, i.e. actually clear `WatchCacheSizes` on the options used to build the getter. This matches the current documentation and the original intent, but it removes a capability that has been observable and usable since v1.28.

I'd favour (1), but I'd rather have sig-api-machinery decide than send a PR that presumes an answer.

One request either way: since the current behaviour has been in place since v1.28, if (2) is chosen it would be good to treat it as a user-facing change with a release note rather than a silent cleanup — clusters relying on it would otherwise regain a watch cache they deliberately turned off, and only notice through memory growth.

1. Start kube-apiserver with `--watch-cache-sizes=foos.example.com#0 --v=3` (watch cache otherwise enabled).
2. Create a CRD with group `example.com` and plural `foos`, and a few objects of that type.
3. Observe `Not using watch cache" resource="foos.example.com"` in the apiserver log, and the absence of `apiserver_watch_cache_capacity{resource="foos.example.com"}` and related `apiserver_watch_cache_*` series.
4. Repeat without the flag: the cache is created and the metrics appear.

Note that there is currently no test covering this — `staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/cmd/server/options/` has no `options_test.go`, which is likely why the regression went unnoticed. Whichever resolution is chosen, a unit test asserting the decorator returned for a custom resource would be worth adding.

Related history: #75677, #90058, #91818, and #109201 (the PR that introduced the current wording — the CRD clause was accurate when written).

Up to and including v1.27, `NewCRDRESTOptionsGetter` cleared `WatchCacheSizes` on the same value it then passed to `ApplyTo`, so the documented behaviour held. The current shape was introduced by e9e4acb ("k8s.io/apiserver: remove skewed completion from EtcdOptions"), which replaced the intermediate `genericapiserver.Config` with `CreateRESTOptionsGetter` and, in doing so, made the `WatchCacheSizes = nil` line ineffective. The behaviour has been consistent from v1.28 through master.

@sttts, since this stems from the `CreateRESTOptionsGetter` refactor, and
@wojtek-t as the author of the dynamic watch cache work — your read on which of the two resolutions is correct would be very welcome.

kubelet: allocation manager checkpoint failure handling leads to state desynchronization and ghost pod allocations

In `pkg/kubelet/allocation/allocation_manager.go`, the In-Place Pod Vertical Scaling (IPPVS) allocation manager handles state persistence via `m.allocated` (backed by disk checkpoints in `state_checkpoint.go`).

During pod admission, resize, and teardown, error handling during disk checkpointing is inconsistent and non-transactional. Specifically, three closely related state management defects lead to split-brain states between in-memory allocation and disk checkpoints, node resource overcommit, and permanent "ghost" resource allocations:

1. **Silent Admission on Checkpoint Failure in `AddPod`**:
   In `AddPod()`, if `m.SetAllocatedResources(logger, pod)` fails (e.g. transient disk write error, permissions, or full disk), `AddPod` logs the error but proceeds to return `ok = true` without rolling back the in-memory allocation or failing pod admission:
   ```
   if ok && utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.InPlacePodVerticalScaling) {
       if err := m.SetAllocatedResources(logger, pod); err != nil {
           // TODO(vinaykul,InPlacePodVerticalScaling): Can we recover from this in some way? Investigate
           logger.Error(err, "SetPodAllocation failed", "pod", klog.KObj(pod))
       }
   }
   return ok, reason, message
   ```
   If Kubelet restarts immediately after, `NewStateCheckpoint` loads stale/missing checkpoint state from disk. `UpdatePodFromAllocation` returns initial unallocated resources, causing Kubelet to overcommit CPU/memory when admitting subsequent pods.

CPU Manager strict reservation can leave an empty default CPUSet

With the static CPU Manager policy and `strict-cpu-reservation`, exclusive allocations can consume every non-reserved CPU and leave `defaultCPUSet` empty.

KEP-4540 discusses shared workloads starving when the shared pool reaches zero. The current implementation has different side effects:

- reconcile skips shared containers when their resolved CPUSet is empty, so an existing container can keep its previous affinity and overlap newly exclusive CPUs;
- a new shared container gets no `CpusetCpus` value because `PreCreateContainer` treats the empty set as unset;
- after a kubelet restart, CPU Manager rejects a checkpoint that has assignments and an empty default CPUSet with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

The allocator removes assigned CPUs from the default set without checking whether the result is empty:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L727-L729

The empty-set handling is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/cpu_manager.go#L511-L519
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/internal_container_lifecycle_linux.go#L31-L36
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ec9448ceef13adbbcd3fa9f09b4d3c1fa54cc674/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L215-L223

An empty shared pool should have defined behavior that does not silently drop CPU affinity, overlap exclusive CPUs, or prevent kubelet from restarting.

The fix might reject the final exclusive allocation, reject configurations that can produce an empty shared pool, or use another policy. This issue does not assume which behavior is preferred.

On a four-CPU Linux node, configure the static policy with CPU 0 reserved:

```
cpuManagerPolicy: static
cpuManagerPolicyOptions:
  strict-cpu-reservation: "true"
reservedSystemCPUs: "0"
systemReserved:
  cpu: "1"
```

1. Remove the old CPU Manager state and start kubelet. The initial default CPUSet is `1-3`.
2. Start a BestEffort Pod so it uses the shared pool.
3. Start a Guaranteed Pod whose CPU and memory requests equal its limits and whose CPU request is `3`.
4. Check `/var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state`. The Guaranteed Pod owns CPUs `1-3` and `defaultCpuSet` is empty.
5. Wait for reconciliation. The BestEffort container cannot be updated to an empty CPUSet and may keep its previous `1-3` affinity.
6. Restart kubelet. CPU Manager state validation fails with `default cpuset cannot be empty`.

A BestEffort Pod created after step 4 also receives no explicit `CpusetCpus` from CPU Manager.

KEP-4540 intentionally archived minimum-shared-CPU proposals and added a shared-pool-size metric:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4540-strict-cpu-reservation

The KEP describes starvation as the zero-pool outcome. It does not describe dropping cpuset enforcement or rejecting the checkpoint after restart.

Watch cache shrinks before burst scale-up

We are load-testing and tuning the performance of our clusters, and we have observed an unusual behavior.

Under sustained bursty traffic, contrary to what we would normally expect, the watch cache size is repeatedly and rapidly halved, and then quickly scaled back up. See figure below.

[image]

This may cause several problems:

1. The watch cache size is directly related to the watcher channel size. When a burst arrives, some clients may request with a small watcher channel size. Once the channel buffer becomes full and blocks over 50ms, the API server terminates those watch connections. This has in fact occurred in our environment: our monitoring shows increases in both terminated watchers and initial events.

2. Every cache resize requires acquiring a lock and copying memory. This operation is relatively expensive, so repeated scale-down and scale-up cycles should ideally be avoided.

This traffic pattern is realistic in our environment because we operate clusters for long-running AI workloads, where Pods may be created or updated in bursts.

Would it make sense to introduce a hysteresis mechanism? For example, if the interval between the two most recent events is significantly shorter than the historical average inter-event interval, the buffer could temporarily avoid scaling down.

Below, I used AI to help me to generate some sample data and charts to illustrate how the cache size changes under different traffic patterns, both with and without this mechanism. These results may help evaluate whether such a change would improve the resizing behavior. see figure below:

[image]

It is also worth noting that, although this algorithm does not directly fix the issue described in [[#139250](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/139250)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/139250), it may still provide benefits for certain traffic patterns. see figure above`3a`.

In particular, it can prevent a burst from causing rapid cache expansion followed by a state where the buffer no longer satisfies the `full` condition, leaving the cache unable to scale down even when additional events arrive.

when burst requests arrive, do not half the cache size and scale it back.

1. Continuously create or update Pods at a high rate until the monitored watch cache size reaches its maximum.
2. Leave the cluster idle for a period of time. The required duration depends on the timeout configured for the API server.
3. Rapidly create or update Pods again, and observe that the monitored watch cache size is quickly halved before growing back to its maximum.

Burndown: Quantity int64 overflow and checked accessors

This tracks the work to fix `resource.Quantity`'s int64 accessor overflow behavior.

The 1.38 work is complete. Every row in Known Gaps is fixed on master. Nothing here needs to merge before code freeze (Nov 16). Everything still open is listed under "Deferred to 1.39".

Make `resource.Quantity` a value type that is safe to share between goroutines and correct for every input it accepts.

- **Done.** Value type semantics. Changing a Quantity never changes another copy of it.
- **Done.** Read-only methods never modify the Quantity, so concurrent reads are safe.
- **Done, except `AsInt64`.** Every method returns the same result whether the value is stored as int64 or `inf.Dec`.
- **Done.** Arithmetic never wraps, and accessors report overflow or saturate.
- **Done.** No input can make an operation use excessive CPU or take a long time to complete.
- **Done, except BinarySI at or above 8Ei.** Serialized output always reflects the current value and format.
- **Decoding done. Ratchets partly done.** Data written by earlier releases still decodes, and every tightened check reuses one ratchet so existing objects stay updatable. The LimitRanger and ResourceQuota ratchets are in. The pod, Node, PVC status and RuntimeClass ratchet is deferred.
- **Open gaps are pinned.** Every fixed behavior and every open gap is pinned by a test on both backends. Open gaps carry a `TODO(#141166)`.

| Expression | 1.37 | 1.38 | Gap |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `NewScaledQuantity(MaxInt64, 1).Value()` | `-10` | `MaxInt64` | multiply wraps around 64 bits |
| `MustParse("100E").Value()` | `0` | `MaxInt64` | conversion fails internally and falls back to zero |
| `MustParse("9223372036854775808").Value()`| `MinInt64` | `MaxInt64` | barely-too-large value becomes negative |
| `MustParse("-9.5Gi").Value()` | `8246196746` | `-10200547328` | bug in unsigned math flips the sign (#138510) |
| `NewQuantity(MinInt64).Neg()` | `MinInt64` | `9223372036854775808` | −MinInt64 doesn't fit in int64, so negation silently does nothing |
| `zero.Sub(MinInt64 quantity)` | `MinInt64` | `9223372036854775808` | similar to above, but using `.Sub()` instead of `.Neg()` |
| `MustParse("1000E").String()` | `"1"` | `"1e21"` | serialization drops the suffix for decimal values above 10^18 (#140459) |
| `ParseQuantity("1e4294967297")` | `10`, no error | `1e2147483647`, no error | exponent is truncated to 32 bits (2³²+1 → 1). In 1.38 it saturates instead. The set of accepted and rejected strings is the same as 1.37 |
| `NewQuantity(MinInt64).Neg(); q.AsInt64()` | `(MinInt64, true)` | `(0, false)` | `AsInt64` reports ok=true for a value that isn't the true result of the operation; same after `zero.Sub(MinInt64 quantity)` |
| `MustParse("1e100").Value()` vs `MustParse("1e100").ToDec().Value()` | `0` vs `MinInt64` | `MaxInt64` on both | same input, different wrong values on the int64 vs Dec backends |
| `MustParse("1e2147483647").Add(MustParse("1"))` | hangs | returns | the inf.Dec fallback aligns scales by writing 10^delta digits; same at Sub, AsScale/RoundUp, BinarySI String, AsFloat64Slow and DRA `quantityKeyAsDec`; reachable through pod-level resources validation and ResourceQuota admission; present in v1.37 and earlier |
| `MustParse("1e2147483647").Add(MustParse("1n"))` | `2e-9` | about `1e2147483647`; the `1n` rounds away from zero into the last kept digit | `int64Amount.Add/Sub` compute the scale delta in int32 and wrap instead of falling back |

- `Value`, `MilliValue` and `ScaledValue` saturate at `MinInt64` or `MaxInt64` instead of wrapping. (#141305)
- New: `AsScaledInt64`, `AsMilliInt64`, `MaxMilliQuantity`, `CacheString`. `DeepCopy` is deprecated because a plain copy is now enough. (#141305, #140674, #142277, #142974)
- `ParseQuantity` no longer expands exponents into digits. It rounds to 29 significant digits. Exponents outside the int32 range saturate. (#143085, #143245, #143648)
- `Add` and `Sub` round away from zero when the operands are more than 29 orders of magnitude apart. (#143075)
- `String()` keeps the magnitude above 10^18, and BinarySI values past `Ei` are written with a decimal exponent. (#140459, #143955, #144019)
- LimitRanger compares exactly. A request within one milli-unit of a bound is no longer rounded onto it. (#141348)
- CEL `isInteger()` and `asInteger()` return true and a value for 19-digit quantities that fit in int64. (#141938, tests in #142229)

These are accepted for 1.38 and tracked under "Deferred to 1.39".

- A stored string with an exponent outside the int32 range reads as the saturated value. 1.37 read the wrapped value.
- A stored value with more than 29 significant digits is rounded when it is read.
- 1.38 can write a string that a 1.37 parser is slow to read. The magnitude cap (#143246) did not merge.
- `AsInt64` returns `(0, false)` for every `inf.Dec`-backed value, including ones that fit.
- BinarySI parsing caps at 2^63-1, so `8Ei` reads as `9223372036854775807` and larger BinarySI values do not round-trip.
- Some checks tightened in 1.38 have no ratchet yet. An update that leaves a stored value unchanged can still be rejected. This needs a quantity past int64, or a negative one.

managedfields.ExtractInto fails with "expected map, got <nil>" when the field manager owns only fields absent from the object (e.g. Secret stringData).

`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields.ExtractInto` (and therefore all generated typed extractors in client-go, e.g. `applycorev1.ExtractSecret`) returns an error when the given field manager owns *only* fields that are not present on the supplied object:

```
unable to convert managed fields for <manager> to unstructured, expected map, got <nil>
```

The most common trigger is a Secret applied via server-side apply with `stringData`. The API server persists the values under `data`, but the managed fields entry records ownership of `f:stringData`, which never appears on any object read back from the API server:

```
managedFields:
- apiVersion: v1
  fieldsType: FieldsV1
  fieldsV1:
    f:stringData:
      f:kubeconfig: {}
  manager: my-manager
  operation: Apply
```

Extracting the fields owned by `my-manager` from the live Secret finds none of them, and `ExtractInto` fails instead of returning an empty applied configuration. The same happens for any manager whose owned fields don't materialize on the object, e.g. a Secret applied with an empty/absent `data` map (manager owns `f:data`, but the field is never persisted).

An empty applied configuration, consistent with `ExtractInto`'s documented behavior for the neighboring case where the manager owns nothing at all: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b037c6852709aa22e06432a1bf90275ea510467f/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/extract.go#L31-L36

In `ExtractInto`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/managedfields/extract.go

```
u := typedObj.ExtractItems(fieldset.Leaves()).AsValue().Unstructured()
m, ok := u.(map[string]interface{})
if !ok {
    return fmt.Errorf("unable to convert managed fields for %s to unstructured, expected map, got %T", fieldManager, u)
}
```

When `ExtractItems` extracts an empty set of leaves, the resulting value's `Unstructured()` is `nil` rather than an empty map[string]interface{}`, so the type assertion fails.

sig/network: API Server validation error message leaks full ClusterIP CIDR range to low-privileged users

When a user attempts to create a Service with an out-of-bounds `clusterIP` configuration (e.g., `1.1.1.1`), the `kube-apiserver` admission and validation layers reject the request but output the exact allocated `--service-cluster-ip-range` string inside the user-facing error message.

While the user must have RBAC permissions to create services to trigger this, it allows low-privileged users or compromised internal ServiceAccounts to systematically discover the internal ClusterIP network topology without having `describe cluster-info` or control plane configuration access.

The validation layer should return a generic error indicating that the requested IP is outside of the permissible cluster range, without explicitly printing the specific network boundaries (CIDR block) of the cluster.

kubelet eviction manager: transient HasDedicatedImageFs failure permanently disables disk-pressure eviction signals

While looking into `pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go`, I noticed a bug in how `HasDedicatedImageFs` failures are handled during eviction manager initialization.

In `synchronize()`, `HasDedicatedImageFs` is called when `m.dedicatedImageFs == nil`. If this call fails (for instance, if CRI or cadvisor isn't ready during early startup), `m.dedicatedImageFs` stays `nil` and `synchronize()` returns the error immediately.

Because `synchronize()` returns early on error, the eviction loop skips:
- `makeSignalObservations`
- `thresholdsMet` calculation
- updating `m.nodeConditions` (including `NodeDiskPressure`)
- setting up signal ranking functions (`m.signalToRankFunc`)

On the next iteration, since `m.dedicatedImageFs` is still `nil`, it attempts `HasDedicatedImageFs` again. If it keeps failing, disk eviction signals (`NodeDiskPressure`, ephemeral storage thresholds) are never initialized or evaluated, disabling disk eviction on the node.

There's already an inline TODO in `eviction_manager.go` acknowledging this:
```
// TODO: This should be refactored to log an error and retry the HasDedicatedImageFs
// If we have a transient error this will never be retried and we will not set eviction signals
```

Additionally, memory and PID pressure checks don't depend on `dedicatedImageFs`, but because `synchronize()` returns early when `HasDedicatedImageFs` fails, memory/PID evaluation is also skipped during those failed cycles.

If `HasDedicatedImageFs` fails:
1. It shouldn't block the rest of `synchronize()` from evaluating memory/PID thresholds.
2. Disk signal evaluation should be skipped for that cycle and retried on subsequent cycles without returning an error that halts the whole sync iteration.

1. Mock or simulate `HasDedicatedImageFs` returning an error on node start.
2. Observe `synchronize()` returning an error on every loop without reaching signal observation logic.
3. Observe that disk pressure signals/conditions are never set.

I can work on a fix for this by decoupling `HasDedicatedImageFs` error handling so transient failures don't block `synchronize()`, and adding test coverage in `eviction_manager_test.go`.

The kubelet immediately rejects the resize with "Resize is infeasible for Guaranteed Pods alongside CPU Manager policy static".

[Feature][Scheduler] PodGroup/CompositePodGroup scheduling failure diagnosis is insufficient for debugging

When a PodGroup (gang) fails to schedule, the diagnostic information surfaced to users — via pod conditions, pod events, and PodGroup conditions — is incomplete, misleading, and does not scale to large gangs. CompositePodGroup failures are even worse: the root CPG gets no conditions at all, and propagated messages lose hierarchy context.

This was tested on a kind cluster built from `master` (v1.37.0-beta.0, commit `7c2b6c32644`) with `GenericWorkload`, `CompositePodGroup`, and `TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling` feature gates enabled.

- #138991 proposes machine-readable scheduling diagnostics for individual Pods, but explicitly excludes Gang Scheduling / WAS-specific diagnostics ("avoid solving feature-specific diagnostics for Gang Scheduling, DRA, or preemption in the first step"). This issue focuses on the complementary problem: aggregated, human-readable diagnosis at the PodGroup and CompositePodGroup level, which is a WAS-specific concern that #138991 does not cover.
- PR #140311 (merged) propagated preemption status messages to PodGroup conditions. This issue extends that idea to all scheduling failure modes, not just preemption.
- KEP-6012 (CompositePodGroup API) defines the `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition type in the API, but the scheduler never patches it — no writer exists. This issue tracks that gap.

| Object | Condition | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `gang-pod-1` | `PodScheduled=False` | `0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).` |
| `gang-pod-2` | `PodScheduled=False` | `pod group is unschedulable, 0/1 placements are available, first placement status: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining` |
| PodGroup `gang-fail` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining, pod group preemption: No preemption victims found for incoming preemptor` |

**Issues:**
- `gang-pod-1` (evaluated first) retains its per-node `FitError`. `gang-pod-2` (evaluated second, after `PlacementFeasible` returned `Unschedulable`) gets a generic group-level message with no per-node diagnosis.
- In a gang with 100 pods, only the first-evaluated pod gets a useful `FitError`. The other 99 pods all get the same generic message. Users cannot tell which pods failed or why.
- The PodGroup condition does not aggregate per-pod failure reasons.

| Object | Condition | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `cpg-pod-1` | `PodScheduled=False` | `0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).` |
| `cpg-pod-2` | `PodScheduled=False` | `pod group is unschedulable, 0/1 placements are available, first placement status: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining` |
| PodGroup `child-pg-1` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (1) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 0 remaining...` |
| PodGroup `child-pg-2` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining...` |
| CompositePodGroup `cpg-root` | **(none)** | **No conditions patched at all** |

**Issues:**
- `child-pg-2` has `minCount: 1` in its spec, but its condition says `minCount (2)`. The "2" is actually the CPG root's `minGroupCount`, propagated verbatim by `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap` (`schedule_one_podgroup.go`). The "scheduled/remaining" counts refer to child **groups**, not pods — but the message doesn't say that.
- `cpg-root` has no conditions. The `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition type is defined in the API (`staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1alpha3/types.go:1387`) but never written — `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` explicitly skips CompositePodGroups.
- Neither pod's message mentions the CPG hierarchy. A user seeing `minCount (2) cannot be satisfied` on `cpg-pod-2` has no way to know this came from `cpg-root` without manually walking `spec.parentCompositePodGroupName` references.

1. **Individual pod `FitError` is destroyed by group-level propagation.** In `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap` (`schedule_one_podgroup.go:755`), when a parent CPG fails, the child's entire `podGroupAlgorithmResult` (including per-pod `podResults`) is replaced with the parent's status. Individual `FitError`s are lost.

2. **`PlacementFeasible` message is ambiguous.** `GangScheduling.PlacementFeasible` (`gangscheduling.go`) uses the same message format for both PodGroup (`MinCount` = pod count) and CompositePodGroup (`MinGroupCount` = child group count): `"minCount (%d) cannot be satisfied: %d scheduled, %d remaining"`. No group name, no indication of what "scheduled/remaining" counts.

3. **No diagnosis aggregation at the PodGroup level.** `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` sets the PodGroup condition message to `podGroupResult.status.Message()` — the raw group-level status. The per-pod `algorithmResult` data (which nodes each pod was placed on, which nodes rejected it, and why) is available at this point but discarded.

4. **CompositePodGroup conditions are never patched.** `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` skips CPGs (`if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil { continue }`). No `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` utility exists.

Design a layered diagnosis mechanism: Pod → PodGroup → CompositePodGroup, where each layer provides the right granularity and cross-references the others.

In `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`, stop overwriting individual pod statuses with generic group messages:

- **Pod individually failed**: keep its `FitError` as-is (already works for the first-evaluated pod).
- **Pod individually succeeded but group failed**: `"pod is schedulable but gang scheduling failed (PodGroup <name>): <group reason>. See PodGroup condition for details."`
- **Pod never evaluated** (gang aborted early): `"pod was not evaluated: gang scheduling aborted early (PodGroup <name>). See PodGroup condition for failure summary."`

This ensures every pod's condition tells the user whether the failure is pod-level or group-level, and where to find details.

Build a structured diagnosis message from `podGroupAlgorithmResult.podResults`, which contains per-pod `SuggestedHost` (placement node) and `FitError.Diagnosis.NodeToStatus` (structured per-node rejection reasons).

**Small gang (≤10 pods)** — list each pod:

```
Gang scheduling failed: 2/5 pods placed, minCount=4.

Placement:
  node-A: pod-1 (cpu:4, mem:1Gi), pod-2 (cpu:4, mem:1Gi)

Failed pods:
  pod-3: node-A: Insufficient cpu; node-B: untolerated taint
  pod-4: node-A: Insufficient cpu; node-B: untolerated taint
  pod-5: not evaluated (gang aborted)
```

This shows the causal relationship: pod-1 and pod-2 consumed 8 cpu on node-A, so pod-3/pod-4 got `Insufficient cpu` on node-A.

**Large gang (>10 pods)** — aggregate by node and by failure signature:

```
Gang scheduling failed: 30/100 pods placed, minCount=80.

Placement by node (30 pods):
  node-A: 15 pods (cpu: 60/64)
  node-B: 10 pods (cpu: 40/64)
  node-C: 5 pods (cpu: 20/64)

Failed pods (70), by failure signature:
  45 pods: Insufficient cpu
  15 pods: Insufficient cpu + untolerated taint
[... 5 more lines]
```

Key design decisions:
- **Failure signature grouping**: extract the set of unique rejection reasons from each pod's `FitError.Diagnosis.NodeToStatus`, group pods with identical reason sets. This preserves the combination relationship (e.g., "Insufficient cpu + untolerated taint" is distinct from "Insufficient cpu") while compressing 100 pods into a few lines.
- **Placement by node with resource usage**: aggregate placed pods per node, showing total requested resources vs. node allocatable. This lets users see why subsequent pods were rejected on that node.
- **Top rejecting nodes**: cross-reference placement and rejection — "node-A rejected 70 pods for Insufficient cpu, and node-A has 60/64 cpu used by placed pods." The causal link is explicit.

- Implement `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` (analogous to existing `PatchPodGroupStatus` in `pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go`).
- In `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`, stop skipping CPGs — patch `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition.
- In `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap`, annotate propagated messages with the source CPG name: `"failed via CompositePodGroup <name>: <reason>"`.
- In `PlacementFeasible`, distinguish pods vs. child groups in the message: `"CompositePodGroup <name>: minGroupCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining child groups"`.

CPG condition format:

```
CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False

Composite gang scheduling failed: 0/2 child groups schedulable, minGroupCount=2.
  child-pg-1: 0/1 pods placed (minCount=1). Failure: Insufficient cpu.
  child-pg-2: 0/1 pods placed (minCount=1). Failure: Insufficient cpu.
```

Current:
```
minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining
```

Proposed (PodGroup):
```
PodGroup gang-fail: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining pods
```

Proposed (CompositePodGroup):
```
CompositePodGroup cpg-root: minGroupCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining child groups
```

- All changes are in scheduler internals (`schedule_one_podgroup.go`, `gangscheduling.go`, `util/utils.go`).
- No API type changes — all information fits in existing `metav1.Condition.Message` fields.
- No changes to the scheduling algorithm itself — only to how results are reported.

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`: build aggregated diagnosis, patch CPG conditions |
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap`: annotate propagated messages with CPG name |
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | New: `buildPodGroupDiagnosis`, `aggregateFailureSignatures`, `buildPlacementMap` |
| `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/gangscheduling/gangscheduling.go` | `PlacementFeasible`: include group name, distinguish pods vs. child groups |
| `pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go` | New: `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` |

DaemonSet pod can be permanently stuck Pending when its target node is saturated by equal-priority pods during mass rescheduling

**TL;DR:** DaemonSet pods get no priority advantage over regular pods. Since a DaemonSet pod can only ever run on the one specific node it targets, if that node fills up with equal-priority pods first, the DaemonSet pod is stuck `Pending` forever — preemption only evicts strictly *lower*-priority pods, so there is no recovery path. Reproducible deterministically in under a minute on vanilla Kubernetes (see "How can we reproduce it" below); also confirmed live on a real-world cluster after 11 days stuck with no self-healing.

After a batch of nodes were recreated (health-check driven remediation) and rejoined the cluster, a DaemonSet pod whose only eligible node (per its DaemonSet-generated node affinity) had already been filled to that node's pod capacity by pods belonging to an unrelated ReplicaSet remained `Pending` indefinitely — until an operator manually deleted another pod on that node to free capacity.

Sequence observed:

1. A node-health event caused several worker and control-plane nodes to be remediated (deleted and recreated) at roughly the same time, on a cluster topology of 3 control-plane + 5 worker nodes.
2. Pods that were running on the deleted worker nodes (from a 300-replica ReplicaSet with no `topologySpreadConstraints`) became unschedulable and queued up as Pending.
3. As replacement nodes rejoined the cluster one at a time, the scheduler bound the queued ReplicaSet pods to the first available node until it hit the kubelet's max-pods ceiling (110), before moving on to spread remaining pods across the other newly-available nodes.
4. The DaemonSet controller's pod for that same node could only ever target that one node (DaemonSet pods are scheduled via a node-specific affinity/nodeName, not floated across the cluster), but by the time it was considered, the node had no remaining pod capacity.
5. The DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods all ran at the same (default, unset) priority, so the DaemonSet pod could not trigger preemption to reclaim a slot on its required node.
6. Result: the DaemonSet pod stayed `Pending` indefinitely — not delayed, but permanently stuck, with no self-healing path — because there is no capacity-reservation or priority mechanism ensuring a DaemonSet pod can still land on its node once that node fills up with regular pods.

**Scheduler event observed on the stuck pod:**

```
Warning  FailedScheduling  (repeating)  default-scheduler
0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity].
no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found
for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
```

**Only available workaround:** manually cordon the saturated node and delete one non-DaemonSet pod on it. The evicted pod reschedules elsewhere (node is cordoned); the DaemonSet pod then binds to the freed slot because DaemonSet pods tolerate `NoSchedule`. This requires manual identification of the affected node/pod per stuck DaemonSet and causes disruption to an unrelated, already-running workload — it is not a fix, and does not scale when multiple DaemonSets or many single-replica workloads are involved.

A DaemonSet is a workload primitive with an implicit scheduling guarantee: exactly one pod per eligible node. That guarantee should not be silently defeated by unrelated workloads racing to fill node capacity during bulk/concurrent node-Ready events. Expected behavior is one of:

- The scheduler/kubelet admission path reserves headroom for DaemonSet pods on a node before admitting other pending pods, similar in spirit to how DaemonSet pods already bypass normal scheduling predicates for taints/tolerations; or
- DaemonSet pods are assigned a priority (or an equivalent mechanism) sufficient to preempt same/lower-priority pods on their required node when no other placement option exists for them, so they are not permanently blocked by a race they cannot participate in; or
- At minimum, this failure mode is called out as a documented limitation with a supported mitigation, rather than silently producing an unrecoverable Pending DaemonSet pod.

The original observation involved a large multi-node cluster and a mass node-remediation event, but neither is actually required to trigger the bug — that context is just *one* way a node ends up saturated by equal-priority pods. The minimal reproduction below removes all of that and triggers the same failure deterministically, in under a minute, on a 3-node [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster running vanilla, publicly-released upstream Kubernetes. No cloud provider, no CNI plugin choice, no node churn simulation needed.

**Prerequisites:** Docker and `kind` installed locally.

```
# 1. Create a 3-node cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name daemonset-repro --config kind-config.yaml
[... 59 more lines]
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
nginx-daemonset-6w8q2   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-worker2
nginx-daemonset-hqq47   0/1     Pending   0          10s   <none>
nginx-daemonset-j7ggb   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-control-plane
```

The pod for the saturated worker is immediately and permanently `Pending`:

```
$ kubectl describe pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47
...
Priority:         0
...
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  21s   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods,
  2 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption:
  0/3 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 2 Preemption is not
[... 10 more lines]
```

Identical signature to the original report: node-pinned `NodeAffinity` on `metadata.name`, both pods at priority `0`, and `No preemption victims found for incoming pod`. This state does not resolve on its own — polling the pod hours later shows the same event repeating, exactly as in the 11-day-stuck pods described further below.

Kubernetes version for this run: `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (vanilla, publicly released upstream build — this repro has no dependency on any downstream distribution or unreleased version).

The steps above deliberately create the blocking pods before the DaemonSet pod, which trivially guarantees a loss. To check whether the failure is an artifact of that ordering, we re-ran it two more ways on the same live cluster, deleting an already-`Running`, steady-state DaemonSet pod and an already-`Running` set of filler pods together, then letting both controllers race to recreate replacements for the freed capacity — the actual dynamic during a real node recovery, where nothing is deliberately sequenced.

- **Fully simultaneous deletion, no pre-existing backlog advantage:** both the DaemonSet pod and 5 filler pods on a node were force-deleted in the same command. The DaemonSet's replacement pod *won* one of the 6 freed slots and stayed `Running`. This is an honest, useful negative result: a genuinely concurrent race between freshly-created pods is probabilistic, not a guaranteed DaemonSet loss — the scheduler has no bias against DaemonSet pods specifically when everything enters the queue at the same moment.
- **Freed single slot with a pre-existing backlog (matches the original incident's actual mechanics):** with 15 filler-pod replicas already sitting `Pending` beforehand — a long-queued backlog, exactly like the 300-replica overflow in the original report — we deleted only the running DaemonSet pod, freeing exactly one slot. A backlog pod created **26 seconds before** the DaemonSet's replacement pod even existed claimed the slot instantly. The DaemonSet's new replacement was left with the identical `FailedScheduling` / `No preemption victims found for incoming pod` signature, confirmed still `Pending` 30+ seconds later.

This second variant is the faithful reproduction of the real-world trigger, and it isn't a coin flip: a DaemonSet controller can only create its replacement pod *after* it observes the old one is gone, which is necessarily later than pods that were already queued and waiting for capacity before the node came back. Against an already-waiting backlog, the DaemonSet pod is structurally late to the scheduling queue every time, not merely unlucky — which is exactly the sequence described in the original incident ("as soon as the first worker node comes back, scheduler tries to assign all the pending pods to that node... the daemonset pod remains in pending state"). The first variant shows the underlying preemption gap has no protective bias either way when pods start even; the second shows why, in the specific conditions that actually occur during a mass-remediation event, the DaemonSet pod reliably loses.

Traced against the `v1.35.0` tag and confirmed live on `v1.36.1` (see the reproduction above). Four pieces combine to produce this failure mode; none of them is broken in isolation — each does exactly what it's documented to do — but the composition leaves DaemonSet pods with no recovery path once their one eligible node saturates.

**1. A DaemonSet pod is hard-pinned to exactly one node, with no fallback**

`pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go`, `ReplaceDaemonSetPodNodeNameNodeAffinity` ([L176-221](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go#L176-L221)) rewrites the pod's `NodeAffinity` into a `RequiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for one specific node before the pod is created. Once that pod exists, it has exactly one place in the entire cluster it can ever bind to — if that node can't admit it, it is `Pending` with no alternative, by design.

**2. The DaemonSet controller never assigns the pod an elevated priority**

`pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go` (1472 lines in this tag) has zero references to `Priority`/`PriorityClassName` anywhere in the file — the controller copies the user's pod template verbatim and leaves priority entirely up to whatever (if anything) the DaemonSet author put in `spec.template.spec.priorityClassName`. Nothing defaults it, validates it, or nudges toward it. Contrast this with core system DaemonSets like `kube-proxy`, which only avoid this failure mode by convention — their manifests explicitly set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical`. That convention is not enforced anywhere in the DaemonSet API or controller, so any user-authored DaemonSet (including the minimal nginx one used in the repro above, and most example manifests in the docs) ships without it.

**3. With no PriorityClassName set, admission assigns priority 0 — identical to any other pod**

`plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go`, `admitPod` ([L162-172](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L162-L172)): on create, if `pod.Spec.PriorityClassName` is empty, the plugin calls `getDefaultPriority()` and stamps the result onto the pod. That resolves to `scheduling.DefaultPriorityWhenNoDefaultClassExists`, defined in `pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go` ([L24-28](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go#L24-L28)) as literal `0` — unless the cluster happens to have a PriorityClass with `globalDefault: true`. A vanilla ReplicaSet pod with no priority class gets exactly the same value. By the time both pods reach the scheduler, there is nothing distinguishing the DaemonSet pod from the ReplicaSet pod.

**4. The preemption path categorically excludes equal-priority pods as victims**

`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go`, `isPreemptionAllowed` ([L349-352](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go#L349-L352)):

```
func (pl *DefaultPreemption) isPreemptionAllowed(nodeInfo fwk.NodeInfo, victim fwk.PodInfo, preemptor *v1.Pod) bool {
	// The victim must have lower priority than the preemptor, in addition to any filtering implemented by IsEligiblePod
	return corev1helpers.PodPriority(victim.GetPod()) < corev1helpers.PodPriority(preemptor) && pl.IsEligiblePod(nodeInfo, victim, preemptor)
}
```

This is a strict `<`, not `<=`. Given step 3, both the DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods on the saturated node carry priority `0`, so this check evaluates `false` for every pod on that node. The scheduler reports `preemption: ... No preemption victims found for incoming pod` — exactly the event captured in this report — and there is no retry path, because nothing about the node's occupancy changes on its own once the ReplicaSet pods are `Running`.

**Putting it together:** (1) removes every fallback placement option for the DaemonSet pod. (2)-(4) remove the only mechanism — preemption — that could reclaim space once the node fills. Each function is working as documented; the gap is structural: a DaemonSet pod using a template without an explicit, elevated `priorityClassName` has no guaranteed recovery path once its one eligible node saturates with equal-or-higher-priority pods. This is why we believe the most direct fix point is (2)/(3) — either give DaemonSet pods an elevated default priority (mirroring the `system-node-critical` convention used by core system DaemonSets) so they can preempt when they have no alternative node, or add a DaemonSet-aware carve-out in `IsEligiblePod`/`isPreemptionAllowed` for a pod's uniquely-eligible node — rather than at (1) or the general scheduling-imbalance behavior tracked in #136782, since fixing spread alone would reduce how often the node saturates but would not remove the permanent-stuck outcome once it does.

In addition to the vanilla kind reproduction above, this was also confirmed on a second, independent real-world cluster — a downstream Kubernetes distribution (3 control-plane + 5 worker RHEL nodes, Antrea CNI; the original incident was observed on both Antrea and Calico clusters, so it isn't CNI-specific;) — separate from the cluster where this was first observed. Two DaemonSet pods were found stuck `Pending` for 11 days at the time of capture:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Stuck pod priority | `nginx-daemonset-2c96z` and `nginx-daemonset-nsb7r`: both `Priority: 0`, no `priorityClassName` |
| FailedScheduling event | `0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.` — repeated **3186 times over 11 days** for each pod. It never self-heals. |
| Node pin (matches code path 1) | Each pod's `nodeAffinity` is a `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for exactly one node — e.g. `{"matchFields":[{"key":"metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["<single-node>"]}]}`. No alternative placement exists. |
| DaemonSet template priority (matches code path 2/3) | `kubectl get ds nginx-daemonset -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.priorityClassName}'` → empty. No elevated priority requested anywhere. |
| Target node saturation | Both target nodes: `capacity.pods=110`, `allocatable.pods=110`, `describe node` confirms `Non-terminated Pods: (110 in total)` — exactly at the ceiling, not over/under. |
| Blocking pods' priority (matches code path 4) | Sampled `nginx-rs-new` replica pods occupying both saturated nodes: `priority=0` on every one checked, and the ReplicaSet template has no `priorityClassName` and no `topologySpreadConstraints`. Identical priority to the stuck DaemonSet pod → `isPreemptionAllowed`'s strict `<` check excludes them all as victims, exactly as traced in the code above. |

Two independently-stuck pods on a cluster unrelated to the one where this was first reported rules out a one-off fluke and confirms every link in the "Where this happens in the code" chain against a live, current build.

- This was first noticed as an apparent regression after node remediations triggered by an unrelated control-plane availability issue, but the scheduling behavior itself is version/platform-agnostic once the preconditions above are met — it is a race between DaemonSet placement and bulk regular-pod placement, not specific to any particular trigger for node churn.
- Related to [#136782](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136782), which describes the scheduler concentrating a burst of newly-schedulable pods onto the first available node rather than spreading them during a scale-up event. That issue is about scheduling *imbalance*; this issue is about the *lack of any recovery path* once a DaemonSet's sole eligible node is filled by equal-priority pods — a fix to the spreading behavior in #136782 would reduce how often this triggers, but would not eliminate it, since any single saturating event is sufficient to strand a DaemonSet pod indefinitely.
- Also related: [#54190](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/54190) ("DaemonSet controller should support preemption"), filed in 2017, which proposed essentially the same fix point identified independently here (point 2/3 above). It appears to have gone unimplemented — this report includes a concrete, current-version reproduction and code trace in case that's useful context for re-opening the discussion.
- Workaround guidance we are currently giving is to set [topologySpreadConstraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints/) on all production workloads to reduce the odds of a single node saturating. This is a mitigation on the "other" workloads, not a fix, and it is not something the platform can enforce or guarantee for arbitrary workloads, so DaemonSets remain structurally exposed to this failure mode.

	staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go:831 +0x2a5

I only have the one occurrence, on 2026-07-27, on a PR that touches nothing outside `pkg/kubelet/prober`. I did not find an existing issue for this test or for a `panic: synthetic error` in this package, open or closed, so I am filing rather than assuming it is known. If triage shows this is long-standing, feel free to fold it into whatever is already tracking it.

N/A (presubmit)

This looks like a genuine cross-test race on a process-global flag, not just timing noise.

1. `fatalOnDecodeError` is a package-level `atomic.Bool` in `etcd3`, so it is process-global for the whole test binary:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L65-L72

2. `TestOnlySetFatalOnDecodeError` flips it and restores the old value from `tb.Cleanup`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L81-L88

3. `TestDeleteWithConflictAndExpectedDecodeError` is the test that disables the panic, because it deliberately stores bytes that cannot be decoded. Its `testCodec.Decode` is what returns `errors.New("synthetic error")` (`cacher_test.go:197`):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher_test.go#L221-L233

4. Watch events are decoded on background goroutines spawned by `concurrentOrderedEventProcessing.scheduleEventProcessing`, and nothing joins those goroutines to the test that created the cacher:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L609-L617

5. `decodeObj` panics outright when the flag is set, on that goroutine, with no `recover` anywhere on the stack:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L878-L888

So a decode error from the test that legitimately expects one can be processed on a leaked goroutine after that test's `Cleanup` has already restored `fatalOnDecodeError` to true, and the panic takes down the binary under an unrelated test's name.

The attribution is provably wrong in this run: `TestDeleteWithSuggestionAndMissingExpectedTransformOrDecodeError` calls plain `testSetup(t)` with no `testCodec` and no `testTransformer`, never calls `setFailing`, and never calls `TestOnlySetFatalOnDecodeError`. It has no way to produce a "synthetic error" at all. The only tests that inject that error are the sibling `...ExpectedTransformError` / `...ExpectedDecodeError` tests above it in the same file.

The comment on the panic ("an error here is due to a coder mistake if the defer does not catch it") assumes a `defer` upstack catches it. On the concurrent event-processing path there is no such defer.

Possible directions, in rough order of how targeted they are. I have not written a patch, and I would rather sig-api-machinery pick, since this touches the fatal-on-decode contract:

1. Make the flag scoped rather than process-global, e.g. carry it on the `watcher` created for that store, so one test's opt-out cannot leak into another test's goroutines.
2. Have the concurrent processing goroutine `recover` and turn the panic into a normal transform error, so the fatal-on-decode behavior still surfaces on the owning watch instead of killing the binary.
3. Ensure the cacher's watch goroutines are drained before `TestOnlySetFatalOnDecodeError`'s `Cleanup` restores the flag, which fixes the ordering without changing production code.

If the concurrent path is only enabled under a particular concurrency setting or feature gate, that would also explain why this shows up rarely rather than every run.

Reproducing it directly is awkward because it depends on goroutine timing at test teardown. `go test -race -count=N ./staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/ -run 'TestDeleteWith'` is where I would start.

No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination

#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.

kubelet: stopping a probe worker does not cancel an in-flight exec probe

Stopping a probe worker does not cancel a probe that is already executing. `worker.stop()` does a non-blocking send on `stopCh`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L204-L211

and `run()` only selects on `stopCh` between probes, after `doProbe` returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L186-L201

So when `RemovePod` / `CleanupPods` / `StopLivenessAndStartup` stops a worker, an exec probe that is mid-flight keeps running against a container that is being killed. It ends only when its own `TimeoutSeconds` elapses, and `runProbeWithRetries` will retry up to `maxProbeRetries` (3) if the attempt errors, so the worst case is roughly `3 * TimeoutSeconds` after `stop()`. `TimeoutSeconds` is user-controlled, so that can be minutes. The worker also records the result of that last probe after it was told to stop.

Between #130487 (v1.35.0) and #140882 this happened to be papered over: workers inherited the pod worker's sync context, which the pod worker cancels at teardown, so in-flight execs died promptly. That was not a fix, it was the cause of #140881. The same cancellation also killed every readiness probe for the entire grace period, which is the much worse bug. #140882 detaches the worker context with `context.WithoutCancel` and restores the pre-1.35 behavior, which reinstates this gap.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659050743.

`stop()` cancels the probe that is currently executing, and the worker goroutine exits promptly instead of waiting out `TimeoutSeconds`.

Pod with an exec readiness probe whose command blocks (`sleep 300`) and `timeoutSeconds: 60`, plus `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1`. Delete the pod while a probe is in flight and watch `--v=4` kubelet logs: the `Exec-Probe runProbe` for that worker has no matching completion until the timeout fires, well after the container is gone.

Suggested fix: give each worker its own context derived from the (detached) manager context and cancel it from `stop()`, roughly:

1. In `newWorker`, `w.ctx, w.cancel = context.WithCancel(ctx)`.
2. `run()` uses `w.ctx` for `doProbe` and adds `<-w.ctx.Done()` to the select.
3. `stop()` calls `w.cancel()` in addition to signalling `stopCh`, so an in-flight `ExecSync` is cancelled.

That keeps the worker lifecycle owned by the prober manager instead of the pod worker, which is what #140882 is after, while still bounding shutdown.

Worth checking as part of this whether cancelling mid-probe can record a spurious result. `doProbe` throws away errored results today, which is what made #140881 invisible, so a cancelled probe should not flip readiness either way. A test for "stop() during an in-flight probe records no result" would be good to have alongside.
