kubelet: serialized pod status sync causes unnecessary cross-pod serialization

The bottleneck in high throughput pod churn (> 5 pods / second / node) seems to be the status update from kubelet. Other controllers rely on this update, so even if the container has started it is not necessarily visible externally.

There are low-hanging opportunities for efficiency improvement: It does a GET before each update, it runs multiple updates for a pod start (though these already coalesce under load), and it does all operations in series on a single worker goroutine, where a batch of pod status updates blocks the next batch.

Proposed fixes:

- Parallelize status syncs with per-pod ordering preserved . This is what #124596 was addressing (closed by triage bot).
- Eliminate the GET — serve the precondition check from the informer/last-known state (also proposed in #123875).
- Two-tier queue — first-time-Ready and deletion-releasing syncs ahead of lower-importance updates; per-pod coalescing means we are already dropping these updates under moderate load - there's no guarantee that clients will observe them as individual updates.

I have a reproducible benchmark harness (kOps + load generator + per-pod tracing across watch/journal/containerd), full artifacts for every number above, and I'm happy to help revive #124596 or review/test an alternative.

If it's helpful, I can also try to figure out how to run the agent-sandbox stress-test on demand against k/k, I think the test is pretty good at capturing a lot of information in a machine readable format, and then generating a report in a human-readable format!

Under sustained pod churn of ~5–9 creates/s per node, the kubelet starts pods quickly (~200ms to containers running when the image is already pulled) but takes 1–2.5 seconds to report that status to the API server. The delay is in the status manager's serialized sync path, and it caps cluster-wide pod-startup throughput for any consumer that keys off pod status (controllers, autoscalers, users). I instrumented this end-to-end on v1.36.2 and can attribute the full latency chain; I believe this revives #123875, which described the same limitation but was closed by the lifecycle bot without triage, along with both fix attempts (#123877, #124596).

https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1204/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2080749074797039616/artifacts/stress-test/report/index.html

Benchmark: 20–40 node clusters (kOps/GCE, n2-standard-8 workers on pd-ssd, c3-standard-22 control plane, v1.36.2), pod create/delete churn (with a wrapping Agent Sandbox CRD). Per-pod lifecycle traced by joining the API watch stream, kubelet journals, and containerd events.

At ~8 pods/s/node (per-pod p50):

| stage | latency |
| ----- | ------ |
| scheduler binding write → kubelet SyncLoop ADD | 0–1ms |
| ADD → pod sandbox creation dispatched (CRI) | ~3ms |
| dispatch → containers running (PLEG Started) | ~150–240ms |
| PLEG Started → status synced to API server | 1.16s (p90 1.96s) |

The last stage scales cleanly with churn: 0.01s at ~1 pods/s/node → 0.22s at ~5/s → 0.82s at ~7/s → 1.16s at ~8/s. Meanwhile kubelet's own pod_start_duration_seconds reports ≤0.5s for 99.9% of pods — the SLI clock stops before the reporting delay begins, so the regression is invisible to the standard dashboards.

What we ruled out:

- API server: PATCH pods/status 6.2ms mean server-side at 373/s; APF wait 0.0ms on all priority levels
- Client rate limiter: fully eliminated as a factor — with [kubeAPIQPS=500](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1283/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2081011556287516672/artifacts/stress-test/report/index.html), rate-limiting waits are 0.00ms across 68k+ main-client requests at peak churn, and the residual delay is still 944ms p50 / 1,287ms p90 at ~9 pods/s/node. (Note that there is still client-side rate limiting, but it is on the POST endpoint, which I believe is because we're limiting events QPS to limit load on the apiserver)
- Kubelet work time: first-sync (pod_worker_duration{create}) 212ms and flat across load; volume mounts negligible; PLEG relist steady at 1.00–1.03s / 27ms duration; zero "housekeeping took longer" warnings in journals.
- Container runtime: containerd events show creations running up to 10-wide concurrently, ~86% idle, pause-sandbox spans 95ms p50.

Why pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go:

1. One goroutine: syncPod and syncBatch share a single goroutine by design ("to avoid sync races", Start()); every pod's status update on a node funnels through it sequentially.
2. Two round trips per sync: syncPod does a GET then a PATCH (~15–30ms wall time per sync at load). Same amplification #123875 flagged.
3. No importance ordering: syncBatch iterates m.podStatuses — a Go map, i.e. random order. A pod's first-ever Ready transition (which controllers block on) has equal standing with terminal bookkeeping of deleted pods.
4. The coalescing trap (the subtle finding): the per-pod versioned status means a deep queue coalesces a pod's Pending→Running→Ready into fewer PATCHes. This makes the lane partially self-defending against relief: going 20→40 nodes halved per-node churn but syncs-per-pod rose from ~2.4 to ~3.6 as the queue shallowed and coalescing unwound — scale-out yields sublinear improvement. https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1276/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2080880843894558720

kube-apiserver: request can hang for 40–90s when its etcd transport is recycled mid-flight (grpc-go v1.72.2 bug, fixed in v1.77.0; affects release-1.34/1.35)

In our CI environment (Calico Felix functional tests, which start a fresh kube-apiserver per test), a LIST of a CRD hung inside the apiserver for 13+ seconds while identical LISTs from other clients, through the same apiserver, succeeded within 300 ms. The stuck request was still blocked on its first attempt of an etcd KV/Range RPC when the client gave up:

```
{"level":"warn","logger":"etcd-client","caller":"v3@v3.6.5/retry_interceptor.go:65","msg":"retrying of unary invoker failed","target":"etcd-endpoints://0xc004ab9680/[...]:2379","method":"/etcdserverpb.KV/Range","attempt":0,"error":"rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled"}
E ... timeout.go:140] "Post-timeout activity" ... method="GET" path="/apis/crd.projectcalico.org/v1/globalnetworksets"
```

etcd (single node, v3.5.24) was healthy throughout: no slow-apply or read-index warnings, and it served all other requests, including the same LIST from other clients, in milliseconds.

The hung request was the first request ever for that CRD on the freshly started apiserver. First requests trigger lazy creation of the CRD's storage, including a new etcd client (one per CRD - #111476). The hang coincided with a burst of transport churn from ~14 CRD storages being created at once:

```
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: connection error: desc = "error reading server preface: read tcp [...]: use of closed network connection"
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: "transport: failed to write client preface: write tcp [...]: use of closed network connection"
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: "transport: Error while dialing: dial tcp [...]: operation was canceled"
```

All requests for that list serviced promptly.

Repeatedly hammer the list CR path on freshly started API server. It is probabilistic and infrequent.

Upstream fix (assuming RCA below is correct)

- grpc/grpc-go#8425 ("Transport close blocks on unresponsive reader"), fixed by grpc/grpc-go#8534 ("transport: Invoke net.Conn.SetReadDeadline in http2_client.Close"), released in grpc-go v1.77.0. Related hardening: grpc/grpc-go#8615 (pickfirstleaf stuck in IDLE), released in v1.76.0.
- Neither was backported to grpc-go 1.72.x.
- kubernetes master picked up the fix incidentally via routine dependency maintenance (#136227, grpc v1.78.0; then #137906, v1.79.3), so 1.36 is fixed. release-1.35 (through v1.35.7) and release-1.34 still vendor grpc-go v1.72.2.

Potential root cause (from Claude):

internal/transport/http2_client.go strands in-flight RPCs when a transport leaves service:

- Close(): calls t.onClose(...) first the subchannel immediately reports the transport dead and new RPCs move to a fresh transport — then waits for GOAWAY write, then blocks on <-t.readerDone with no deadline, and only after that errors the in-flight streams. If the dying connection goes mute (no FIN/RST reaches the reader), in-flight streams wait indefinitely.
- GracefulClose(): calls t.onClose(...) and then waits for active streams to drain with no deadline; in-flight streams are never errored at all.

So an RPC that lands on a transport just as it is being recycled is stranded on attempt 0: the etcd retry interceptor never sees the attempt finish, so it never retries, while every new RPC succeeds on the replacement transport. The etcd client defaults to WaitForReady(true), so nothing bounds the attempt client-side. The only recovery paths are the etcd client keepalive configured in storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go (30s ping / 10s timeout → ~40–86s) or the HTTP request's own context ending (server --request-timeout, or the caller disconnecting — which is what we observed).

Two things make first-requests-to-CRDs a reliable trigger window: per-CRD lazy storage creation churns subchannels exactly when the request is issued, and with ResilientWatchCacheInitialization a LIST arriving before the CRD's watch cache is ready delegates straight to etcd (cacher/delegator.go), putting the user request directly on the brand-new transport.

Caveat: the chain above is established from the logs plus reading the vendored code; we have not reproduced it with a patched grpc-go to bisect.

WatchList informer retries indefinitely when an Aggregated API server never sends the initial-events-end Bookmark

A kubernetes aggregated API server accepted a WatchList request and sent initial events but never sent the `initial-events-end` Bookmark. The watch connection was open for several minutes and was aborted by API server with error `Timeout or abort while handling`. Since the watch connection lasted longer than one second and got events, [handleAnyWatch()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa94f417962c7c4a3798e042dd0ce24cc9374a1e/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1094) in reflector returned `(false, nil)`.

Relector's [watchList()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/aa94f417962c7c4a3798e042dd0ce24cc9374a1e/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L870) kept on retrying instead of falling back to list. Because of this the informer never completed the inital sync. In the impacted case, the affected informer was one of per resource quota monitor informers in Kubernetes Controller Manager. Since [QuotaMonitor.IsSynced()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3473c0534f55f8354abb35bddc8ae2cad0e73d88/pkg/controller/resourcequota/resource_quota_monitor.go#L295) requires all informers to report HasSynced(), it never became true and the Resource Quota controller waited on this and quota workers did not start. This caused `ResourceQuota.status.used` values stale and new pods were rejected because the stale quota status value indicated the quota was full.

The reflector should recover instead of retrying WatchList indefinitely when an aggregated API server does not complete the initial watch events stream. The key concern is that one misbehaving APIService should not block an informer permanently.

  1. Start an aggregated API server which accepts a WatchList request.
  2. Send few events.
  3. After more than one second, close the stream without an `initial-events-end` bookmark or `watch.Error` event.
  4. Observe that the reflector retries WatchList indefinitely and the informer never syncs.

APF queueset can panic ("slice bounds out of range") and crash the apiserver when a queue holding a lingering request is removed after a DesiredNumQueues reduction

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go`, a request that has finished its main service but still occupies seats during its `AdditionalLatency` (a "lingering" request, e.g. a mutating request whose work estimate reserves seats for its watch fan-out) is removed from `requestsExecuting` immediately in `finishRequestLocked`, while releasing its seats and calling `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` is deferred to an `EventAfterDuration` callback that fires `AdditionalLatency` later.

`removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` decides whether to drop an excess queue using:

```
if len(qs.queues) > qs.qCfg.DesiredNumQueues &&
    r.queue.requestsWaiting.Length() == 0 &&
    r.queue.requestsExecuting.Len() == 0 {   // does not check seatsInUse
    qs.queues = removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, r.queue.index)
    ...
}
```

It does not check `seatsInUse`. So if `DesiredNumQueues` has been reduced (excess queues draining by attrition) and a queue Q holds a lingering request `r` plus another request `s`, then when `s` finishes it sees Q as empty (0 waiting, 0 executing — `r` was already removed from the executing set) and removes Q, even though `r`'s seats still linger. `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes` only fixes up the `index` field of the *kept* queues, so the removed Q keeps a now-stale `index`, and `r.queue` still points at it. When `r`'s lingering timer later fires, its deferred `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked(r)` calls `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, <stale index>)` a second time:

- if the stale index is out of range for the now-shorter slice, `queues[index+1:]` panics with `slice bounds out of range`;
- otherwise it removes a different, live queue, silently corrupting fairness/seat accounting and stranding that flow's requests.

The panic runs in the goroutine spawned by `eventclock.Real.EventAfterDuration` (`go func(){ t := <-ch; f(t) }()`), which has no `recover`, so it crashes the whole apiserver process.

The queue should not be removed while a lingering request still holds seats in it, and it should never be removed twice.

Unit-level, with the queueset's fake event clock (test in `package queueset`):

1. Build a queuing queueset with `DesiredNumQueues: 3, HandSize: 1` and ample concurrency.
2. `StartRequest` two requests with the same hash (so they share queue index 2): `r` with `WorkEstimate{InitialSeats:1, FinalSeats:1, AdditionalLatency: time.Second}` (lingering) and `s` normal.
3. Reconfigure to `DesiredNumQueues: 1` (the three queues remain, draining by attrition).
4. `r.Finish(...)` then `s.Finish(...)`.
5. Advance the fake clock past `AdditionalLatency`.

Result on current master: `panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [3:2]` in `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes`, from the lingering timer callback. (A regression test is attached; it panics before the fix and passes after.)

Trigger requires an operator to reduce a PriorityLevelConfiguration's `queuing.queues` (so excess queues are draining) together with the right concurrent traffic and timing, so probability is low; but the consequence (apiserver panic, or silent fairness corruption) is severe, and it is reachable through supported configuration. This is a robustness bug on configuration change, not a security issue (no unprivileged trigger, no escalation).

Fix: add `&& r.queue.seatsInUse == 0` to the `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` guard so a queue is not removed while a lingering request still holds its seats; the queue is then removed exactly once, by the lingering request's own deferred call after its seats are released.

DRA device health timeout does not trigger a PodStatus update at the expiration deadline

DRA device health expiration is evaluated lazily. `getHealthInfo` compares `LastUpdated` with the device timeout only when health information is read,`updateHealthInfo` also checks for expired devices that are missing from a complete plugin response, but it runs only when another `NodeWatchResourcesResponse` is received,There is no timer, deadline queue, or periodic worker that transitions a device to `Unknown` when its health-check timeout expires.
﻿
For example:
﻿
1. A plugin reports an allocated device as `Healthy` with a short `health_check_timeout_seconds` value.
2. The stream remains connected, but the plugin stops sending health responses.
3. The timeout expires.
4. No `changedDevices` result is produced because `updateHealthInfo` is not called.
5. No resource update notification is sent for Pods using the device.
﻿
The next call to `getHealthInfo` will calculate `Unknown`, but that read is normally part of rebuilding Pod status. The health timeout itself does not enqueue the affected Pod, so `AllocatedResourcesStatus` can continue showing the previous health value until another pod sync or unrelated update occurs.
﻿
The normal notification path exists only while processing a stream response,
﻿
The default kubelet sync frequency is one minute and is configurable, so the user-visible delay is unrelated to the device-specific health timeout and can be longer:
﻿
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2192afa9f369883debb4bd43a1f9177aeab80a8e/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go#L78-L80

When a reported device reaches its health-check deadline without a fresh report, kubelet should transition that device to `Unknown` and enqueue every affected Pod for a status update at, or shortly after, the deadline.

The health protocol states that devices not present in the complete list become `Unknown` after a timeout:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2192afa9f369883debb4bd43a1f9177aeab80a8e/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/dra-health/v1alpha1/api.proto#L71-L74

KEP-4680's test plan also calls out both behaviors:

- marking devices as `Unknown` after a timeout period;
- properly sending update notifications for affected Pods.

https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4680-add-resource-health-to-pod-status

A deterministic test can use a fake DRA health stream and an allocated device referenced by a Pod:

1. Start `HandleWatchResourcesStream` with a fake stream.
2. Send a `Healthy` response for the allocated device with a short timeout.
3. Consume the initial Pod update notification.
4. Keep the stream open and send no further responses.
5. Advance a fake clock beyond the device deadline, or wait for the short timeout in an integration-style test.
6. Assert that the DRA manager sends another update for the affected Pod.
7. Rebuild the Pod status and assert that the device is `Unknown` with an empty stale-health message.

With the current implementation, step 6 times out because there is no deadline-driven execution path.

DRA health streams from multiple plugin endpoints can overwrite or clear the active driver's health state

During a seamless DRA plugin upgrade, kubelet may have multiple registered plugin endpoints for the same driver. The DRA plugin manager intentionally supports this:
﻿
Regular DRA RPCs select a preferred plugin, favoring the most recently registered connected endpoint,However, health monitoring starts an independent `NodeWatchResources` stream for every registered endpoint,All of those streams call the handler with only the driver name. The endpoint identity or registration generation is not passed to the DRA manager,Health information is also stored per driver, not per plugin endpoint
﻿
This allows responses from old and new endpoints to reconcile the same driver cache concurrently. Because each `NodeWatchResourcesResponse` is a complete list for the driver, a response from the old endpoint can overwrite health information reported by the new endpoint.
﻿
There is a second race during endpoint removal. Deregistration cancels that endpoint's health stream,When any health stream exits, its handler unconditionally clears all health information for the driver,
﻿
Therefore, an old endpoint being deregistered can clear health information that was already reported by the new endpoint.
﻿
The cache transition caused by `clearDriver` also does not notify affected Pods. Pod update notifications are sent only from the normal response-processing path when `updateHealthInfo` returns changed devices,This can leave `AllocatedResourcesStatus` with stale `Healthy` or `Unhealthy` values until another pod sync occurs, even though the internal lookup now returns `Unknown`.

Kubelet should have one authoritative health stream per driver. During a plugin upgrade, health updates should come only from the most recently registered applicable endpoint, as specified by KEP-4680:
﻿
> For seamless plugin upgrades, where multiple instances of a plugin might run concurrently, the Kubelet will always watch the most recently registered plugin for health updates.
﻿
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4680-add-resource-health-to-pod-status
﻿
When ownership moves to a new endpoint:
﻿
- the old stream should be canceled or ignored;
- responses from an older registration generation must not overwrite current state;
- termination of an old stream must not clear state owned by the new stream;
- if the authoritative stream is lost and device health becomes `Unknown`, affected Pods should receive a resource update notification.

A deterministic unit test can use two fake endpoints registered under the same driver name:
﻿
1. Register endpoint A and let its health stream report device `pool/device` as `Healthy`.
2. Register endpoint B for the same driver and let its stream report the same device as `Unhealthy`.
3. Send another `Healthy` response from endpoint A.
4. Observe that the shared driver cache can be changed by the non-authoritative endpoint A.
5. Deregister endpoint A, which cancels its stream.
6. Observe that A's deferred `clearDriver(driverName)` removes the state reported by endpoint B.
7. Observe that this cache clear does not place an update for the affected Pod on the DRA manager update channel.
﻿
The test should assert that only endpoint B can update the cache after B becomes authoritative, that A's termination cannot clear B's state, and that losing the authoritative stream notifies affected Pods when their reported health changes to `Unknown`.

DRA: Allocator reads device counter consumption from possibly modified slice

The structured allocator derives per-pool state about already-allocated devices from the current ResourceSlice contents. Slices are mutable, so a driver can republish a pool without a previously-allocated device, or with different `ConsumesCounters` for it - and when that happens, the allocated device's contribution silently disappears from the allocator's accounting. This affects two features with different severity:

**1. PartitionableDevices: counter availability can be over-committed.**

`checkAvailableCounters` (`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, mirrored in the incubating and stable allocators) computes per-pool availability by starting from the counter set totals and subtracting the consumption of allocated devices **found in the current slices**. An allocated device that is no longer published (or whose `ConsumesCounters` changed) no longer subtracts anything, so the pool appears to have more counters free than it physically does, and new allocations can over-commit the shared counters of a device that is still in use.

**2. DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139795): the enforcement baseline loses allocated peers.**

`compatibilityGroupsBaselineForPool` deliberately copies the counters pattern (its comment: "exactly like checkAvailableCounters does for counters"): group *values* come from the allocation-time snapshot in the claim status, but counter-set *membership* still comes from the current slice. If the allocated device is not in the republished slice, its intersection contribution drops out of the feature-on baseline and a later incompatible device can be admitted onto the counter set. Notably, the feature-off version-skew skip (`groupedCounterSetsFromState`) is built purely from snapshots and keeps protecting the same counter set - the enforcement path is less conservative than the skip path.

Accounting and enforcement for already-allocated devices should depend only on allocation-time state, never on the current slice contents, which the compatibility-groups KEP already designates as unsafe for enforcement (that is the snapshot's entire purpose).

Pod & Container statuses not reporting memory requests accurately when memory QoS is enabled and memory.min is set

Historically, memory requests in Kubernetes were not mapped to Linux cgroup constructs (unlike CPU requests, which map to cpu.shares / cpu.weight). Because cgroups did not enforce or track memory requests, kubelet status reporting logic (convertToAPIPodLevelResourcesStatus and convertContainerStatusResources) bypassed cgroups for memory requests and instead relied on spec values or previous status values.

With the introduction of MemoryQoS (MemoryQoS feature gate using TieredReservationMemoryReservationPolicy), memory.min is configured on cgroup v2 for Guaranteed pods based on memory requests and Since memory.min (Guaranteed) and memory.low (Burstable) now reflect memory requests in cgroups when MemoryQoS is enabledmemory.low is configured on cgroup v2 for Burstable pods based on memory requests.

PodStatus and ContainerStatus memory requests are never read back from cgroup state; they are always populated by preserving old status values or aggregating from container/pod specs

Since memory.min (Guaranteed) and memory.low (Burstable) now reflect memory requests in cgroups when MemoryQoS is enabled, Pod status should reflect the values:
- GetPodCgroupConfig / cgroup managers be updated to read memory.min / memory.low as actual cgroup memory request values when MemoryQoS is active and memory.min and memory.low are set

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3d3f9b2f4665b059b50536f114bc7fb1dc831586/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2472

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3d3f9b2f4665b059b50536f114bc7fb1dc831586/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2254

1. Enable Feature Gates: Enable MemoryQoS=true (with memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation) and PodLevelResources=true.
2. Deploy a Guaranteed Pod: Create a pod with requests.memory: 1Gi and limits.memory: 1Gi. Kubelet sets memory.min = 1073741824 on the cgroup v2 path.
3. kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.resources}'
Observed Result: .status.resources.requests.memory reports 1Gi (spec value). It ignores the cgroup memory.min value (2Gi) because kubelet does not read memory.min into status.

Pods that are terminated via node drain / eviction (not caused by
memory pressure) are being reported with
`containerStatuses[*].state.terminated.reason = "OOMKilled"` and
`exitCode = 143` (SIGTERM), even when there is no evidence of memory
pressure at the time of termination.

This was originally reported against kOps
(kubernetes/kops#18040), but the classification logic that sets this
field lives in kubelet/the container runtime rather than the cluster
provisioning tool, so filing here with sig-node's attention.

For non-OOM terminations such as node drains, liveness-probe-induced
restarts, or manual pod deletions, we'd expect:
- `container.state.terminated.reason` to NOT be `OOMKilled` when the
  exit code is 143 (SIGTERM implies graceful termination, not a
  kernel OOM kill which uses SIGKILL/137), or
- the pod-level `status.reason` to indicate `Evicted` / node shutdown
  while the container termination reason stays consistent with the
  actual signal received.

This misclassification breaks downstream tooling (alerting,
observability platforms) that rely on
containerStatuses[*].state.terminated.reason to distinguish real OOM
events from expected evictions/restarts.

CRD with identical per-version selectableFields but differing per-version schemas is rejected due to internal hoisting

Creating a multi-version `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` CRD that declares the **same** `selectableFields` on two served versions whose **schemas differ** is rejected by the apiserver:

```
The CustomResourceDefinition "widgets.example.com" is invalid:
spec.selectableFields: Invalid value: "": may only be set when validations.schema is included
```

The error is doubly confusing: the manifest sets only `spec.versions[*].selectableFields` (valid per the v1 API), yet the error references top-level `spec.selectableFields` — a field that does not exist in the v1 API the user submitted.

**Root cause (from reading the source):** `Convert_v1_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec_To_apiextensions_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec` (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/conversion.go`) hoists each of the four per-version fields (`subresources`, `schema`, `additionalPrinterColumns`, `selectableFields`) to the internal top-level spec **independently**, whenever that field is identical across all versions. So with identical `selectableFields` but differing schemas:

- `selectableFields` **is** hoisted to internal `spec.SelectableFields` (and cleared per-version),
- `schema` is **not** hoisted (internal `spec.Validation` stays nil),

and internal validation then rejects the combination the conversion itself created (top-level `selectableFields` requires a top-level `validations.schema`). The user's input was never invalid; the independent hoisting manufactured the invalid internal state.

Per-version `selectableFields` to be accepted on any served version, independent of whether the other versions' schemas are identical. KEP-4358 field selectors are declared per-version in v1; whether two versions happen to share a schema should not change the validity of identical selector declarations.

**Real-world impact:** any multi-version CRD mid-graduation — the standard pattern of serving two versions where the newer one drops deprecated fields — cannot offer the same field selector on both served versions. We hit this graduating a CRD whose new version removes two deprecated fields; controllers watching via field selector on the old version could not keep the selector when the new version was added. Workarounds: declare `selectableFields` on only one version (losing field selectors on the others), or keep the version schemas byte-identical (defeating the point of graduation).

Apply this CRD:

```
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: widgets.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: widgets
    singular: widget
[... 30 more lines]
```

→ rejected with the error above.

Control matrix (verified against kube-apiserver v1.35.0):

| per-version schemas | selectableFields | result |
|---|---|---|
| differ | on one version only | accepted |
| differ | identical on both | **rejected** |
| identical | identical on both | accepted (both hoist together) |

The identical-schemas row confirms the failure is the hoisting *interaction*, not the field declarations themselves.

Possible fixes:

- Couple the hoisting: hoist `selectableFields` (and `additionalPrinterColumns`/`subresources`) only when `schema` is also hoisted; or
- Relax the spec validation to accept internal top-level `selectableFields` without a top-level schema when every version carries a schema.

Either preserves round-tripping while accepting the valid v1 input. Independent of the fix, the error message would benefit from mentioning that identical per-version declarations can trigger it, since `spec.selectableFields` is not settable in the v1 API.

Structured GPU device health reporting in device manager

**What would you like to be added?**

A structured, backward-compatible health signal in the device plugin API so Kubelet can distinguish DEGRADED (ECC error, thermal throttle, NVLink down) from UNHEALTHY (gone), and surface it via a metric + optional probe.

Today the device manager treats a device as healthy purely based on whether `ListAndWatch` reports it in the healthy list. There is no queryable per-device health reason, so GPU degradation silently corrupts training workloads and out-of-tree operators (NVIDIA GPU Operator, Fugoku GPU device plugin) reimplement health checks.

**Proposed change (additive, v1beta1):**
- New `DeviceHealth` message: `state` (HEALTHY/UNHEALTHY/DEGRADED), `reason` (e.g. "ecc_error"), `last_transition_time`.
- Optional `health_detail` field on `Device` (nil for old plugins -> unchanged behavior).
- New Kubelet metric `kubelet_device_health_state{resource,device,state}`.
- Optional `HealthCheck` unary RPC (Kubelet skips if plugin doesn't implement).

**Design doc:** https://github.com/richardokonicha/kubernetes/blob/feature/gpu-device-health-reporting/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/README.md (draft)

**Why is this needed?**

AI/ML workloads need a standard, upstream health signal instead of every GPU operator reinventing it. Reduces duplication and gives schedulers/operators a uniform signal for drain/cordon/reschedule.

**Comments welcome on:**
1. Additive proto approach (backward compat) — acceptable?
2. Metric name / labels
3. Whether `HealthCheck` RPC is worth the surface area vs passive `ListAndWatch` only

kubelet preemption during init leaves pod stuck in Init:N/M with no recreation or cleanup

On a resource-constrained node, the kubelet preempted a lower-priority pod to admit a critical pod while it was still running init containers.

`kube-admission-5f9b89fdb5-bbpsp` in namespace `kube-admission` has been stuck at `Init:1/2` for days:

- `secret-init` completed (exit 0)
- `cert-controller` never started; state is `waiting: PodInitializing`
- `status.phase: Failed`, `status.reason: Preempting`, message: *"Preempted in order to admit critical pod"*
- `DisruptionTarget` condition: `reason: TerminationByKubelet`, message: *"Pod was preempted by Kubelet to accommodate a critical pod."*
- `restartPolicy: Always`, `restartCount: 0` on all containers

The pod object is never deleted, the init sequence is never retried, and the ReplicaSet does not create a replacement.

If a pod is preempted mid-init, it should not sit in `Init:N/M` indefinitely. Either:

1. the kubelet deletes the pod so the ReplicaSet recreates it, or
2. the ReplicaSet treats the preempted pod as failed and creates a replacement on its own.

Evicted pods get a clear stale status and are eventually cleaned up. Preemption during init seems to fall through the cracks.

1. Schedule multiple burstable pods with `priorityClassName: normal` onto a resource-constrained node.
2. Use multiple init containers so preemption can land between them.

tainteviction controller does not durably retry pod deletion on denial

**What happened?**

When the taint-eviction controller evicts a pod for a `NoExecute` taint, it performs a small fixed number of delete retries over a few tens of milliseconds and then gives up. Each scheduled eviction is a one-shot timed worker with no rate-limited requeue, so once those attempts are exhausted the eviction is abandoned.

If a validating admission webhook persistently denies the pod `DELETE`, every attempt fails almost immediately and the controller stops trying. When the denial persists with no change to the node taint and no `deletionTimestamp` on the pod, no such event is generated, so the pod keeps running on the tainted node indefinitely — defeating the intent of `NoExecute`.

**What did you expect to happen?**

The taint manager should handle pod-deletion denials gracefully rather than silently abandoning the deletion: durably retry with backoff until the pod is gone.

**How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?**

1. Register a `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` on `pods` `DELETE` that always returns `allowed: false`.
2. Apply a `NoExecute` taint to a node hosting a pod that does not tolerate it (or let the node controller add one, e.g. by making a node `NotReady`/unreachable).
3. Observe: the taint manager attempts eviction, all deletes are denied, and after the attempts are exhausted the pod stays `Running` with no further eviction attempts.

kube_apiserver clusterip_allocator available_ips missing for ServiceCIDR allocators after apiserver restart

Cluster runs with `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` enabled, a legacy `--service-cluster-ip-range` (/22), and an additional `ServiceCIDR` (/16).

During a rolling kube-apiserver restart, the extension CIDR gauge disappears from `/metrics` on new apiserver pods for a long time. The legacy CIDR gauge keeps reporting.

```
$ kubectl get servicecidr
NAME                       CIDRS           AGE
kubernetes                 10.0.0.0/22     30d
service-cidr-extension-1   10.1.0.0/16     7d
```

On a newly started apiserver pod (minutes after it is Ready):

```
$ curl -ks https://127.0.0.1:6443/metrics --cert ... | grep clusterip_allocator_available_ips
kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips{cidr="10.0.0.0/22"} 1018
# no series for cidr="10.1.0.0/16"
```

After the first ClusterIP allocation in the extension range, the /16 series appears:

```
kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips{cidr="10.0.0.0/22"} 1018
kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips{cidr="10.1.0.0/16"} 65534
```

During a rolling update this produces a multi-endpoint gap: old apiserver pods stop reporting the extension CIDR, new pods do not report it until allocator activity, so no apiserver endpoint exports the gauge for ~1-2 hours even though the cluster can still allocate ClusterIPs from the extension range.

`kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips` should be populated when a ServiceCIDR allocator becomes ready after informer sync, not only after a subsequent allocate/release.

1. Enable `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator`.
2. Run kube-apiserver with a legacy `--service-cluster-ip-range` and apply a `ServiceCIDR` for a second range.
3. Confirm both CIDRs are Ready: `kubectl get servicecidr`.
4. Restart one kube-apiserver pod.
5. Scrape `/metrics` from the new pod before creating any new ClusterIP Service in the extension range.
6. Observe the extension CIDR has no `available_ips` gauge; legacy CIDR does.

`EnableMetrics()` on the IPAddress-based allocator registers the recorder but does not call `setAvailable()`. The gauge is only updated on allocate/release paths in `ipallocator.go`.

Related to multi-CIDR accounting in #134509, but this is a separate reporting gap on fresh apiserver processes.

CEL map-list concatenation preserves duplicate new keys from the right operand

Schema-aware CEL map-list concatenation keeps duplicate new keys from the right operand instead of merging them.

`addToMapList` builds an index for the left operand, but does not add a key to that index when it appends the first new element from the right operand. A later element with the same key is therefore appended again.

For a map list keyed by `key1,key2`, if `x.mapList` contains two existing entries, this expression currently produces four entries and preserves both values `9` and `10`:

```
x.mapList + [
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 9},
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 10},
]
```

This breaks the merge-by-key semantics implemented for `x-kubernetes-list-type: map`. CEL policies that construct or inspect associative lists can observe the wrong size/value. Mutation expressions can also emit duplicate map keys, causing the admission request to be rejected instead of applying the later value.

The first new key from the right operand should be appended and indexed. A later element with that key should overwrite it in place, so the example has one `new,key` entry with value `10`.

Add this case to `TestListAdd` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/common/values_test.go` using the existing `x.mapList` fixture:

```
{
    name: "map list + literal list merges duplicate new keys",
    expression: "size(x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}]) == 3 && (x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}])[2].value == 10",
}
```

Then run:

```
GOWORK=off go test ./pkg/cel/common -run TestListAdd -count=1
```

The case fails with `Expected true with typed values but got false` on current `master`.

The behavior is in the map-list concatenation support merged by #140292. Updating `keyToIdx` immediately after appending a new key fixes the regression and makes the test pass.

utilyaml: YAMLReader/YAMLOrJSONDecoder corrupts UTF-16 input, causing misleading "yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character"

`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml.YAMLOrJSONDecoder` (via the underlying `YAMLReader`/`LineReader`) corrupts UTF-16 encoded input: a valid, BOM'd UTF-16 LE YAML document comes out of `YAMLReader.Read()` one byte longer than it went in — an odd-length UTF-16 stream — and the downstream yaml parser then fails with `yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character`. The error blames the user's file for being truncated when the file is actually valid; the truncation is introduced by the reader itself.

The yaml parser is not at fault: go-yaml is a libyaml port and handles BOM'd UTF-16 natively — `yaml.v2`, `yaml.v3` and `sigs.k8s.io/yaml` all parse the same bytes fine when handed the unmangled stream.

The corruption is in `LineReader.Read()`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.36.2/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go#L447-L461

`bufio.Reader.ReadLine()` (L456) splits at the raw `0x0a` byte — a UTF-8 assumption — and strips it, then `buffer.WriteByte('\n')` (L459) re-appends a *single-byte* UTF-8 newline. Mid-stream this happens to round-trip: each two-byte `0a 00` newline loses its `0a` to `ReadLine`, gains a fresh `0a` from `WriteByte`, and the orphaned `00` leads the next line, so the bytes reassemble in order. But at EOF the orphaned final `00` comes back as one more "line" and gets its own appended `0a`, so the stream grows by one byte and every subsequent UTF-16 code unit boundary is intact except the total length is now odd. A 314-byte document exits the reader as 315 bytes ending `... 0a 00 0a`.

This is byte-for-byte the encoding Windows PowerShell 5.1 produces with a plain `>` redirect, so "I wrote a manifest on Windows and the controller says my YAML is broken" is the practical failure mode.

One of:

- BOM-detected UTF-16 input parses successfully. There is 10-year-old precedent for exactly this: kubectl has transcoded UTF-16 at the file-reading layer since 2016 (#39008), and still does — https://github.com/kubernetes/cli-runtime/blob/master/pkg/resource/visitor.go#L558-L561 wraps every file in `unicode.BOMOverride(unicode.UTF8.NewDecoder())` before the decoder sees it. That protection lives only in cli-runtime's `FileVisitor`; every other consumer of `YAMLOrJSONDecoder`/`YAMLReader` (controllers, operators, anything decoding user-supplied streams) is exposed.
- Or an early, explicit error ("unsupported encoding: UTF-16; convert to UTF-8") instead of silent corruption plus a misleading parser error.

Encode any valid manifest as UTF-16 LE with BOM (what PowerShell `echo ... > file.yaml` writes):

```
$ { printf '\xff\xfe'; iconv -f UTF-8 -t UTF-16LE svc.yaml; } > svc-utf16.yaml
```

```
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"os"

	utilyaml "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml"
)
[... 12 more lines]
```

Output (apimachinery v0.36.2):

```
Decode err: error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character
reader in: 314 bytes, out: 315 bytes
```

The same file parses fine with `sigs.k8s.io/yaml.Unmarshal` directly, and with `kubectl apply -f` (thanks to the cli-runtime transcoder).

Real-world sighting: this is the root cause of fluxcd/flux2#1126 (2021) — kustomize-controller validated user manifests through kustomize's legacy `kunstruct` factory, which delegates to `NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder`, and PowerShell-authored files failed with this exact error. Full RCA with byte traces: https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/1126#issuecomment-4967789882. Flux escaped by rewriting its generator, but the trap remains armed for any other consumer.

Verified present in v0.20.2 through v0.36.2; `LineReader` is unchanged on master.

Happy to send a PR. Two possible directions — transcode on BOM detection at `YAMLReader`/`YAMLOrJSONDecoder` entry (can be done with stdlib `unicode/utf16`, no new dependency, mirroring what cli-runtime does with `x/text`), or reject non-UTF-8 input early with a clear error. Whichever SIG API Machinery prefers.

Track assumed pods in a cycle to simplify gang scheduling feasibility check

In the Kubernetes scheduler, when scheduling a pod group (gang), we need to check if the gang's `MinCount` constraint can be met. This check is performed in the `PlacementFeasible` function of the `gangscheduling` plugin.

During a pod group scheduling cycle, we evaluate pods one by one. If a pod is successfully scheduled in the simulation, it is "assumed" in the snapshot of the cache.

To determine if a subsequent pod in the same group can be scheduled, we need to know how many pods were *already scheduled* before the current cycle started (`alreadyScheduledCount`), and how many have been scheduled *during* the current cycle.

Currently, `alreadyScheduledCount` is calculated by comparing all scheduled pods in the snapshot with the list of pods that were unscheduled at the start of the cycle:

```
unscheduledUIDs := sets.New[types.UID]()
for _, pod := range podGroupInfo.GetUnscheduledPods() {
    unscheduledUIDs.Insert(pod.UID)
}

alreadyScheduledCount := 0
for _, scheduledPod := range podGroupState.ScheduledPods() {
    if !unscheduledUIDs.Has(scheduledPod.UID) {
        alreadyScheduledCount++
    }
[... 1 more lines]
```

This approach is inefficient as it requires:
1. Building a set of UIDs for all unscheduled pods.
2. Iterating over all scheduled pods (which includes both previously scheduled and assumed in this cycle pods) and performing a lookup in the set.

We can simplify this logic by introducing a way to query how many pods have been assumed *during the current scheduling cycle* directly from the pod group state snapshot.

We propose adding a new method to the `PodGroupState` interface:
```
// AssumedInThisCycleCount returns the number of assumed pods in the current scheduling cycle.
// For live state, this always returns 0.
AssumedInThisCycleCount() int
```

With this method, `alreadyScheduledCount` can be calculated as:
```
scheduled := podGroupState.ScheduledPodsCount()
assumedInThisCycle := podGroupState.AssumedInThisCycleCount()
alreadyScheduledCount := scheduled - assumedInThisCycle
```

This eliminates the need to build the `unscheduledUIDs` set and iterate over `ScheduledPods()`.

Watch client shutdown: three remaining bugs from #131505

In 2025 I fixed several watch client shutdown bugs: #131266 (reflector Stop deadlock), #131321 (VeryShortWatchError), #131706 (watch test body cleanup). Thanks again to @wojtek-t and @liggitt for those reviews.

The test work in #131505 turned up three more bugs. They were documented there as TODOs but never fixed. I've verified all three still exist on master (843726939e9) and plan to send one small PR per bug:

1. **Response body leak.** `Request.Watch` doesn't close `resp.Body` when content-type negotiation fails. Tracked in #140464.

2. **Error event after Stop.** `StreamWatcher.receive` selects between the done channel and the error send. When both are ready Go picks at random, so a decode error racing with `Stop()` reaches the consumer about half the time. First reported back in 2015 (#6433) and again recently in #139782. The open fix #139783 adds the http2 error string to `IsProbableEOF`, which helps that case, but the race allows any decode error through after Stop. My PR will check the done channel first so a stopped watcher just closes its result channel.

3. **Broken error unwrapping.** `StreamWatcher.receive` and the client watch decoder wrap decode errors with `%v`, which severs `errors.Is`/`errors.As`. Consumers end up string-matching the message. Config Sync, for example, matches the literal "unable to decode an event from the watch stream: context canceled" text to detect shutdown. Small enough to fix without its own issue.

Each PR is small, structured as a failing test commit followed by the fix, with race detector and stress output in the description.

Currently in the pod by pod preemption, we do a special check that verifies if on the node selected for a given pod via NominatedNodeName, there are any ongoing preemptions (victim pod has DeletionTimestamp and condition reason is PodReasonPreemptionByScheduler).
This check is not enough for workload aware preemption as we can trigger preemptions on nodes that are not selected to run the pods from PodGroup, but removing them is actually necessary to fit a pod group (for example due to the inter pod constraints).
With improvements to pod by pod preemption, allowing pod to preempt pod groups across multiple nodes, the same issue can arise in default preemption.

One possible solution for this problem is to add additional scheduling attempt in WAP that will ignore nodes with DeletionTimestamp and PodReasonPreemptionByScheduler condition and will only evaluate preemptor pods on nodes from NominatedNodeName. If that scheduling attempts succeeds we will not run the victim selection algorithm assuming that the ongoing preemption should be enough to allow the pod group to fit onto the cluster.

Using kubernetes/mount-utils ends up in re-formatting the filesystem

Using [FormatAndMount](https://github.com/kubernetes/mount-utils/blob/d06d436a17294305776494aa876d6e8e38c9200c/mount.go#L189) library from kubernetes/mount-utils ends in re-formatting partially broken filesystem instead of failing erroring out.

If filesystem is partially broken (i.e primary superblock of filesystem got corrupted) instead of silently re-formatting the device library should error out.

It will be tricky to reproduce issue, but I will list steps:

Incident timeline: how a killed  fsck  leads to data loss

• **T0 — Initial provisioning**: The application (pod) is scheduled onto the node for the first time. During the  NodeStageVolume  request, the CSI driver formats the disk with a filesystem (ext4) and mounts it.
• **T1 — Data written, then there is reboot of node**: The application writes a significant amount of data. Before this data is fully flushed to disk, the node restarts unexpectedly, leaving the filesystem in a dirty (inconsistent) state.
• **T2 — Re-stage triggers fsck**: The node comes back online and the pod is rescheduled. The CSI node driver receives a fresh  NodeStageVolume  request for the same volume. Because it uses mount-utils'  FormatAndMount , it detects an existing filesystem and unconditionally runs  fsck  to repair it.
• **T3 — fsck killed mid-repair**: While  fsck  is still running, the node restarts again (or the  fsck  process is killed). Interrupting  fsck  mid-write can corrupt the filesystem's primary superblock.
• **T4 — Silent reformat wipes data**: The node comes back online and the driver receives another  NodeStageVolume  request. This time, the filesystem check reports no filesystem (because  blkid  can only read the now-corrupted primary superblock). Treating the disk as unformatted,  FormatAndMount  reformats it as ext4 — wiping all previously written data, even though the data was still recoverable via backup superblocks.

Update validation methods incorrectly call create validation methods (ValidateObjectMeta)

Currently, many update validation methods in the codebase call their corresponding create validation methods. This pattern results in `ValidateObjectMeta` (and by extension `ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively(Create, ...)`) being called during an update validation pass.

This has two main negative consequences:
1. It will break any future ratcheting of metadata.
2. It causes redundant validation, as `ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively` may be called multiple times during the update pass (once explicitly for the update, and once implicitly via the create validation method).

In `staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apis/apiregistration/validation/validation.go` during PR #139505:
```
func ValidateAPIServiceUpdate(ctx context.Context, newAPIService *apiregistration.APIService, oldAPIService *apiregistration.APIService) field.ErrorList {
	allErrs := validation.ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively(ctx, operation.Update, &newAPIService.ObjectMeta, &oldAPIService.ObjectMeta, false, nil, field.NewPath("metadata"), utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.DeclarativeValidationBeta))
	allErrs = append(allErrs, ValidateAPIService(ctx, newAPIService)...) // <-- Calls create validation
	// ...
```

As noted by @lalitc375 in `https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139505#discussion_r3546302067`, this pattern is very common in the validation code for native types. Most of the update validation methods call the create validations method, which in turn calls `ValidateObjectMeta`.

We need to solve this problem horizontally across the codebase to ensure update validation passes only run update-specific logic and do not inadvertently trigger create-specific validations.

_Originally raised by @jpbetz in [kubernetes/kubernetes#139505 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139505#discussion_r3540859399)_

Add linter rule to ensure safe use of `+k8s:monotonic` DV marker

**Description:**

`+k8s:monotonic` validation marker enforces that integer fields are non-decreasing during updates. However, a monotonic marker alone is not sufficient to guarantee monotonicity. To prevent API design flaws where a monotonic field can be reset or bypass decrease prevention checks, we need to enforce the correct combination of markers.

**Proposed linter rule:**

Any field marked with `+k8s:monotonic` :
- Must have a `+k8s:minimum` marker to prevent it from being initialised with or set to negative values.
- Must be marked with `+k8s:required` or if it is optional, it must explicitly prevent unsetting during updates by `+k8s:update=NoUnset`

To implement this, the kube-api-linter must be updated to support matching specific tag values in the `dependenttags` linter (e.g. recognize `dependsOn: +K8s:update=NoUnset` instead of just key-level matches).

kubectl: autocomplete --dry-run with '=' and value suggestions (none/server/client)

Improve shell completion for the `--dry-run` flag on mutating `kubectl` commands
(`apply`, `create`, `delete`, `patch`, `scale`, …) so that:

- `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>` completes to **`--dry-run=`** (with no trailing
  space and no file listing), and
- `kubectl apply --dry-run=<TAB>` suggests the valid values **`none` / `server` /
  `client`**.

**I'm working on this.** There is a cross-repo dependency: `--dry-run` carries an
optional value (it sets `NoOptDefVal` to support the deprecated bare `--dry-run`),
and cobra currently offers no way for a program to make a flag complete as
`--flag=`. I've opened an opt-in enhancement upstream in cobra to enable it:

- spf13/cobra#2433 — adds `Command.MarkFlagAppendEqual`

Once that lands and is vendored, the kubectl side is a small change in
`AddDryRunFlag` (registering value completion for `none/server/client` and
calling `MarkFlagAppendEqual("dry-run")`).

For a flag with `NoOptDefVal` set, the only syntax that actually assigns a value
is `--dry-run=value`; `--dry-run value` (space-separated) treats `value` as a
positional argument and errors. Yet today `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>`
completes to `--dry-run ` (with a space) and then offers file completion, which:

- nudges users toward the non-working space-separated form, and
- gives no hint of the valid values (`none`, `server`, `client`).

Guiding users to `--dry-run=client` / `--dry-run=server` via completion makes the
flag more discoverable and steers them away from the deprecated bare `--dry-run`.

Evaluate node stability risks and support hybrid workload Memory QoS in KEP 2570

The current Memory QoS (KEP-2570) implementation brings vital cgroups v2 protections, but enforcing `memory.min` as the default, one-size-fits-all solution for Guaranteed pods creates severe operational risks for mixed workloads.

Mapping memory requests to the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is structurally necessary to satisfy node-local agents (NRI plugins, telemetry daemons) without injecting synchronous HTTP calls to the `kube-apiserver` during pod startup. However, the chosen cgroup primitive (`memory.min` for Guaranteed) fundamentally breaks node elasticity.

The KEP assumes all Guaranteed pods require strict, kernel-level memory locking. In reality, users often set requests equal to limits solely to prevent Kubelet eviction (e.g., for ML inference or periodic batch jobs). These workloads might allocate a large heap but sit idle for long periods. When mapped to `memory.min`, the kernel is legally forbidden from reclaiming their idle page cache. Locking unused memory behind a hard wall destroys the node's ability to safely maximize resource utilization and share capacity with neighboring pods.

Because the Kubelet applies this logic universally by default via `TieredReservation`, existing cluster behavior will change drastically. When Guaranteed pods hoard idle cache behind a node-wide `memory.min` wall, the node exhausts shareable memory much faster. During memory pressure, instead of gracefully and proportionally reclaiming page cache, the kernel hits a hard wall and is forced to immediately OOM-kill BestEffort and Burstable pods.

Relying exclusively on node-level configurations forces a single profile onto all workloads. Administrators cannot safely run a latency-sensitive database (requiring strict `memory.min` protection) alongside an elastic web application on the exact same machine. Applying `memory.high` globally means a large workload might be aggressively throttled well before it consumes its physical free capacity. This node-level rigidity defeats the purpose of high-density Kubernetes colocation.

---

We propose modifying the Memory QoS architecture to establish `memory.low` as the global default baseline, while allowing opt-in escalation for hard protections via node-level flags or per-pod APIs (DRA).

Instead of forcing Guaranteed pods to `memory.min`, the Kubelet should map all pod memory requests (Guaranteed and Burstable) to `memory.low` by default.

* **Maximum Elasticity & Bin-Packing:** This protects memory during normal operations, but during a catastrophic node-level emergency, the kernel retains the flexibility to reclaim idle cache rather than hitting a hard boundary that triggers artificial OOM kills.
* **Industry Validation:** This matches the `fbtax2` architecture utilized at scale by Meta, which explicitly favors `memory.low` because it is "work-conserving" and safely handles system memory overcommit without thrashing.
* **CRI Visibility:** Mapping to `memory.low` successfully populates the CRI payload, satisfying local node agents instantly without API server queries.

**Action Item:** Expand `memoryReservationPolicy` to include a `SoftReservation` mode (or update the default behavior of `TieredReservation`) where all requests are mapped to `memory.low`.

For specialized, dedicated hardware pools (e.g., dedicated database nodes), administrators should be able to explicitly toggle `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation` to universally map Guaranteed workloads to `memory.min`.

* **Action Item:** Ensure that even when `memory.min` is enforced, the Kubelet redundantly populates `memory.low` with the same value in the CRI payload so node daemons retain a uniform schema regardless of the enforcement mechanism.

Because Kubelet-level enforcement is too blunt for hybrid clusters, fine-grained hard memory locks (`memory.min`) and custom proactive throttling thresholds (`memory.high`) should be managed via **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)**.

* **Industry Validation:** Organizations like Alibaba Cloud already recognize the upstream limits of KEP-2570, resorting to external Koordinator agents and custom annotations to inject per-pod Memory QoS policies.
* **Action Item:** Transition application cgroup routing out of Kubelet defaults. The Kubelet should focus on protecting the node (`kube-reserved`), while users request strict memory isolation via DRA `ResourceClaims` that instruct the container runtime to append `memory.min` or `memory.high` on a per-pod basis.

---

We would love to get SIG-Node's feedback on:

1. Shifting the baseline cgroups v2 mapping strategy from `memory.min` to `memory.low` for Guaranteed & Burstable workloads to prevent aggressive OOM starvation.
2. The viability of expanding `memoryReservationPolicy` to give administrators explicit `SoftReservation` / `HardReservation` choices in the upcoming beta cycles.
3. The long-term roadmap for offloading specialized, per-pod Memory QoS configurations (like hard locking and custom throttling factors) to Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA).

kubectl port-forward: no way to suppress 'Handling connection for' messages

`kubectl port-forward` unconditionally prints "Handling connection for <port>" to stderr on every connection. There is no flag to suppress these messages.

For long-running tunnels with frequent connections, this produces a constant stream of noise that buries actual errors on the same file descriptor.

A `--quiet` or `--verbosity` flag (or gating behind `-v` log levels) so users can suppress informational messages while preserving real errors on stderr.

```
kubectl port-forward pod/any-pod 5432:5432
```

Connect to localhost:5432 from another terminal. Each connection prints:

```
Handling connection for 5432
```

There is no way to disable this without filtering all of stderr, which risks hiding real errors.

The message originates from a hardcoded `fmt.Fprintf(o.Out, "Handling connection for %d\n", port)` in `pkg/cmd/portforward/portforward.go` with no verbosity check.

Gating it behind `klog.V(1)` or similar would be sufficient.

RestartAllContainers/ContainerRestartRules e2e time out on Hyper-V-isolated Windows (capz-windows-master-hyperv)

`ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows-hyperv-serial-slow`

The process-isolated equivalent `ci-kubernetes-e2e-capz-master-windows-serial-slow` is **green** for the same specs — the failure is specific to Hyper-V isolation.

All `RestartAllContainers` variants under `[sig-node] Pod Extended`, `[FeatureGate:ContainerRestartRules] [FeatureGate:RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits]` (each times out):

- `[sig-node] Pod Extended (RestartAllContainers) ... should restart all containers on regular container exit`
- `[sig-node] Pod Extended (RestartAllContainers) ... should restart all containers on sidecar container exit`
- `[sig-node] Pod Extended (RestartAllContainers) ... should restart init and sidecar containers on init container exit`
- `[sig-node] Pod Extended (RestartAllContainers) ... should allow multiple RestartAllContainers actions and not introduce a loop`

Source: `test/e2e/common/node/container_restart_policy.go`.

These specs have **never passed** on `capz-windows-master-hyperv` — since the `RestartAllContainers` specs were introduced / the `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits` feature gate was enabled on the Hyper-V job.

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-windows-signal#capz-windows-master-hyperv

For `RestartAllContainers`, the kubelet restarts containers *in place*. It kills and removes all containers but keeps the pod sandbox, assuming the sandbox survives.

Under Windows Hyper-V isolation, the sandbox is a Utility VM (UVM) shared by all containers in the pod. When a workload container is killed, hcsshim can tear down that shared UVM by mistake. The container's init process (`sh -c "sleep ..."`) exits, but its orphaned child keeps stdio open, so the guest never reports the exit to the host. After SIGKILL, hcsshim's 30-second watchdog then force-closes the whole UVM.

The sandbox becomes `NotReady`, and the pod goes to `PodFailed` before any container is restarted.

* /openapi/v3/version

This also happens for other APIService like KEDA if they expose a spec at the same path.

I expect a consistent response for every request, which always shows the spec of the apiserver.

```

Kubernetes
Kubernetes
Kubernetes
Kubernetes metrics-server
Kubernetes
[... 1 more lines]
```

The issue can still be reproduced in Kubernetes 1.36.x although we are running an older version

I assume the problem is caused by the following loop: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e36a405b2b14485d0ff68c55171df815552c8163/staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/controllers/openapiv3/aggregator/aggregator.go#L281-L292
It iterates over all known api-services to find the first one that can handle the request path. Since iterations for maps have no fixed order in golang, the metrics-server could be the first api-service to be checked and therefore returns the wrong specification.

Generic apiservers can load their front-proxy (request-header) authenticator dynamically from the `kube-system/extension-apiserver-authentication` ConfigMap: the front-proxy CA bundle, the allowed proxy client CNs, and the `X-Remote-User`/`X-Remote-Group`/... header names. Two controllers watch that ConfigMap and republish the values in memory:

- `ConfigMapCAController.loadCABundle` (`staging/.../dynamiccertificates/configmap_cafile_content.go:145-164`) reads the CA and stores it in `c.caBundle`.
- `RequestHeaderAuthRequestController.sync` (`staging/.../headerrequest/requestheader_controller.go:240-245`) reads the header/CN bundle and stores it in `exportedRequestHeaderBundle`.

Both handle delete by *re-enqueuing* a sync:

```
// headerrequest_controller.go:143 ; configmap_cafile_content.go:125
DeleteFunc: func(obj interface{}) { c.queue.Add(c.keyFn()) }
```

…and both sync paths **return on lister NotFound without clearing state**:

```
// headerrequest_controller.go:240
func (c *RequestHeaderAuthRequestController) sync() error {
    configMap, err := c.configmapLister.Get(c.configmapName)
    if err != nil { return err }            // NotFound -> bail, keep old exportedRequestHeaderBundle
    return c.syncConfigMap(configMap)
}

// configmap_cafile_content.go:145
func (c *ConfigMapCAController) loadCABundle() error {
    configMap, err := c.configmapLister.ConfigMaps(c.configmapNamespace).Get(c.configmapName)
[... 4 more lines]
```

So deleting the ConfigMap makes both controllers spin on `configmap "extension-apiserver-authentication" not found`, but the previously loaded CA bundle, allowed-CN list, and header names stay in memory and keep authenticating requests.

On ConfigMap deletion (or an empty/invalid CA / empty `requestheader-allowed-names`), the controllers should clear their published state: `VerifyOptions()` becomes unavailable (no CA verifier), the CN/header providers return empty, and subsequent front-proxy request-header authentication **fails**. As written, NotFound is treated as "keep retrying with the old trust" rather than "revoke."

kubelet /configz leaks --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys)

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

kube-scheduler: `/configz` endpoint serves the HTTPS extender client private key (`tlsConfig.keyData`) in cleartext base64

kube-scheduler registers the external `KubeSchedulerConfiguration` with the component-base `/configz` runtime endpoint. At startup it converts the internal config to the **external v1** type and sets it on configz:

```
// cmd/kube-scheduler/app/server.go:189-191
if cz, err := configz.New("componentconfig"); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("unable to register configz: %w", err)
} else if err := cz.Set(externalConfig); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("unable to set configz: %w", err)
}
```

`configz` serves that config with plain stdlib JSON — no redaction:

```
// staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:145
b, err = json.Marshal(configs)
```

The external v1 extender TLS type exposes `KeyData` (PEM **private key** bytes) as a plain JSON field, with no `datapolicy`/redaction tag:

```
// staging/src/k8s.io/kube-scheduler/config/v1/types.go:399
KeyData []byte `json:"keyData,omitempty"`
```

Note the **internal** `ExtenderTLSConfig.KeyData` carries `datapolicy:"security-key"`, but configz serves the **external** type, which does not — so the tag is never honored here. Because `[]byte` is JSON-encoded as base64, the scheduler's full extender client private key is returned verbatim in the `/configz` body whenever an HTTPS extender is configured with inline `tlsConfig.keyData`.

`/configz` must not serve private key material. `ExtenderTLSConfig.KeyData` (and arguably `CertData`/`CAData`) should be redacted or omitted from the external config registered with configz.

Possible user confusion from differing zpage information

I've been look at the zpages support which went to beta in 1.36 ( [KEP-4828](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/4828-component-flagz/README.md) ) and I wanted to provide some feedback on where I think the current design might cause some user confusion, based on differences in output between the `/configz` and `/flagz` output.

From reading the KEP and some testing I understand that the `/flagz` endpoint returns the values set by command line flags passed to the component *or* default values where no explicit configuration flag has been passed. In contrast to this `/configz` returns the running configuration of the component taking into account flags, default values, and configuration files.

As a result, where components have values set from configuration files as well as command line flags, the responses from `/flagz` and `/configz` will be different. Looking at a standard Kubeadm 1.36 cluster, in that setup it occurs in the kube-proxy and kubelet components, as the others either don't use configuration files (kube-scheduler and kube-controller) or don't have a `/configz` endpoint (kube-apiserver).

As an example in the kubelet there are several significant differences in what's returned by `/flagz` and `/configz`, some of them are :-

- `/flagz` reports that anonymous authentication is enabled for the kubelet, however this is disabled in the kubelets configuration file, so in reality it is not enabled.
- `/flagz` reports that the cgroupDriver is `cgroupfs` (this is the default, there's no explicit flag set by the component) but the configuration file sets `systemd` which is reported by `/configz`
- `/flagz` reports `rotate-certificates` is `false`, but this is enabled in the configuration file `rotateCertificates` setting.

This could be particularly tricky for the `kube-apiserver` as there is no `/configz` endpoints, so no obvious path for cluster admins to check the full running configuration.

Currently in the [zpages documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/zpages/) there is no mention of `/configz` which may lead to cluster administrators being unaware of its presence or unaware of the difference in output between `/flagz` and `/configz`

As the goal of this feature is to support cluster administrators in diagnosing issues with running clusters, it would be great to explain the differences between these two endpoints, and ensure that they're available for all components.

client-go: kubeconfig migration writes credential-bearing `~/.kube/config` as world-readable (0644)

When a client-go based tool (kubectl, helm, any controller, or anything using `clientcmd.NewDefaultClientConfigLoadingRules().Load()`) runs for the first time against a legacy `~/.kube/.kubeconfig`, the loader silently migrates it to `~/.kube/config` using:

```
// staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/clientcmd/loader.go:320 (func Migrate, called from Load)
err = os.WriteFile(destination, data, 0666)
```

Under the default `0022` umask this creates the destination as `0644` — world-readable — even though the source `.kubeconfig` was `0600`. Kubeconfigs carry bearer tokens and `client-key-data` / `client-certificate-data`. The migration is automatic and silent: a single first-time `kubectl get pods` downgrades a private credential file to world-readable and leaves it that way until someone manually `chmod`s it.

The migrated kubeconfig should be created `0600` (or preserve the source file's restrictive permission bits), consistent with `WriteToFile` in the same package — never widened to world-readable.

Run this single self-contained snippet from the root of a Kubernetes checkout (it provides `k8s.io/client-go`). It sets up a throwaway `HOME` with a private legacy kubeconfig, triggers the real `clientcmd` loader under `0022` umask, and prints the resulting permission + credential leak.

```
set -e
H="$(mktemp -d /tmp/kc-home.XXXXXX)"          # throwaway HOME
mkdir -p "$H/.kube"
cat >"$H/.kube/.kubeconfig" <<'YAML'           # legacy source, private
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: poc
  cluster: { server: https://127.0.0.1:6443 }
users:
[... 43 more lines]
```

Expected output (observed on Ubuntu 20.04, Kubernetes master `v1.37.0-alpha.2-98-g121abd026c8`):

```
source mode      : 0600
migrated mode    : 0644
world-readable   : true
has bearer token : true
has client-key   : true
```

A `0600` source containing a token and client key is migrated to a `0644`, world-readable file that still contains both credentials.

- Sink: `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/clientcmd/loader.go:320`, `ClientConfigLoadingRules.Migrate`, invoked from `Load`. The default migration rule maps legacy `~/.kube/.kubeconfig` → `~/.kube/config`.
- Suggested fix: `os.WriteFile(destination, data, 0600)`, matching `WriteToFile` in the same file. A stricter variant preserves the source bits when more restrictive: `os.WriteFile(destination, data, sourceInfo.Mode().Perm())`.
- Same class as the separately-recorded `kubeadm config migrate` (0644) and kube-scheduler `--write-config-to` keyData leaks — shared tooling writes sensitive runtime config with a public mode instead of preserving confidentiality.

[Flaking Test] [sig-cli] sig-cli tests are intermittently failing due to client-go common code

### Issue Overview
In recent testing, sig-cli tests are experiencing intermittent flakes. The actual tests are passing, but they are failing during setup (BeforeEach) or cleanup (DeferCleanup).

The failure manifests as an authentication drop: the ClientSet loses its authentication context between the test execution and the AfterEach cleanup, resulting in system:anonymous forbidden errors when attempting to create resources (like oauthclients) or delete resources (like namespaces).

The issue stems from how the ClientSet is constructed and retained in test/e2e/framework/framework.go.

**The Bug**
The ClientSet is created from a local variable (config) rather than the persistently stored framework configuration (f.clientConfig).

**Local Scope Issue:** The local config variable goes out of scope after BeforeEach() completes.

**Shallow Copy Flaw: T**he ClientSet holds a shallow copy that points to structures potentially tied to that local stack frame or shared memory.

**Why it surfaced now (Kubernetes v1.36):** This bug has always existed but was previously masked by strong references in the TLS transport cache. Kubernetes v1.36 introduced active garbage collection.

**The Flake:** Because the failure depends on when the active Garbage Collector (GC) drops the transport memory (once the local variable's strong reference expires), the unauthenticated client defaults to system:anonymous. This makes it a flake rather than a consistent failure.

In test/e2e/framework/framework.go:BeforeEach() (lines 220-234):

**Current Code:**

Go
config, err := LoadConfig() // Line 221 - local stack variable
config.QPS = f.Options.ClientQPS
config.Burst = f.Options.ClientBurst
// ...
f.clientConfig = rest.CopyConfig(config) // Line 232 - shallow copy stored
f.ClientSet, err = clientset.NewForConfig(config) // Line 233 - BUG: uses local 'config', not 'f.clientConfig'

Construct the ClientSet using the copied, persistent configuration storage (f.clientConfig) rather than the short-lived local stack variable. This ensures the framework maintains a strong reference to the configuration throughout the entire lifecycle of the test.

**Fixed Implementation:**

Go
func (f *Framework) BeforeEach(ctx context.Context) {
    // Load config ONCE and store it
    config, err := LoadConfig()
    ExpectNoError(err)

    config.QPS = f.Options.ClientQPS
    config.Burst = f.Options.ClientBurst

    // Store a DEEP COPY (not shallow)
    f.clientConfig = rest.CopyConfig(config)

    // IMPORTANT: Use the stored copy, not the local variable
    f.ClientSet, err = clientset.NewForConfig(f.clientConfig)

    // Even if someone modifies kubeconfig file later,
    // f.ClientSet still has the original credentials in memory
}
